\newpage

# HOW TO USE THIS PACK

1. **The pack is in two parts.** Part A holds the twenty question papers. Part B holds the answer key, marking scheme, curriculum blueprint, cognitive-level distribution, quality-control summary and examiner notes for each paper. **Photocopy Part A for the candidates only.**
2. **Each paper stands alone.** A paper may be used as an end-of-topic test as soon as its sub-strand has been taught, or several papers may be combined into a terminal mock.
3. **Edit page one of a paper before printing.** The school name, the academic year and the examination title are meant to be changed to suit your school.
4. **Timing.** Each paper is set for 2 hours: about 40 minutes for Section A and 80 minutes for Section B. Candidates who are new to the format should be given the full time.
5. **Figures.** Every figure is drawn in pencil style and prints clearly in black and white. Check the photocopies before the examination; a figure that has printed faintly should be redrawn on the chalkboard.
6. **Marking.** Section B answers are marked against the points listed in the marking scheme. The italic *Marking note* under each part states what is compulsory for the mark, what alternatives are acceptable, and the common errors. Accept any other correct and relevant answer.
7. **Recording.** Use the mark-sheet grids in this pack to record the papers written by each candidate, and the Section A answer sheet for the objective test.
8. **Difficulty.** Every paper is built to approximately 30% easy, 50% moderate and 20% challenging items, weighted by marks. A class average of 50-60% on a paper is normal at the first attempt.

\newpage

# INSTRUCTIONS TO THE INVIGILATOR

1. Seat the candidates so that no candidate can see another's work. Collect all notes, textbooks and mobile telephones before the papers are given out.
2. Give out the question paper and the answer booklet together. Candidates may use a pencil, a ruler and an eraser; calculators are not required for any paper in this pack.
3. Read out the instructions on page one of the paper and announce the starting time and the finishing time on the chalkboard.
4. Remind the candidates that **Section A carries 40 marks and Section B carries 60 marks**, and that all questions in both sections must be answered.
5. Allow no talking, no lending of instruments and no leaving of the room in the first and the last fifteen minutes.
6. Announce the time remaining thirty minutes and ten minutes before the end.
7. At the end, collect the answer sheets first and then the answer booklets, counting them against the number of candidates before anyone leaves.
8. Report any irregularity in writing to the head teacher on the same day.

## 2. The curriculum areas in full

*The wording of every content standard and indicator below is taken from the NaCCA Common Core Programme Science Curriculum (B7/JHS1 - B9/JHS3), 2021 edition. The curriculum areas (topics) are the teaching headings used in the blueprint of each paper to group the items under an indicator.*

### STRAND 1: Diversity of Matter

#### Sub-Strand 1: Materials — Paper 1

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.1.1.1** — Show an understanding of formation of binary chemical compounds and their uses (Acids, Bases and Salts).
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.1.1.1.1* — Identify by name binary chemical compounds and discuss their uses.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.1.1.1.2* — Discuss the formation of binary chemical compounds.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.1.1.1.3* — Describe the characteristics of common acids, bases and salts.
- **Content standard B9/JHS3.1.1.2** — Demonstrate knowledge of atomic bonding in the formation of chemical compounds.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.1.1.2.1* — Recognise that chemical bond results from the attraction between atoms in a compound.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 1.1 Elements, Compounds and Chemical Symbols; 1.2 Binary Compounds in the Home and Community and Their Uses; 1.3 Formation and Formulae of Binary Compounds; 1.4 Acids, Bases and Salts and the pH Scale; 1.5 Chemical Bonding in the Formation of Compounds.

#### Sub-Strand 2: Living Cells — Paper 2

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.1.2.1** — Demonstrate knowledge of specialist cells of dicotyledonous plants and humans, their formation and functions for the existence of the plants and humans.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.1.2.1.1* — Discuss the concepts of specialised cells and how they are formed in dicotyledonous plants and humans.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.1.2.1.2* — Examine the functions of specialised cells in dicotyledonous plants such as epidermal, guard cells, cambium, xylem in relation to the existence of the plants.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.1.2.1.3* — Examine the functions of specialised animal cells such as nerve, blood cells, muscle cells and sperm cells in relation to the existence of humans.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 2.1 Cells, Tissues and the Meaning of Specialised Cells; 2.2 How Specialised Cells Are Formed in Plants and Humans; 2.3 Specialised Cells of Dicotyledonous Plants; 2.4 Specialised Cells of the Human Body; 2.5 Adaptation of Specialised Cells to Their Functions.

### STRAND 2: Cycles

#### Sub-Strand 1: Earth Sciences — Paper 3

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.2.1.1** — Demonstrate an understanding of the Nitrogen cycle as a repeated pattern of change in nature, and how it relates to the environment.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.2.1.1.1* — Explain the process of the nitrogen cycle as a repeated pattern in nature.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.2.1.1.2* — Describe the importance of the nitrogen cycle to the environment.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 3.1 Nitrogen in Nature and the Idea of a Cycle; 3.2 Nitrogen Fixation and Nitrification; 3.3 Assimilation, Ammonification and Denitrification; 3.4 Importance of Nitrogen and of the Nitrogen Cycle to the Environment; 3.5 Interference with the Nitrogen Cycle and How to Prevent It.

#### Sub-Strand 2: Life Cycle of Organisms — Paper 4

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.2.2.1** — Demonstrate an understanding of the life cycle of grasshopper and assess how their activities affect humans.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.2.2.1.1* — Describe the life cycle of the grasshopper as a form of incomplete metamorphosis.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.2.2.1.2* — Examine how the activities of the grasshopper affect humans.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 4.1 The Grasshopper: Body Parts and Habitat; 4.2 The Life Cycle of the Grasshopper: Egg, Nymph and Adult; 4.3 Incomplete and Complete Metamorphosis Compared; 4.4 Activities of the Grasshopper and Their Effects on Humans; 4.5 Controlling Grasshoppers on the Farm.

#### Sub-Strand 3: Crop Production — Paper 5

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.2.3.1** — Show an understanding of differences in maturities of different crops grown in different soils and different seed beds.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.2.3.1.1* — Observe and describe differences in maturation of crops grown in different soils and on different seed beds.
- **Content standard B9/JHS3.2.3.2** — Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of uses of different crops at different maturity stages.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.2.3.2.1* — Observe and record the uses of different crops at different maturity stages.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.2.3.2.2* — Evaluate the importance of knowledge of maturity stages of different crops to human beings.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 5.1 Crop Maturity and the Stages of Growth; 5.2 Soils, Seed Beds and Their Effect on Maturity; 5.3 Observing and Recording the Maturity of Crops; 5.4 Uses of Crops at Different Maturity Stages; 5.5 Importance of Knowing the Maturity Stages of Crops.

#### Sub-Strand 4: Animal Production — Paper 6

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.2.4.1** — Demonstrate understanding of the preparation of feed for domestic and commercial animals.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.2.4.1.1* — List the ingredients and the method of preparation of different feed for different domestic and commercial animals.
- **Content standard B9/JHS3.2.4.2** — Demonstrate skills and knowledge of feeding domestic and commercial animals.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.2.4.2.1* — Describe and select appropriate feed for different domestic and commercial animals.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.2.4.2.2* — Differentiate between different types of feed for different stages of domestic and commercial animals.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.2.4.2.3* — Perform the feeding of domestic and commercial animals.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 6.1 Feed Ingredients and the Preparation of Feed; 6.2 Ruminants, Monogastrics, Poultry and the Feed They Take; 6.3 Selecting and Recording Feed on the Farm; 6.4 Feed for the Different Stages of Growth; 6.5 Feeding Practice on the Farm.

### STRAND 3: Systems

#### Sub-Strand 1: The Human Body System — Paper 7

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.3.1.1** — Demonstrate understanding of the blood circulatory system, health problems associated with the system and its relationship with the respiratory system in humans.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.3.1.1.1* — Explain the concept of the circulatory system, state the function of each part of the system and the health challenges associated with it.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.3.1.1.2* — Explain the concept of respiration and show how the respiratory and circulatory systems complement each other.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 7.1 Blood: Composition and Functions; 7.2 The Heart and the Blood Vessels; 7.3 The Circulation of Blood in the Body; 7.4 Health Challenges of the Circulatory System and Blood Pressure; 7.5 Respiration and the Work of the Two Systems Together.

#### Sub-Strand 2: The Solar System — Paper 8

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.3.2.1** — Demonstrate knowledge of other non-planetary bodies such as comets, asteroids, and their relationship with the solar system.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.3.2.1.1* — Understand the movement of non-planetary bodies in the solar system.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 8.1 The Solar System and Its Members; 8.2 Asteroids and the Asteroid Belt; 8.3 Comets and Their Movement; 8.4 Meteoroids, Meteors and Meteorites; 8.5 Comparing the Non-Planetary Bodies and Studying Them.

#### Sub-Strand 3: Ecosystem — Paper 9

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.3.3.1** — Recognise the interdependence of organisms in an ecosystem and appreciate their interaction to maintain balance in the system.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.3.3.1.1* — Conduct research into the composition of an ecosystem and discuss how the components depend on each other for survival.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 9.1 Ecosystem, Habitat and the Components of an Ecosystem; 9.2 Interdependence: Producers, Consumers and Decomposers; 9.3 Food Chains and Food Webs; 9.4 Interference with the Balance of an Ecosystem; 9.5 Protecting the Balance of an Ecosystem.

#### Sub-Strand 4: Farming Systems — Paper 10

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.3.4.1** — Demonstrate knowledge and skills in the preparation of different types of manure from animal and plant waste.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.3.4.1.1* — List and explain the different plant and animal waste used in preparing different types of manure.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.3.4.1.2* — Demonstrate the preparation of different types of manure.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.3.4.1.3* — Prepare different types of manure.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 10.1 Manure and the Types of Manure; 10.2 Plant Wastes and Animal Wastes Used in Making Manure; 10.3 Choosing Manure for Different Soils and Conditions; 10.4 Preparing Compost: Method and Conditions; 10.5 Practical Work, Application and Safety.

### STRAND 4: Forces and Energy

#### Sub-Strand 1: Energy — Paper 11

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.4.1.1** — Show understanding of the concept of conservation of energy and ways of conserving energy.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.4.1.1.1* — List the ways to conserve energy, for example ironing in bulk, using energy-efficient appliances and switching off appliances when they are not in use.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.4.1.1.2* — Explain the importance of energy conservation in daily life.
- **Content standard B9/JHS3.4.1.2** — Demonstrate understanding in and the capability to do calculations involving energy.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.4.1.2.1* — Explain how to calculate energy consumed over a period of time.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.4.1.2.2* — Describe how images are formed in cameras.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.4.1.2.3* — Describe the formation of shadows.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.4.1.2.4* — Demonstrate the formation of an eclipse.
- **Content standard B9/JHS3.4.1.3** — Evaluate the application of light energy in life.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.4.1.3.1* — Demonstrate that light changes path when it travels from one medium to a different medium.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 11.1 Ways of Conserving Energy; 11.2 The Importance of Energy Conservation; 11.3 Calculating the Energy Consumed; 11.4 The Camera and the Formation of Images; 11.5 Shadows: Umbra and Penumbra; 11.6 Eclipses of the Sun and of the Moon; 11.7 Light Changing Path from One Medium to Another.

#### Sub-Strand 2: Electricity and Electronics — Paper 12

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.4.2.1** — Construct electrical circuits and illustrate how electrical energy is transformed into other forms of energy, and perform electrical calculations.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.4.2.1.1* — Demonstrate transformation of electrical energy to other forms of energy in both series and parallel circuits, and perform simple calculations involving the flow of current in circuits.
- **Content standard B9/JHS3.4.2.2** — Demonstrate an understanding of forward and reverse bias and explain the behaviour of LEDs, diodes, resistors and capacitors in electronic circuits.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.4.2.2.1* — Describe forward bias and reverse bias and explain the relationship among the components, such as LEDs, diodes, resistors and capacitors, in an electronic circuit.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 12.1 Electric Circuits and Circuit Symbols; 12.2 Series and Parallel Circuits; 12.3 Transformation of Electrical Energy; 12.4 Current, Voltage, Resistance and the Relation V = IR; 12.5 Diodes and LEDs: Forward Bias and Reverse Bias; 12.6 Resistors and Capacitors in Electronic Circuits.

#### Sub-Strand 3: Conversion and Conservation of Energy — Paper 13

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.4.3.1** — Show an understanding of conversion and conservation of energy and their application to life.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.4.3.1.1* — Describe how energy can be converted from one form to another and show how conservation of energy occurs.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.4.3.1.2* — Describe how conversion and conservation of energy are applied in life.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 13.1 Forms of Energy; 13.2 Conversion of Energy from One Form to Another; 13.3 The Law of Conservation of Energy; 13.4 Energy Conversion Compared with Energy Conservation; 13.5 Application of Conversion and Conservation in Life; 13.6 Finding Opportunities to Conserve Energy and Reporting on Them.

#### Sub-Strand 4: Force and Motion — Paper 14

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.4.4.1** — Demonstrate understanding of the concept of pressure and explain how pressure acts in everyday life.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.4.4.1.1* — Explain the concept of pressure and show how pressure relates to force; perform activities that work on the principle of pressure in the daily lives of humans.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.4.4.1.2* — Demonstrate the application of Newton's third law of motion in life.
- **Content standard B9/JHS3.4.4.2** — Demonstrate understanding of Newton's laws of motion and ability to apply the laws to solve problems in everyday life.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.4.4.2.1* — Explain Newton's laws of motion and their applications to daily life.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 14.1 Pressure: Meaning, Formula and Unit; 14.2 Pressure in Everyday Life; 14.3 Calculations on Pressure; 14.4 Newton's Third Law: Action and Reaction; 14.5 Newton's First and Second Laws and Inertia; 14.6 Using the Relation f = ma, and Momentum.

#### Sub-Strand 5: Agricultural Tools — Paper 15

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.4.5.1** — Demonstrate knowledge and skills in making simple agricultural tools for on-farm activities.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.4.5.1.1* — Identify materials used in making simple agricultural tools.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.4.5.1.2* — Discuss and write activities involved in making simple agricultural tools.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.4.5.1.3* — Manufacture simple agricultural tools.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 15.1 Simple Agricultural Tools and Their Uses; 15.2 Materials Used in Making Simple Tools; 15.3 Connecting the Parts of a Tool; 15.4 Processes Involved in Making a Tool; 15.5 Constraints and Precautions in Making Tools; 15.6 Making, Testing and Caring for Tools.

### STRAND 5: Humans and the Environment

#### Sub-Strand 1: Waste Management — Paper 16

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.5.1.1** — Demonstrate an understanding of the scientific ways of waste management.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.5.1.1.1* — Investigate the scientific methods used in waste management.
- **Content standard B9/JHS3.5.1.2** — Demonstrate an understanding of the impact of waste on an environment, innovative waste management technologies for sustainable development and waste management practices in Ghana.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.5.1.2.1* — Describe innovative ways of waste management for sustainable development.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 16.1 Types and Sources of Waste; 16.2 Impact of Waste on the Environment; 16.3 Scientific Methods of Waste Management; 16.4 Scientific Principles Behind the Methods; 16.5 Innovative Waste Management for Sustainable Development; 16.6 Waste Audits and Waste Management Practices in Ghana.

#### Sub-Strand 2: Human Health — Paper 17

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.5.2.1** — Demonstrate knowledge of common non-communicable diseases of humans, their causes, symptoms, effects and prevention.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.5.2.1.1* — Explain the symptoms, effects and prevention of some non-communicable diseases and analyse the risk factors associated with them.
- **Content standard B9/JHS3.5.2.2** — Demonstrate understanding of the relationship of health and disease, the concept of common diseases in the environment and how to control them.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.5.2.2.1* — Explain the concepts of health and disease and show their relationship.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.5.2.2.2* — Explain the concept of common diseases in an environment.
- **Content standard B9/JHS3.5.2.2** — Demonstrate knowledge of selected fungal diseases of humans, their causes, symptoms, effects and prevention.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.5.2.2.1* — Explain the nature of fungal diseases with special emphasis on ringworm, candidiasis and fingernail and toenail infection, their causes, symptoms, effects on humans and their prevention.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 17.1 Health and Disease and Their Relationship; 17.2 Non-Communicable Diseases and Their Risk Factors; 17.3 Cancer: Causes, Signs and Prevention; 17.4 Common Diseases in a Community; 17.5 Fungal Diseases of Humans; 17.6 Managing Disease: the Individual, the Community and Government.

#### Sub-Strand 3: Science and Industry — Paper 18

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.5.3.1** — Analyse the scientific concepts, principles and processes applied in industries in and outside their community.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.5.3.1.1* — Investigate the scientific concepts, principles and processes involved in industries in their environment.
- **Content standard B9/JHS3.5.3.2** — Demonstrate an understanding of the concept of industry, the science underpinning the processes of production in industries, and the technologies in indigenous industries and western industries.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.5.3.2.1* — Explain the concept of industry and distinguish between modern and indigenous industries.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.5.3.2.2* — Examine indigenous industries in their communities and show the scientific processes in the stages of production.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 18.1 The Concept of Industry and Types of Industry; 18.2 Industries and Their Products in Ghana; 18.3 Scientific Processes in Modern Industries; 18.4 Indigenous Industries of Ghana; 18.5 The Science in Indigenous Processes and Practices; 18.6 Technology in Indigenous and Modern Industries.

#### Sub-Strand 4: Climate Change and Green Economy — Paper 19

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.5.4.1** — Demonstrate an understanding of the natural and human factors that influence climate change and a green economy.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.5.4.1.1* — Examine various natural and human factors that influence climate change and green economy in their localities.
- **Content standard B9/JHS3.5.4.2** — Evaluate the effectiveness of initiatives that address the issue of climate change and green economy in Ghana and the world at large.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.5.4.2.1* — Assess data on climate change and green economy actions or activities globally, including Ghana and other countries.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 19.1 Climate, Climate Change and the Greenhouse Effect; 19.2 Natural Factors that Influence Climate Change; 19.3 Human Factors that Influence Climate Change; 19.4 Minimising Human Activities that Cause Climate Change; 19.5 The Green Economy; 19.6 Climate Change and Green Economy Initiatives in Ghana and Beyond.

#### Sub-Strand 5: Understanding the Environment — Paper 20

- **Content standard B9/JHS3.5.5.1** — Demonstrate knowledge and skills in the use of plant roots, stems, leaves, flowers and fruits for agricultural and non-agricultural purposes.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.5.5.1.1* — Show and list the uses of different plant parts for agricultural and non-agricultural purposes.
  - *Indicator B9/JHS3.5.5.1.2* — Demonstrate the use of different plant parts for agricultural and non-agricultural purposes.
- Curriculum areas assessed: 20.1 Plant Parts and Their Functions; 20.2 Plant Parts Used for Planting and Propagation; 20.3 Other Agricultural Uses of Plant Parts; 20.4 Non-Agricultural Uses of Plant Parts; 20.5 Making Agricultural Materials from Plant Parts; 20.6 Making Non-Agricultural Materials and Using Plants Sustainably.

They are reproduced above exactly as published; no code has been invented.*

**Strand 1: Diversity of Matter | Sub-Strand 1: Materials | B9/JHS3.1.1.1 and B9/JHS3.1.1.2**

# BEACON EDUCATIONAL CONSULT

## INTEGRATED SCIENCE (SCIENCE)

### BECE-STYLE MOCK EXAMINATION (PAPER 1)

**Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)  
**Time:** 2 hours (Suggested: Section A - 40 min; Section B - 80 min)  
**Total Marks:** 100  
**Academic Year:** 2026/2027 Academic Year

---

### INSTRUCTIONS

1. Write your name and class clearly in the spaces provided on your answer sheet.
2. This paper has TWO sections: Section A and Section B.
3. Answer ALL the questions in both sections.
4. Section A has 40 multiple-choice questions. Each question carries 1 mark. Choose the best answer (A, B, C or D) and record it on the answer sheet provided.
5. Section B has 6 theory questions totalling 60 marks. Write your answers clearly and neatly in your answer booklet. Study the figures carefully before you answer the questions on them.
6. Write all chemical symbols and formulae correctly, using a capital letter for the first letter of a symbol and a small letter for the second.
7. Use a pencil and a ruler where a table or a diagram is required. Do not use correction fluid.
8. Hand in your answer sheet and your answer booklet at the end of the examination.

---

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

*Answer ALL questions. Each question carries 1 mark. Choose the BEST answer and write its letter (A, B, C or D) against the question number on your answer sheet.*

**1.** An element is best described as a substance that

A. cannot be broken down into simpler substances by a chemical change
B. can be separated into its parts by filtering
C. is always a shiny solid at room temperature
D. is formed when two liquids are stirred together

**2.** A chemical compound is formed when

A. a liquid is heated until it boils
B. two solids are poured into the same container
C. a solid is ground into a fine powder
D. two or more elements combine chemically in a fixed proportion

**3.** Which of the following is a compound?

A. Copper
B. Water
C. Oxygen
D. Air

**4.** The chemical symbol for sodium is

A. Nd
B. Na
C. Sd
D. So

**5.** Kofi wrote the symbols of four elements as Fe, Cu, K and Mg. The element represented by K is

A. calcium
B. carbon
C. potassium
D. krypton

**6.** The MAIN difference between a mixture of iron filings and sulphur and the compound iron(II) sulphide is that in the compound the

A. two substances are present in any proportion the pupil chooses
B. iron and the sulphur keep their own properties
C. iron filings can be picked out with a magnet
D. iron and the sulphur are chemically joined and cannot be separated with a magnet

**7.** Table salt, which is found in every Ghanaian kitchen, is the compound

A. potassium chloride
B. calcium carbonate
C. sodium chloride
D. sodium carbonate

**8.** A pupil is given a white solid and asked to show that it is a compound and not a mixture. The BEST evidence would be that the solid

A. has a fixed composition and properties different from those of the elements in it
B. is white in colour
C. dissolves in water to give a clear solution
D. can be ground into a powder

**9.** A binary compound is a compound made up of

A. two molecules of the same element
B. two different elements
C. any number of elements and a mixture
D. two different mixtures

**10.** Which of the following is a binary compound?

A. Calcium trioxocarbonate(IV)
B. Sodium hydrogen carbonate
C. Sugar solution
D. Magnesium oxide

**11.** The common name of the binary compound hydrogen oxide, which is used for drinking, cooking and washing, is

A. bleach
B. water
C. vinegar
D. kerosene

**12.** A trader at Makola market sells a white powder used to make soap harder and to treat water. The compound calcium oxide is commonly called

A. quicklime
B. common salt
C. washing powder
D. baking soda

**13.** Iron(II) sulphide is formed when

A. sulphur is dissolved in water and poured on iron
B. iron filings are stirred into powdered sulphur in a beaker
C. iron and sulphur are heated together until they glow
D. iron is left in water until it rusts

**14.** Hydrogen chloride gas dissolves in water to give a solution that is used in industry for cleaning metals. The solution is

A. sodium hydroxide solution
B. lime water
C. hydrochloric acid
D. salt solution

**15.** Which pair of compounds commonly found in the home are BOTH binary compounds?

A. Vinegar and baking soda
B. Water and table salt
C. Sugar and marble
D. Fertiliser and detergent

**16.** An atom that has lost or gained one or more electrons is called

A. a mixture
B. a compound
C. an ion
D. a molecule

**17.** When a sodium atom loses one electron it becomes

A. a sodium ion with a single positive charge
B. a sodium ion with a single negative charge
C. a sodium molecule
D. a chlorine atom

**18.** A molecule is best described as

A. the smallest part of a mixture
B. two or more atoms chemically combined together
C. a charged particle formed from an atom
D. a particle that carries no mass

**19.** The molecular formula of magnesium oxide is

A. MgO2
B. Mg2O3
C. Mg2O
D. MgO

**20.** The formula of the compound formed between sodium (valency 1) and oxygen (valency 2) is

A. NaO2
B. NaO
C. Na2O
D. Na2O2

**21.** In the formula CaCl2, the figure 2 shows that

A. the chlorine carries two positive charges
B. two calcium atoms are present in the compound
C. the compound has two molecules in all
D. two chlorine atoms are combined with one calcium atom

**22.** Which of the following statements is TRUE about carbon(IV) oxide and iron(II) sulphide?

A. Each is a binary compound, but one is a gas of non-metals and the other a solid containing a metal
B. Both are gases at room temperature
C. Both are made of two metals joined together
D. Neither of them has a fixed formula

**23.** Ama models the compound water with balls and sticks. The model she builds should show

A. two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom
B. a single ball labelled water
C. two hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms standing apart
D. one hydrogen atom joined to two oxygen atoms

**24.** A characteristic property of acids is that they

A. feel soapy and have no effect on litmus
B. are always solids at room temperature
C. taste bitter and turn red litmus paper blue
D. taste sour and turn blue litmus paper red

**25.** Which of the following is a base?

A. Carbon(IV) oxide
B. Sodium hydroxide
C. Hydrochloric acid
D. Sodium chloride

**26.** Bases that dissolve in water are called

A. indicators
B. solvents
C. alkalis
D. salts

**27.** The acid found in the lime and the orange sold at the roadside is

A. citric acid
B. nitric acid
C. ethanoic acid
D. sulphuric acid

**28.** A salt is formed when

A. two acids are mixed together
B. the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal
C. an acid is poured into water
D. a base is heated strongly

**29.** A solution turns red litmus paper blue and feels soapy between the fingers. The solution is

A. alkaline
B. a strong acid
C. acidic
D. neutral

**30.** On the pH scale, a neutral solution such as pure water has a pH of

A. 0
B. 10
C. 14
D. 7

**31.** A solution with a pH of 2 is

A. a strong alkali
B. a weak alkali
C. a strong acid
D. a weak acid

**32.** Universal indicator is preferred to litmus paper when testing a solution because it

A. can be used only once
B. shows how strong or weak the acid or alkali is, not only which one it is
C. measures the volume of the solution
D. changes to a single colour for all solutions

**33.** A farmer finds that his soil is too acidic for his crop. The MOST suitable material to add to the soil is

A. common salt, because it is neutral
B. vinegar, because it is a liquid
C. more acid, because crops need acid
D. lime, because it is a base and will neutralise the acid

**34.** A chemical bond is best described as

A. the space between two atoms in a molecule
B. the heat given out when a compound is formed
C. the force of attraction that holds atoms together in a compound
D. the charge carried by the nucleus of an atom

**35.** An ionic bond is formed when

A. electrons are transferred from a metal atom to a non-metal atom
B. two atoms are pressed closely together
C. protons move from one atom to another
D. electrons are shared equally between two non-metal atoms

**36.** A covalent bond is formed by

A. the complete transfer of electrons
B. the loss of protons by one atom
C. the attraction between two ions
D. the sharing of electrons between atoms

**37.** Which of the following substances contains an ionic bond?

A. Water
B. Carbon(IV) oxide
C. Sodium chloride
D. Copper

**38.** The bonding found in copper wire used for house wiring is

A. metallic bonding
B. no bonding at all
C. ionic bonding
D. covalent bonding

**39.** Sodium chloride has a much higher melting point than water chiefly because

A. its molecules are much heavier than those of water
B. it is a white solid while water is a liquid
C. it dissolves easily in water
D. the strong attraction between its oppositely charged ions needs a lot of heat to overcome

**40.** Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but its solution in water does. This is because in the solution the

A. molecules break down into atoms
B. ions are free to move and carry the charge
C. electrons leave the chlorine and move freely
D. water itself is a very good conductor

## SECTION B: THEORY (60 marks)

*Answer ALL questions. Write your answers in your answer booklet. The marks for each question are shown in brackets.*

### Question 1  [10 marks]

At Osu Presbyterian Basic School, Adwoa's class collected the following materials from the school store and from home: copper wire, iron filings, powdered sulphur, table salt, water and air. The teacher asked the class to sort the materials and to study one of them more closely.

**(a)** Explain the terms **element** and **compound** as used in chemistry.

**(b)** Copy and complete the table below in your answer booklet by writing the correct chemical symbol of each element.

| Element | Chemical symbol |
| --- | --- |
| Iron | |
| Sodium | |
| Copper | |

**(c)** The class put iron filings and powdered sulphur in a dish and stirred them. In another dish, the teacher heated the same two materials together until they glowed and a black solid, iron(II) sulphide, was formed.

State **three** differences between the material in the first dish and the black solid in the second dish.

**(d)** Describe a simple test the class could carry out to show that the material in the **first** dish is a mixture, and state the result they would expect.

---

### Question 2  [12 marks]

Mr Mensah, a Basic 9 teacher, brought to class a packet of table salt, a bottle of water, a lump of quicklime from a building site and a piece of marble from a mason's yard. He told the class that some of these materials are binary compounds.

**(a)** What is a **binary compound**? Give **one** example of a binary compound found in the home.

**(b)** Copy and complete the table below in your answer booklet.

| Common name | Chemical name | One use in the home or community |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Table salt | | |
| Quicklime | | |

**(c)** Describe how **iron(II) sulphide** is formed from its elements, stating what is seen during the reaction.

**(d)** Using the combining powers (valencies) given in brackets, write the **molecular formula** of the binary compound formed between:

(i) sodium (1) and oxygen (2)  **[1 mark]**

(ii) magnesium (2) and chlorine (1)  **[1 mark]**

(iii) aluminium (3) and oxygen (2)  **[1 mark]**

---

### Question 3  [10 marks]

A Basic 9 class at Tamale tested four solutions, P, Q, R and S, with universal indicator and matched the colours against the colour chart. Fig. 1 shows where each solution lay on the pH scale.

![Fig. 1: The pH of four solutions tested by the class.](/home/user/figures/pencil_fig46.png)

*Fig. 1: The pH of four solutions tested by the class.*

**(a)** From Fig. 1, state the pH of solution **P** and the pH of solution **R**.

**(b)** Using Fig. 1, state whether each of the solutions **P**, **Q** and **S** is a strong acid, a weak acid, a weak alkali or a strong alkali.

**(c)** A pupil dipped a piece of **blue litmus paper** into solution Q and a piece of **red litmus paper** into solution S.

(i) State what she observed in each case.  **[2 marks]**

(ii) Give **one** reason why a pupil should never taste a solution in the laboratory in order to find out whether it is an acid.  **[1 mark]**

**(d)** Explain why universal indicator was more useful to this class than litmus paper would have been.

---

### Question 4  [10 marks]

Acids, bases and salts are used every day in Ghanaian homes, on farms and in industry. A farmer at Techiman found that the soil of his maize plot had become too acidic, and a trader complained of a burning feeling in her stomach after a heavy meal.

**(a)** State **three** characteristic properties of bases.

**(b)** Name **one** acid and **one** salt found in a Ghanaian home, and state a use of each.

**(c)** The farmer was advised to spread **lime** on his acidic plot.

(i) Name the kind of chemical reaction that takes place in the soil when the lime is added.  **[1 mark]**

(ii) Write the general word equation for this reaction.  **[1 mark]**

(iii) State how the farmer could check that the treatment has worked.  **[1 mark]**

**(d)** The trader took an antacid tablet and the burning feeling went away. Using your knowledge of acids and bases, explain why the tablet worked.

---

### Question 5  [10 marks]

Fig. 2 shows the electron arrangement of the atoms of two elements, X and Y. Study the figure carefully and answer the questions that follow.

![Fig. 2: The electron arrangement of the atoms of two elements, X and Y.](/home/user/figures/pencil_fig47.png)

*Fig. 2: The electron arrangement of the atoms of two elements, X and Y.*

**(a)** Using Fig. 2, write the **electron configuration** of an atom of X and of an atom of Y.

**(b)** State the number of electrons in the outermost shell of each atom, and explain what each atom will do with its outermost electrons in order to become stable.

**(c)** X and Y combine to form a compound.

(i) Name the type of bond formed between X and Y.  **[1 mark]**

(ii) Write the formula of the compound formed.  **[1 mark]**

(iii) Explain how the bond is formed.  **[1 mark]**

**(d)** State **two** properties you would expect the compound formed by X and Y to have.

---

### Question 6  [8 marks]

Chemical bonds hold the atoms of every compound together, and the kind of bond present decides how a substance behaves. A Basic 9 group was given dry table salt, salt solution and a length of copper wire to study.

**(a)** Copy and complete the table below in your answer booklet.

| Type of bond | How the bond is formed | One substance that has it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ionic | | |

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

**1.** The cell is best described as

A. a group of tissues working together
B. the smallest unit of a living thing that can carry out the processes of life
C. the outer covering of a living thing
D. the smallest particle of any substance

**2.** A specialised cell is a cell that has

A. the same shape as every other cell in the body
B. no cell membrane around it
C. lost its nucleus and cannot divide
D. a particular shape and structure that suit it to one special job

A. organ, tissue, cell, organ system
B. tissue, cell, organ, organ system
C. cell, tissue, organ, organ system

**4.** A group of similar cells that work together to do the same job is called

A. an organ
B. an organism
C. an organ system
D. a tissue

**5.** Which of the following is a specialised cell?

B. A bacterium in the soil
C. A grain of pollen dust
D. A red blood cell

**6.** Specialisation of cells is an advantage to a plant or an animal because

A. it stops the cells from dividing
B. each kind of cell carries out its own job very well, so the whole body works efficiently

**7.** A pupil observed cells from two parts of the same plant and found that they differed in shape. The BEST explanation is that the cells

B. transpiration

A. support the leaf blade

**21.** The xylem vessel is well suited to its work because it is

A. a short living cell packed with cytoplasm

**22.** Besides carrying water, the xylem also helps the plant by

A. giving support to the stem because of its strong, thickened walls

**23.** The cambium of a dicotyledonous stem is important because it

A. controls water loss from the stem

**24.** A farmer cut a ring of bark, including the cambium, right round the trunk of a young orange tree. The tree later died. The BEST explanation is that

**27.** The red colour of the red blood cell is due to

A. cytoplasm

C. the cell wall

**28.** A mature human red blood cell is unusual because it has

**29.** The MAIN function of the white blood cells is to

**30.** Messages are carried from the brain to the muscles of the leg by

A. nerve cells

**32.** The cells that bring about movement of the parts of the body by shortening are the

A. red blood cells
B. sperm cells
C. muscle cells
D. nerve cells

**35.** The biconcave disc shape of the red blood cell is important because it

**36.** Muscle cells contain many mitochondria because they

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

**1.** The percentage of nitrogen in the air is about

A. 21%
B. 50%
C. 78%
D. 0.03%

**2.** Nitrogen gas in the air cannot be used directly by green plants because it is

A. too heavy to rise from the ground
B. unreactive, so plants cannot take it in through their roots in that form
C. present in the air in very small amounts
D. poisonous to the roots of plants

**3.** A natural cycle is best described as

A. a change that takes place only once in nature
B. the movement of the earth round the sun
C. a series of changes that is repeated over and over again in nature
D. a chain of animals feeding on one another

**4.** The nitrogen cycle is described as a repeated pattern in nature because

A. nitrogen passes from the air to the soil, into living things and back to the air again, over and over
B. the amount of nitrogen in the air keeps rising every year
C. it takes place only in the rainy season
D. nitrogen is used up completely each year and replaced by rain

**5.** In which form do green plants take up nitrogen from the soil?

A. As nitrogen gas trapped in the soil air
B. As protein washed from dead leaves
C. As ammonia gas rising from the soil
D. As nitrates dissolved in the soil water

**6.** Nitrogen is needed by living things chiefly for the making of

A. vitamin C
B. fats and oils
C. starch and sugar
D. proteins

**7.** Which of the following shows that nitrogen does not disappear from nature?

A. Nitrogen gas is made fresh in factories every year
B. The air gains new nitrogen from the sun
C. The nitrogen in a dead plant returns to the soil and is used again by other plants
D. Nitrogen is destroyed when a plant dies

**8.** The process by which nitrogen gas from the air is changed into compounds that plants can use is called

A. nitrogen fixation
B. denitrification
C. transpiration
D. ammonification

**9.** Nitrogen-fixing bacteria are found in the

A. water of streams and rivers only
B. stomach of cattle only
C. root nodules of leguminous plants
D. leaves of all green plants

**10.** Which of the following crops grown in Ghana bears root nodules?

A. Rice
B. Cowpea
C. Cassava
D. Maize

**11.** Besides bacteria, nitrogen in the air is also fixed by

A. lightning during a thunderstorm
B. the moon at full moon
C. the heat of the sun at noon
D. the wind blowing over the sea

**12.** During a thunderstorm, lightning causes nitrogen and oxygen in the air to combine to form oxides of nitrogen, which

A. rise and form a layer above the clouds
B. dissolve in rain water and reach the soil as nitrates
C. are breathed in directly by animals
D. turn back into nitrogen gas at once

**13.** The change of ammonium compounds in the soil into nitrates is called

A. nitrogen fixation
B. assimilation
C. denitrification
D. nitrification

**14.** Nitrification is carried out by

A. nitrifying bacteria in the soil
B. earthworms in the soil
C. the roots of grasses
D. the heat of the sun on the soil

**15.** The relationship between a leguminous plant and the bacteria in its root nodules is best described as one in which

A. both the plant and the bacteria gain
B. only the plant gains and the bacteria are killed
C. neither the plant nor the bacteria gains anything
D. only the bacteria gain and the plant is harmed

**16.** A farmer at Ejura plants cowpea on a plot that has carried maize for three seasons. The MAIN scientific reason for his choice is that cowpea

A. has deeper roots that break up rocks
B. is harvested earlier than maize
C. has bacteria in its root nodules that add nitrogen compounds to the soil
D. uses less water than maize

**17.** The taking in of nitrates by plants and their use in making plant protein is called

A. denitrification
B. evaporation
C. nitrification
D. assimilation

**18.** Animals obtain the nitrogen they need for growth by

A. feeding on plants or on other animals and digesting the protein in them
B. drinking water that contains nitrogen gas
C. absorbing nitrates through their skin
D. breathing in nitrogen gas from the air

**19.** The breaking down of the protein in dead plants and animals into ammonium compounds is called

A. nitrogen fixation
B. ammonification
C. nitrification
D. assimilation

**20.** Ammonification in the soil is brought about mainly by

A. nitrates dissolved in water
B. sunlight falling on the soil
C. green plants
D. decomposers such as bacteria and fungi

**21.** Besides dead bodies, nitrogen compounds are returned to the soil by

A. the carbon dioxide breathed out by animals
B. the urine and droppings of animals
C. the water vapour lost from leaves
D. the heat given out by the soil at night

**22.** The process by which nitrates in the soil are changed back into nitrogen gas is called

A. ammonification
B. fixation
C. nitrification
D. denitrification

**23.** Denitrifying bacteria are MOST active in a soil that is

A. well drained and loose
B. dry and sandy
C. waterlogged and poorly aerated
D. covered with growing legumes

**24.** Which process returns nitrogen to the air and so completes the nitrogen cycle?

A. Assimilation
B. Denitrification
C. Nitrification
D. Ammonification

**25.** A farmer who drains a waterlogged field helps his crops chiefly because draining

A. reduces the activity of denitrifying bacteria and keeps more nitrates in the soil
B. turns the soil into clay
C. adds nitrogen gas directly to the soil
D. kills all the bacteria in the soil

**26.** Nitrogen is important to the environment chiefly because it

A. keeps the earth warm at night
B. is needed by all living things for making the proteins used in growth and repair
C. is used by plants for respiration
D. gives plants their green colour directly

**27.** A plant short of nitrogen usually shows

A. very dark green leaves and rapid growth
B. yellowing of the leaves and stunted growth
C. roots growing above the soil
D. thick woody stems and no leaves

**28.** The nitrogen cycle is important to farmers because it

A. raises the temperature of the soil
B. prevents weeds from growing
C. keeps returning nitrogen compounds to the soil for the next crop

A. contains nitrogen gas trapped between its particles

**31.** Decomposers are important in the nitrogen cycle because they

A. make protein for the use of animals

C. break down dead bodies and waste, returning nitrogen compounds to the soil

**32.** A pupil said, 'Without the nitrogen cycle, life on earth would be difficult.' The BEST reason for this statement is that

A. the air would contain no oxygen

A. transpiration
B. denitrification

A. increases the number of nitrifying bacteria

**37.** Which of the following practices would MOST likely reduce the amount of nitrogen returned to a soil?

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

**1.** Animal feed is best described as

A. any material eaten by farm animals that supplies them with nutrients
B. any grass that grows on the farm land
C. the medicine given to sick animals
D. the water given to animals in the morning

**2.** A mixture of feed ingredients prepared to meet the daily needs of an animal is called a

A. supplement
B. roughage
C. vaccine
D. ration

**3.** Which of the following feed ingredients is used mainly as a source of energy?

A. Fish meal
B. Maize grain
C. Common salt
D. Oyster shell

**4.** Groundnut cake, soya bean meal and fish meal are added to poultry feed mainly to supply

A. water
B. protein
C. fibre
D. carbohydrate

**5.** Oyster shell and bone meal are included in a layer ration chiefly to supply

A. protein for growth of muscle
B. energy for movement
C. vitamin C for health
D. calcium for the formation of strong egg shells and bones

**6.** Premix is added to a home-mixed ration in a small quantity because it supplies

A. most of the energy in the ration
B. the bulk that fills the stomach
C. most of the protein in the ration
D. vitamins and trace minerals, which are needed in very small amounts

**7.** When mixing feed by hand on a clean floor, the farmer should

A. pour all the ingredients into one heap and leave them
B. spread the ingredient of the largest quantity first and add the smaller ones on top, then mix thoroughly

**8.** Before mixing premix into a large quantity of feed, the farmer should first

A. add the premix to the drinking water only
B. dissolve the premix in a bucket of water
C. mix the premix with a small quantity of maize meal and then add it to the rest
D. roast the premix over a fire

**9.** Mixed feed should be stored in a cool, dry room on pallets MAINLY to

A. make the feed heavier
B. prevent dampness, which causes mould to grow in the feed
C. help the feed to ferment before use
D. allow rats to reach the feed easily

**10.** Cattle, sheep and goats are grouped together as

A. monogastrics
B. poultry
C. pets
D. ruminants

**11.** An animal with a simple, one-chambered stomach is described as a

A. herbivore of four stomachs
B. monogastric animal
C. ruminant
D. polygastric animal

**12.** Which of the following animals is a monogastric farm animal?

A. Goat
B. Sheep
C. Pig
D. Cow

**13.** The largest compartment of the stomach of a ruminant is the

A. abomasum
B. omasum
C. rumen
D. reticulum

**14.** The compartment of the ruminant stomach in which digestive juices are produced, like the stomach of a human being, is the

A. abomasum
B. omasum
C. reticulum
D. rumen

**15.** Ruminants are able to feed on grass and other fibrous material because

A. they swallow stones that grind the grass
B. their saliva contains an enzyme that digests cellulose
C. they chew the grass into powder with their front teeth
D. micro-organisms in the rumen break down the fibre (cellulose) for them

**16.** Grass, hay, silage and crop residues are examples of

A. roughages
B. concentrates
C. mineral supplements
D. vitamin premixes

**17.** Feed such as maize, wheat bran and groundnut cake, which is rich in nutrients and low in fibre, is described as

A. forage
B. roughage
C. concentrate
D. bulk feed

**18.** A fowl has no teeth. The part of its digestive system that grinds the grain is the

A. gizzard
B. liver
C. cloaca
D. crop

**19.** Which of the following would be the MOST suitable feed for a flock of local fowls kept in a deep litter house?

A. Fresh elephant grass only
B. Dry maize stalks only
C. A balanced poultry mash with clean water
D. Palm oil mixed with sand

**20.** The BEST reason for keeping a daily record of the feed given on a poultry farm is that the record

A. is required before the birds can drink water
B. makes the farm look busy
C. shows how much feed the birds use and helps the farmer work out his costs and profit
D. shows the colour of the feed used

**21.** A farmer notices white and green mould on a bag of feed. He should

A. reject the bag, because mouldy feed contains poisons that can kill the animals
B. dry the feed in the sun and feed it to the young animals
C. mix it with fresh feed and use it quickly
D. give it to the laying birds only

**22.** Which of the following is the BEST guide when selecting feed for a farm animal?

A. The day of the week on which it is bought

C. The colour of the sack the feed comes in

**23.** A pupil wishes to compare the feed taken by a goat and by a pig on a school farm. The BEST method is to

A. guess the amount from the size of each animal
B. weigh the feed given to each animal each day and record it in a table
C. ask the animals' owner only once
D. count the number of times each animal drinks water

**24.** Clean drinking water must be available to farm animals at all times because water

A. replaces the protein in the feed
B. makes the feed cheaper to buy
C. is needed for digestion, for transport of nutrients and for the production of milk and eggs
D. prevents the animals from eating

**25.** A farmer who must change his birds from one brand of feed to another should

A. give the two feeds in equal amounts for one year
B. mix the new feed with the old one and increase it gradually over several days
C. stop feeding the birds for two days before the change
D. change to the new feed suddenly in one day

**26.** Animals are commonly grouped by stage of growth as

A. cheap, costly and very costly animals
B. small, medium and imported animals
C. young, growing and mature animals
D. wild, tame and trained animals

**27.** The first milk produced by a cow after calving, which protects the calf against disease, is called

A. whey
B. butter
C. silage
D. colostrum

**28.** The feed given to day-old chicks up to about four weeks is the

A. finisher mash
B. cattle lick
C. chick starter mash
D. layer mash

**29.** A ration given to birds that have started laying must be rich in

A. fat only
B. sand and grit only
C. calcium and protein
D. fibre only

**30.** Feed for young, growing animals must contain more protein than feed for mature animals because protein is needed for

A. keeping the animal warm at night
B. colouring the skin of the animal
C. replacing the water lost in urine
D. the building of new body tissue as the animal grows

**31.** The small quantity of concentrate given to piglets while they are still suckling is known as

A. creep feed
B. finisher feed
C. dry feed
D. silage

**32.** Which of the following changes should a farmer make as his broilers move from the starter stage to the finisher stage?

A. Feed the birds only maize stalks
B. Give the birds only water for the last two weeks
C. Give the birds the chick mash again
D. Change to a finisher ration, which has more energy and slightly less protein

**33.** A fattening bull and a lactating (milking) cow are given different rations because

A. animals at different stages and levels of production need different amounts of nutrients

D. feed is given according to the colour of the animal

**34.** A farmer feeds his growing kids the same low-protein feed he gives his mature goats. The MOST likely result is that the kids will

A. grow faster than normal

**35.** Feeding troughs and drinkers should be washed regularly MAINLY to

A. make the animals eat more slowly

**36.** In the hot season, farm animals are best fed

A. in the cool hours of the early morning and the evening

**37.** A poultry farmer should provide enough feeder space for all the birds so that

A. every bird, including the weaker ones, gets its share of the feed

**38.** Which of the following is the BEST sign that the feeding programme on a poultry farm is working well?

**39.** A school farm has plenty of fresh grass but the goats are still thin at the end of the dry season. The BEST advice is to

A. stop feeding the goats for a few days

D. add a concentrate supplement and a mineral lick to the dry forage available

**40.** Which of the following practices on a livestock farm shows the BEST use of knowledge of feeding?

A. Grouping the animals by stage of growth and giving each group a suitable ration and clean water

D. Leaving the animals to find all their own feed throughout the year

C. glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy

**36.** Breathing differs from respiration in that breathing

**40.** Which of the following statements BEST explains why the balance of an ecosystem must be protected?

D. Only large animals matter in an ecosystem

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

**1.** Manure is best described as

A. the water used to irrigate a vegetable bed
B. material of plant or animal origin added to the soil to supply nutrients and improve it
C. a chemical made in a factory for killing weeds
D. the seed kept for planting the next season

**2.** Which of the following is an ORGANIC manure?

A. Sulphate of ammonia
B. Well-rotted cow dung
C. Superphosphate
D. Muriate of potash

**3.** The chief difference between manure and an inorganic fertiliser is that manure

A. supplies nutrients far more quickly than fertiliser
B. is always made in a factory
C. contains no plant nutrients at all
D. comes from plant and animal waste and also improves the structure of the soil

**4.** A mixture of animal dung and the bedding material from the animal house is known as

A. farmyard manure
B. green manure
C. liquid fertiliser
D. mulch of stones

**5.** Compost is best described as

A. dried cow dung burnt to ash
B. decayed plant and animal waste that has been rotted down together
C. fresh grass spread on the soil surface
D. a chemical dissolved in water

**6.** A crop such as mucuna grown and then ploughed into the soil while still fresh and green provides

A. bone meal
B. farmyard manure
C. green manure
D. compost

**7.** Which of the following is the MAIN advantage of using manure rather than fertiliser alone?

B. Manure cannot be made on the farm
C. Manure improves the structure of the soil and its ability to hold water as well as supplying nutrients
D. Manure works on the very day it is applied

**8.** Which of the following best explains why manure is described as a way of recycling?

A. It is carried from one village to another
B. Waste materials from plants and animals are returned to the soil to grow new crops
C. It is burnt and the ash thrown away
D. It is bought again every season

**9.** Which of the following is a PLANT waste used in making manure?

B. Bone meal
C. Poultry droppings
D. Cocoa pod husks

**10.** Which of the following is an ANIMAL waste used in making manure?

B. Saw dust
C. Pig dung
D. Cassava peels

**11.** Poultry droppings are valued in manure making chiefly because they are rich in

A. water only
B. nitrogen
C. plastic material
D. sand

**12.** Bone meal added to the soil supplies mainly

A. phosphorus and calcium
B. carbon dioxide
C. nitrogen only
D. potassium only

**13.** Wood ash from the kitchen fire is useful in the garden because it supplies

A. protein
B. humus in large amounts
C. potassium (potash)
D. nitrogen gas

**14.** Which of the following materials must NOT be put into a compost heap?

A. Dry leaves from the school compound
B. Pieces of plastic and broken glass
C. Vegetable peels from the kitchen
D. Weeds pulled from the garden before they seed

**15.** Human excreta (night soil) can be used as manure, but it must first be

A. mixed with drinking water
B. composted or treated thoroughly to destroy disease-causing organisms
C. spread fresh on vegetables ready for harvest
D. left uncovered beside the classroom

**16.** Saw dust and wood shavings rot slowly in a compost heap because they

A. contain no carbon at all
B. are too rich in nitrogen
C. contain much woody material and little nitrogen
D. are always wet when added

**17.** A farmer at Techiman has plenty of cocoa pod husks, cassava peels and poultry droppings. These materials are useful because they

A. contain no nutrients for crops
B. are available free on the farm and can be rotted down into good manure
C. can be fed directly to the growing crop
D. must be burnt before they are of any value

**18.** Manure is especially useful on a sandy soil because it

A. removes all the air from the soil
B. helps the soil to hold water and nutrients
C. makes the soil drain even faster
D. turns the sand into clay

**19.** On a heavy clay soil, well-rotted manure helps by

A. opening up the soil so that air and water can move through it
B. sealing the surface against rain
C. making the soil stickier when wet
D. removing the humus from the soil

**20.** Fresh poultry droppings should be rotted before use because, when fresh, they

A. are so strong that they can scorch and kill young plants
B. turn the soil into stone
C. contain no nitrogen at all
D. are too weak to be of any use

**21.** In an area of heavy rainfall, manure is best worked into the soil rather than left on the surface because, on the surface, it

A. turns into fertiliser
B. is eaten by the crop at once
C. becomes too dry to rot
D. is easily washed away by the rain

**22.** A vegetable gardener wants a manure that acts quickly on his lettuce. He should choose

A. fresh saw dust
B. dry maize stalks
C. well-rotted poultry manure
D. coarse wood shavings

**23.** Manure is best applied to a field

A. on the day the crop is harvested
B. only when the crop begins to flower
C. two to three weeks before planting, so that it mixes with the soil
D. once in five years, in large heaps

**24.** A farmer who uses manure year after year will find that his soil

A. becomes darker, richer in humus and easier to work
B. loses all its nutrients
C. can no longer hold any water
D. becomes hard and stony

**25.** The first step in preparing compost from household and garden waste is to

A. sort the waste and remove materials that will not rot
B. burn the waste to ashes
C. cover the waste with cement
D. pour chemicals over the waste

**26.** A compost heap is built in layers so that

A. animals can feed on each layer
B. rain cannot reach the heap at all
C. the different materials are well mixed and rot evenly
D. the heap looks attractive to visitors

**27.** Which of the following is added in thin layers to a compost heap to introduce the organisms that cause decay?

A. Good topsoil or old compost
B. Clean river sand
C. Dry cement powder
D. Broken bottles

**28.** A compost heap is watered from time to time because the organisms that cause decay

A. use water as their only food
B. are killed by any water
C. turn the water into nutrients
D. need moisture in order to work

**29.** The compost heap is turned over every two or three weeks MAINLY to

A. cool the heap down to the temperature of the air
B. make the heap smaller for storage
C. let air into the heap and mix the materials so that they rot evenly
D. remove the small organisms from the heap

**30.** The inside of a well-made compost heap becomes hot. This heat is produced by

A. the direct rays of the Sun on the heap
B. the water poured on the heap
C. the activity of micro-organisms breaking down the waste
D. a chemical added by the farmer

**31.** The heat of a well-made compost heap is useful because it

A. prevents the materials from rotting
B. destroys many weed seeds and disease-causing organisms
C. attracts insects to the heap
D. dries the heap completely

**32.** Compost is ready for use when it is

A. dry, hard and dusty like cement
B. wet, slimy and foul smelling
C. still green and sharp smelling
D. dark brown, crumbly and smells like fresh earth

**33.** A heap that is packed too tightly and kept very wet begins to smell badly because

A. the materials are too dry to decay
B. too many weed seeds are present
C. the heap is too small to rot
D. air cannot enter, so the waste rots without oxygen

**34.** A compost pit or heap on a school compound should be sited

A. away from classrooms and from any well or stream, in a shady place
B. on the bank of the nearest stream
C. inside the school kitchen
D. in front of the headteacher's office

**35.** Before building the heap, large materials such as maize stalks and pod husks should be

A. tied into bundles and left whole
B. soaked in kerosene
C. dried and burnt to ash
D. cut or chopped into smaller pieces

**36.** Covering a compost heap with palm fronds or grass helps to

A. keep the heap cold at all times
B. stop the materials from rotting
C. prevent air from ever entering
D. keep the heap moist and warm and protect it from heavy rain and the Sun

**37.** A pupil pushes a stick into the heap and pulls it out after a few minutes. A warm, moist stick shows that

A. the heap is working well
B. the heap must be removed at once
C. the heap is too dry
D. the heap has finished rotting

**38.** Which of the following is the BEST safety practice when handling manure?

A. Handle the manure with bare hands and eat soon after
B. Store the manure in the classroom
C. Smell the manure closely to test it
D. Wear gloves or use a tool, and wash the hands with soap afterwards

**39.** A class prepared compost in two pits. Pit 1 was turned every two weeks and kept moist; pit 2 was never turned. After three months, the compost in pit 1 was ready while pit 2 was not. The BEST conclusion is that

A. turning and moistening the heap speed up the rotting of the waste
B. compost is always ready in three months
C. pit 2 contained the wrong materials
D. compost can only be made in pits

**40.** Which of the following shows the BEST use of waste on a school farm?

A. Burning all the waste at the edge of the field
B. Throwing all the waste into the nearby gutter
C. Leaving the waste in heaps around the classrooms
D. Sorting the waste, composting what will rot and using the compost on the garden beds

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

**1.** Conservation of energy, as used in everyday life, means

B. destroying the energy that is not needed

**2.** Which of the following is a way of conserving energy in the home?

B. be stored only in the form of heat
C. be created in a power station when needed
D. neither be created nor destroyed, but only changed from one form to another

**18.** A machine is supplied with 500 J of energy and gives out 350 J of useful energy. The energy that has been wasted is

A. 850 J
B. 500 J
C. 150 J
D. 350 J

**19.** A lamp is supplied with 100 J of electrical energy and produces 10 J of light. According to the law of conservation of energy, the other 90 J

A. has been changed into heat energy
B. has been destroyed inside the lamp
C. was never supplied at all
D. is stored in the wires for later use

**20.** A ball thrown upwards slows down as it rises. During the rise, its kinetic energy is

A. destroyed by the air
B. changed into chemical energy
C. changed into potential energy
D. changed into sound energy only

**21.** A pendulum bob swinging to and fro finally comes to rest. The energy of the bob has been

A. changed into chemical energy in the bob
B. changed mainly into heat and sound by friction and air resistance
C. stored in the string for later use
D. completely destroyed by gravity

**22.** Energy is said to be wasted in a machine when it is

A. changed into kinetic energy
B. stored in the moving parts
C. changed into a form that is not useful for the job being done
D. destroyed inside the machine

**23.** A motor is supplied with 1 200 J of energy. It gives out 700 J of kinetic energy, 60 J of sound energy and the rest as heat. The heat produced is

A. 440 J
B. 640 J
C. 1 960 J
D. 500 J

**24.** The chief difference between energy conversion and energy conservation is that conversion is

A. a change of energy from one form to another, while conservation is the careful use of energy to avoid waste
B. the storing of energy, while conservation is the sale of energy
C. possible only in machines, while conservation is possible only in living things
D. the careful use of energy, while conservation is a change of form

**25.** Switching off the lights in an empty classroom is an example of energy

A. conversion
B. conservation
C. creation
D. destruction

**26.** A pupil winds a torch that lights a lamp. The change from the turning of the handle to the light of the lamp is an example of energy

A. storage only
B. creation
C. conservation
D. conversion

**27.** Which pair of actions shows conservation of energy and conversion of energy, in that order?

A. A fan turning when switched on; ironing all the clothes at once
B. Ironing all the clothes at once; a fan turning when switched on
C. Burning a heap of refuse; leaving a bulb on all night
D. Boiling a full kettle for one cup; a stone falling from a wall

**28.** Both energy conversion and energy conservation are important to a country because together they

A. make the energy that is available do more useful work
B. remove the need for fuels of every kind
C. destroy the energy that cannot be used
D. create new energy for the power stations

**29.** A pupil says, 'Since energy is never destroyed, there is no need to conserve it.' The best reply is that

A. energy can be created whenever it is needed
B. the law of conservation of energy is not true for machines
C. energy is in fact destroyed whenever it is used
D. the energy wasted is changed into forms such as heat that cannot easily be used again

**30.** At the Akosombo hydro-electric station, the energy of the stored water is converted into electrical energy. The energy chain is

A. electrical → mechanical → kinetic → potential
B. chemical → kinetic → potential → electrical
C. kinetic → potential → chemical → electrical
D. potential → kinetic → mechanical → electrical

**31.** A biogas plant on a farm converts

A. light energy into chemical energy
B. electrical energy into chemical energy
C. chemical energy in animal and plant waste into a fuel gas that burns to give heat
D. heat energy in the soil into chemical energy

**32.** In a solar home system, the battery is included mainly to

A. store energy so that the lamps can work at night
B. increase the voltage of the panel
C. cool the solar panel during the day
D. change the current into sunlight

**33.** Which of these is a renewable source of energy used in Ghana?

A. Diesel
B. Petrol
C. Sunlight
D. Liquefied petroleum gas

**34.** Cooking with a well-made clay stove instead of an open fire saves fuel mainly because

A. the firewood contains more energy in a stove
B. the food needs less energy when a stove is used
C. the stove creates extra heat energy
D. more of the heat produced reaches the pot instead of escaping into the air

**35.** A family that dries its clothes in the sun instead of using an electric drier is practising

A. energy destruction by avoiding electricity
B. energy conversion from heat to chemical energy
C. energy conservation by using a free, renewable source
D. energy creation by using the sun

**36.** An energy audit of a school means

A. a careful survey of where and how energy is used and wasted in the school
B. a test of the strength of the school's wiring
C. a list of all the money paid for electricity only
D. a record of the number of pupils in each class

**37.** In carrying out an energy audit, the FIRST step should be to

A. buy new appliances for every room
B. switch off the main supply to the school
C. ask the electricity company to change the meter
D. list all the appliances and note their power ratings and the hours they are used

**38.** A group found that the computer laboratory air conditioners run all night, that two security lamps burn all day and that a tap of hot water drips. The BEST single recommendation is to

A. close the computer laboratory to pupils
B. fit timers and switches, and repair the faults, so that energy is used only when it is needed
C. replace the whole wiring of the school
D. remove the air conditioners from the laboratory

**39.** Which measurement would be the MOST useful evidence in a report on energy conservation in a school?

A. The number of pupils who read the report
B. The number of lamps in the school
C. The cost of the paper used for the report
D. The number of units (kWh) recorded on the meter before and after the changes

**40.** A school replaces 20 filament lamps of 100 W each with LED lamps of 10 W each, used for 5 hours a day. The energy saved each day is

A. 9 kWh
B. 10 kWh
C. 1 kWh
D. 90 kWh

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

*Answer ALL questions. Each question carries 1 mark. Choose the BEST answer and write its letter (A, B, C or D) against the question number on your answer sheet.*

**1.** Pressure is best described as

A. the total force acting on a surface
B. the force acting normally on each unit area of a surface
C. the weight of a body divided by its volume
D. the force needed to lift a body

**2.** The formula for pressure is

A. pressure = force + area
B. pressure = force ÷ area
C. pressure = force × area
D. pressure = area ÷ force

**3.** The SI unit of pressure is the

A. pascal
B. joule
C. newton
D. newton metre

**4.** One pascal is the same as

A. one newton per square metre
B. one joule per square metre
C. one newton square metre
D. one newton per metre

**5.** For a given force, the pressure exerted on a surface increases when the area of contact is

A. turned upside down
B. kept exactly the same
C. made larger
D. made smaller

**6.** Two boxes of the same weight rest on the floor. The box that exerts the greater pressure is the one with the

A. greater height above the floor
B. rougher surface in contact with the floor
C. larger area of contact with the floor
D. smaller area of contact with the floor

**7.** Which of the following is measured in newtons?

A. Area
B. Force
C. Pressure
D. Mass

**8.** A force acting on a very large area produces

A. a small pressure
B. a large pressure
C. a large area
D. no force at all

**9.** A knife is sharpened before use because a sharp edge

A. increases the weight of the knife
B. has a larger area, so it exerts a larger force
C. reduces the force the hand must apply to zero
D. has a very small area, so it exerts a large pressure on the material

**10.** A tractor that works on soft farmland is fitted with wide tyres mainly to

A. increase the pressure on the soil so that it grips
B. spread its weight over a large area and so reduce the pressure on the soil
C. reduce the weight of the tractor
D. make the tractor heavier

**11.** The foundation of a building is made wider than the wall above it in order to

A. increase the pressure on the soil
B. allow water to pass under the wall
C. reduce the weight of the building
D. spread the load over a greater area and reduce the pressure on the soil

**12.** A person drinks through a straw. The drink rises in the straw because

A. the straw pulls the drink upwards with a force
B. the drink becomes lighter inside the straw
C. the air inside the straw pushes the drink up
D. the pressure inside the straw is lowered and the atmosphere pushes the drink up

**13.** Air is pumped into a car tyre until it is hard. The air inside the tyre

A. presses equally on all parts of the inside of the tyre
B. presses only on the valve
C. presses only on the bottom of the tyre
D. loses its pressure as soon as the pump is removed

**14.** At a washing bay, water from a hose cleans better when a narrow nozzle is fitted because the

A. water becomes heavier in the narrow nozzle
B. water leaves through a smaller area and so strikes the car with greater pressure
C. nozzle increases the volume of water used
D. water is cooled by the narrow nozzle

**15.** Walking on soft sand is easier in flat sandals than in shoes with narrow heels because flat sandals

A. make the person lighter on the sand
B. press the sand with a greater force
C. spread the weight over a larger area, lowering the pressure on the sand
D. increase the pressure under the foot

**16.** Which of these is an application of pressure in everyday life?

A. Using a pulley to raise a load
B. Using a syringe to draw up a liquid
C. Using a lever to lift a stone
D. Using a thermometer to measure temperature

**17.** A force of 200 N acts on an area of 4 m². The pressure exerted is

A. 204 Pa
B. 0.02 Pa
C. 50 Pa
D. 800 Pa

**18.** A box exerts a pressure of 300 Pa on a floor through an area of 2 m². The force exerted by the box is

A. 302 N
B. 600 N
C. 150 N
D. 0.0067 N

**19.** A block of weight 480 N rests on a face of area 0.24 m². The pressure on the ground is

A. 20 000 Pa
B. 115.2 Pa
C. 500 Pa
D. 2 000 Pa

**20.** A girl of weight 500 N stands on one foot of area 0.025 m². The pressure she exerts on the ground is

A. 2 000 Pa
B. 12.5 Pa
C. 20 000 Pa
D. 500 Pa

**21.** A pressure of 4 000 Pa is produced by a force of 1 200 N. The area over which the force acts is

A. 4 800 000 m²
B. 0.3 m²
C. 3.3 m²
D. 3 000 m²

**22.** A crate exerts a pressure of 1 500 Pa when it stands on a face of 0.4 m². When the same crate stands on a face of 0.2 m², the pressure becomes

A. 3 000 Pa
B. 1 500 Pa
C. 750 Pa
D. 6 000 Pa

**23.** Newton's third law of motion states that

A. for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction
B. action is always greater than reaction
C. force is equal to mass times acceleration
D. a body continues at rest unless a force acts on it

**24.** The action and the reaction described by Newton's third law

A. act on the same body
B. are always unequal in size
C. act on two different bodies
D. act in the same direction

**25.** A boy pushes a wall with a force of 50 N. The force with which the wall pushes back on the boy is

A. 25 N
B. zero
C. 50 N
D. 100 N

**26.** A swimmer moves forward in water by pushing the water

A. sideways, so that the water lifts her up
B. backwards, so that the water pushes her forwards
C. forwards, so that the water pushes her forwards
D. downwards, so that the water pushes her backwards

**27.** A gun recoils when it is fired. The recoil is explained by the fact that

A. the air pushes the gun backwards
B. the burning powder pushes only the bullet
C. the gun is heavier than the bullet
D. the bullet is pushed forward and the gun is pushed back with an equal force

**28.** When a balloon full of air is released and the air rushes out backwards, the balloon

A. moves backwards with the escaping air
B. stays still because the two forces cancel
C. rises straight up because air is light
D. moves forward because the escaping air pushes the balloon the other way

**29.** A man standing in a small canoe steps forward on to the bank. The canoe moves backwards because

A. the water pushes the canoe backwards
B. the canoe is lighter than the man
C. the force he exerts backwards on the canoe is matched by the force the canoe exerts forwards on him
D. his weight increases as he steps

**30.** A pupil says that action and reaction always cancel each other, so nothing can ever move. The mistake in this statement is that the two forces

A. are never really equal in size
B. act at different times, so one comes first
C. act on different bodies, so they cannot cancel each other
D. are both pushes and never pulls

**31.** Newton's first law of motion states that a body remains at rest, or moves with uniform velocity in a straight line, unless

A. it is placed on a rough surface
B. its weight is removed
C. its mass is increased
D. an external force acts on it

**32.** The tendency of a body to remain in its state of rest or of uniform motion is called

A. inertia
B. pressure
C. momentum
D. acceleration

**33.** Passengers in a bus are thrown forward when the driver brakes suddenly. This is explained by

A. Newton's first law, since the passengers tend to continue moving forward
B. Newton's third law, since the seat pushes them
C. the law of conservation of energy
D. the increase in the weight of the passengers

**34.** Newton's second law of motion leads to the relation

A. F = m + a
B. F = a/m
C. F = m/a
D. F = ma

**35.** Wearing a seat belt in a vehicle is important mainly because the belt

A. removes the inertia of the passenger
B. reduces the speed of the vehicle
C. provides the force needed to stop the passenger moving forward in a sudden stop
D. increases the mass of the passenger

**36.** A force of 20 N acts on a mass of 4 kg. The acceleration produced is

A. 5 m/s²
B. 24 m/s²
C. 80 m/s²
D. 0.2 m/s²

**37.** A body of mass 50 kg is given an acceleration of 2 m/s². The force acting on it is

A. 100 N
B. 0.04 N
C. 52 N
D. 25 N

**38.** The momentum of a moving body is given by

A. force × time
B. mass × acceleration
C. mass × velocity
D. mass ÷ velocity

**39.** A loaded lorry and an empty lorry move at the same speed. The loaded lorry is harder to stop because it has

A. a smaller mass but a greater speed
B. less momentum than the empty lorry
C. greater momentum, so a larger force is needed to stop it in the same time
D. no inertia at all

**40.** A trolley of mass 2 kg is pushed with a force of 6 N on a smooth bench. If the force is doubled and the mass is kept the same, the acceleration

A. stays at 3 m/s²
B. also doubles, from 3 m/s² to 6 m/s²
C. becomes 12 m/s²
D. is halved, from 3 m/s² to 1.5 m/s²

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

**1.** Waste is best described as

A. any material that can be sold at a market
B. any material that is harmful to living things
C. material that is no longer wanted by the person or place that produced it
D. material that has been buried in the ground

**2.** Which of the following is an example of biodegradable waste?

B. A rusted tin
C. An empty water sachet
D. Cassava peels

**3.** Waste that cannot be broken down by micro-organisms is described as

A. organic
B. non-biodegradable
C. liquid
D. compostable

A. Water used in washing clothes
B. Empty tins of milk
C. Yam peels
D. Ash from the kitchen fire

**5.** Used syringes, expired drugs and soiled bandages from a clinic are classified as

A. construction waste
B. clinical (hospital) waste
C. agricultural waste
