**6.** Which of the following is an example of industrial waste?

A. Peels from a kitchen
B. Leaves from a school compound
C. Oil and chemicals discharged from a factory
D. Sweepings from a classroom

A. organic waste
B. plastic waste

D. electronic waste

**8.** Old mobile phones, dead batteries and broken television sets are called

A. building waste
B. agricultural waste
C. food waste
D. electronic waste (e-waste)

**9.** Choked gutters filled with rubbish in a town are MOST likely to cause

A. an increase in the oxygen of the air

A. provides a breeding place for mosquitoes

C. attracts useful bees to the area
D. increases the amount of drinking water

**11.** A heap of rotting refuse close to a house is a health risk chiefly because it

A. uses up the carbon dioxide of the air

**12.** Burning rubbish in the open in a town pollutes the air mainly by releasing

B. nitrogen only

**13.** Liquid that drains from a heap of waste and enters a stream is harmful because it

A. adds oxygen to the water

**14.** Plastic waste left in farm soil for many years will MOST likely

**15.** Animals grazing near a rubbish dump sometimes die after feeding there because they

A. eat too much grass at the dump

**17.** The process by which waste materials are treated and used again to make new articles is called

A. evaporation
B. littering

D. dumping

**18.** Composting is a method of waste management in which

A. plant and food waste are allowed to decay to form manure
B. waste is sorted and stored in bags for sale
C. waste is burnt at a very high temperature

**19.** Burning waste in a closed furnace at a very high temperature is known as

A. composting
B. incineration
C. sorting
D. sedimentation

**20.** A sanitary landfill differs from an ordinary rubbish dump because in a sanitary landfill the waste is

A. poured into a river to be carried away

C. placed in a lined pit, spread in layers and covered with soil

**21.** The FIRST step in managing waste scientifically in a school is to

A. bury all the waste in one deep hole
B. sweep all the waste into the gutter

**22.** Which of the following wastes is MOST suitable for composting?

**23.** The three Rs of waste management are

A. rake, roast and return

A. composting
B. incineration

A. sunlight alone

A. kill the earthworms in the heap

A. methane

**1.** According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), health is

**14.** The BEST general way of preventing many non-communicable diseases is to

**15.** Cancer is a disease in which

B. Skin cancer

A. prevent the breasts from paining

A. Taking painkillers at the first sign of pain

A. a tsetse fly

D. a cockroach

## SECTION A: OBJECTIVE TEST (40 marks)

*Answer ALL questions. Each question carries 1 mark. Choose the BEST answer and write its letter (A, B, C or D) against the question number on your answer sheet.*

**1.** Climate is BEST described as

A. the condition of the atmosphere of a place on one day
B. the average weather conditions of a place over many years
C. the temperature recorded at noon on a given day
D. the amount of rain that falls in a single month

**2.** Which of the following is a difference between weather and climate?

A. Weather changes from day to day, while climate is the average over many years
B. Weather affects plants, while climate affects only animals
C. Weather is found in towns, while climate is found in villages
D. Weather is measured only at night, climate only by day

**3.** Climate change means

A. the movement of clouds across the sky
B. a lasting change in the average weather pattern of a place or of the earth
C. the change from morning sunshine to afternoon rain
D. the change of seasons within one year

**4.** Which of the following is evidence of climate change in Ghana?

A. The occurrence of harmattan in December
B. The sun rising in the east every morning
C. Rainy seasons that begin later and are less reliable than before
D. The change from day to night

**5.** The gradual rise in the average temperature of the earth is known as

A. humidity
B. ozone formation
C. condensation
D. global warming

**6.** Which of these gases is a greenhouse gas?

A. Nitrogen
B. Argon
C. Carbon dioxide
D. Helium

**7.** The greenhouse effect is important to life on earth because without it the earth would be

A. without an atmosphere at all
B. much wetter than it is now
C. much colder than it is now
D. unable to turn on its axis

**8.** Which of the following is a NATURAL factor that influences climate change?

A. Volcanic eruptions that throw ash and gases into the atmosphere
B. The cutting down of forests for timber
C. The burning of petrol in motor vehicles
D. The burning of refuse in a town

**9.** A change in the amount of energy given out by the sun can affect the earth's climate because the sun

A. supplies the water found in the oceans
B. is the main source of the heat that warms the earth
C. controls the rotation of the earth on its axis
D. produces the carbon dioxide of the atmosphere

**10.** Ocean currents influence the climate of coastal lands by

A. changing the length of the day
B. producing the winds that blow in space
C. carrying warm or cold water that heats or cools the air above it
D. adding salt to the air over the land

**11.** Large quantities of ash and gas thrown out by a volcano may cool the earth for some years because the ash

A. increases the speed of the earth's rotation
B. absorbs all the carbon dioxide of the air
C. blocks part of the sunlight from reaching the earth's surface
D. destroys the water vapour in the clouds

**12.** Methane released naturally from swamps and wetlands contributes to climate change because methane is

A. an acid that burns plant leaves
B. a greenhouse gas that traps heat in the atmosphere
C. a gas that destroys rain clouds
D. a gas that cools the atmosphere

**13.** Which of the following is a natural event that can start a wildfire?

A. A lightning strike during a dry storm
B. A hunter smoking out grasscutters
C. A farmer clearing land by fire
D. A cigarette thrown into dry grass

**14.** Which statement about natural factors of climate change is correct?

A. They began only after factories were built
B. They affect only the climate of the oceans
C. They can be completely stopped by governments
D. They have acted on the earth's climate long before human beings appeared

**15.** The burning of fossil fuels such as petrol, diesel and coal adds to climate change chiefly by releasing

A. water into the oceans
B. nitrogen into the soil
C. oxygen into the atmosphere
D. carbon dioxide into the atmosphere

**16.** Deforestation increases the carbon dioxide of the atmosphere because trees

A. store oxygen inside their trunks
B. give out carbon dioxide while they grow
C. take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis when they are alive
D. prevent the wind from blowing the gas away

**17.** Which human activity in Ghana contributes MOST directly to the loss of forest cover?

A. Logging and the clearing of land for farming and settlement
B. Weaving kente cloth
C. Sweeping the school compound
D. Fishing with hook and line

**18.** Galamsey (illegal small-scale mining) affects the environment mainly by

A. destroying forest and farmland and polluting rivers with mud and chemicals
B. increasing the rainfall over the mining area
C. cooling the rivers so that fish grow faster
D. adding humus to the soil of the area

**19.** Bush burning before planting contributes to climate change because it

A. cools the soil for the next crop
B. adds nitrogen gas to the atmosphere
C. releases carbon dioxide and destroys the plants that take it in
D. increases the humus of the soil permanently

**20.** Which of these would release the LEAST greenhouse gas for a journey of ten kilometres?

A. Travelling in a taxi alone
B. Riding on a motorcycle
C. Driving alone in a car
D. Riding a bicycle

**21.** Keeping large herds of cattle adds to climate change because the animals

A. drink the water of the rivers
B. take in all the oxygen of the air
C. trample the soil into dust
D. release methane as they digest their food

**22.** Compared with natural factors, human factors in climate change are important chiefly because they

A. can be controlled or reduced by the actions people take
B. have been acting for a much longer time
C. cannot be measured by any instrument
D. affect only the countries that are cold

**23.** Which of the following would help MOST to reduce the carbon dioxide released in a town?

A. Burning refuse in every compound
B. Using buses and bicycles instead of many private cars
C. Cutting the trees along the streets
D. Leaving lights on throughout the night

**24.** Afforestation helps to fight climate change because the new trees

A. prevent the sun from shining on the earth
B. absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere as they grow
C. release carbon dioxide as they grow
D. stop the wind from blowing over the land

**25.** A school replaces its filament bulbs with LED bulbs. This action helps to fight climate change because the LED bulbs

A. use less electricity for the same amount of light
B. need no electricity at all to work
C. give out more heat than the old bulbs
D. produce oxygen while they are on

**26.** Which farming practice would reduce the release of greenhouse gases?

A. Burning the farm before every planting season
B. Clearing weeds by hoeing and composting them instead of burning them
C. Cutting down the shade trees on the farm
D. Using more diesel pumps for irrigation

**27.** The use of a biogas digester in a school reduces climate change because it

A. produces carbon dioxide from the air
B. prevents waste from decaying at all
C. captures the methane from waste and burns it as fuel instead of letting it escape
D. sends the methane straight into the air

**28.** Which of the following best describes the idea of 'reduce, reuse and recycle' in the fight against climate change?

A. It is a way of increasing the waste produced
B. It is a method of burning waste more completely
C. Using less, using again and remaking materials saves the energy and fuel needed to make new ones
D. It has no connection with energy use

**29.** A community wants to reduce its contribution to climate change at the least cost. The BEST first step would be to

A. buy electric cars for every household
B. import solar panels for every house at once
C. build a wind farm on the outskirts of the town
D. plant and protect trees and stop bush burning in the community

**30.** A green economy is one that

A. improves the well-being of people while reducing damage to the environment
B. stops all industries from working
C. grows only green vegetables for export
D. uses only money printed on green paper

**31.** Which of the following is a renewable source of energy?

A. Diesel
B. Petrol
C. Sunlight
D. Coal

**32.** Which of these is an example of a 'green job'?

A. Mining gold with mercury in a river
B. Driving a lorry that carries firewood
C. Selling charcoal from cut forest trees
D. Installing and maintaining solar panels

**33.** A hotel installs solar water heaters and plants trees on its grounds. These actions show that the hotel is

A. trying to increase its use of fossil fuels
B. practising a green economy by using clean energy and protecting the environment
C. avoiding the payment of electricity bills only
D. reducing the number of its workers

**34.** Which of the following pairs gives a green economy action and its correct benefit?

A. Using solar lamps - less kerosene burnt and less carbon dioxide released
B. Draining a wetland for building - more fish in the river
C. Cutting forest for charcoal - more rainfall in the area
D. Burning tyres for fuel - cleaner air in the town

**35.** A green economy is said to be sustainable mainly because it

A. uses up natural resources as quickly as possible
B. makes the largest profit in the shortest time
C. depends entirely on imported technology
D. meets the needs of people today without spoiling the environment for those to come

**36.** The Green Ghana Day, on which millions of tree seedlings are planted, is an initiative aimed MAINLY at

A. providing firewood for export
B. restoring the forest cover of the country
C. building more roads in the forest zone
D. increasing the number of mining sites

**37.** Ghana's programme to replace old street lights with solar and LED lights is an example of

A. a method of producing more waste
B. an attempt to stop the use of electricity
C. a plan to increase the use of diesel generators
D. a national action to use energy more efficiently and cut emissions

**38.** Which of the following would be the BEST measure of how well a tree-planting initiative has worked?

A. The number of seedlings that are still alive and growing after two years
B. The number of people who attended the launching ceremony
C. The number of seedlings handed out on the day
D. The amount of money spent on the ceremony

**39.** The table below shows the share of electricity from renewable sources in three countries.

| Country | Share from renewable sources |
|---|---|
| Country X | 12% |
| Country Y | 45% |
| Country Z | 28% |

Which conclusion is supported by the data?

A. All three countries use the same amount of renewable energy
B. Country Z produces more electricity than Country Y
C. Country X has the cleanest electricity supply of the three
D. Country Y depends least on fuels that release greenhouse gases for its electricity

**40.** A country reports that it has cut its greenhouse gas emissions, yet its forests continue to disappear. The BEST judgement on the report is that

A. forests have no connection with greenhouse gases
B. the claim needs to be checked against measured data, since losing forest usually raises emissions
C. the country should simply be praised for its effort
D. the report must be correct, because governments do not make mistakes

D. mixed with petrol to make it stronger

**34.** A class making compost from plant parts should

A. use only dry sand and water
B. cut the material into small pieces, keep the heap moist and turn it regularly
C. cover the heap with a sheet of plastic and never open it
D. pour kerosene on the heap to speed up decay

**35.** A scarecrow made from maize stalks and dry palm fronds is set in a field in order to

A. attract insects for pollination
B. provide shade for the crop
C. supply nutrients to the soil
D. frighten birds away from the ripening crop

**36.** Which test would BEST show a class that the rope they have made from plant fibre is fit for use?

A. Measuring the length of the rope only
B. Hanging a known load on the rope and checking that it does not break or stretch too much
C. Smelling the rope after it has dried
D. Looking at the colour of the rope

**37.** A group wants to make a mat for the school library from plant materials. The MOST suitable material is

A. green leaves cut that morning
B. fresh flowers from the garden
C. dried strips of raffia, straw or palm leaf
D. roots dug from the school farm

**38.** Plant material to be used for weaving is first dried in the sun mainly because drying

A. makes the material tough and prevents it from rotting or shrinking after weaving
B. removes all the fibre from the material
C. adds colour to the material
D. makes the material heavier to handle

**39.** A class strips the bark completely round the trunk of a young tree to obtain fibre. The BEST judgement on this action is that it is

A. right, because the tree has many other branches
B. wrong, because the fibre of bark is of no use
C. wrong, because removing a complete ring of bark kills the tree
D. right, because the bark grows back within a week

**40.** Which practice shows the MOST sustainable use of plant parts by a community?

A. Burning the bush to make the plants sprout faster
B. Uprooting plants before they have produced seed
C. Harvesting only mature stems and leaves and planting new seedlings to replace what is taken
D. Cutting whole trees for every basket that is needed

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) In a formula, accept the figures written on the line (Na2O) or as subscripts, but do not award the mark where a symbol is wrongly written, for example NA or nA for Na. (3) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed. (6) Where a candidate names a material sold or used in his or her own community that the scheme does not list, award the mark if the chemistry is correct.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Element** - a substance that cannot be split into two or more simpler substances by an ordinary chemical change; it is made of only one kind of atom (1 mark).
- **Compound** - a substance formed when two or more elements combine chemically in a fixed proportion by mass, and whose properties differ from those of the elements in it (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Award the mark for the idea, not for the exact wording. Do not award a mark where a candidate says a compound is 'two things mixed together'.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Iron - **Fe** (1 mark).
- Sodium - **Na** (1 mark).
- Copper - **Cu** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The second letter must be a small letter. Do not award the mark for FE, NA or CU, nor for the Latin name alone.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- The first dish holds a **mixture**; the black solid is a **compound** (1 mark).
- In the mixture the iron and the sulphur **keep their own properties**; in iron(II) sulphide the properties are **new and different** from those of iron and of sulphur (1 mark).
- The mixture can be made in **any proportion** and the parts **separated by physical means** (a magnet); the compound has a **fixed proportion** by mass and can be broken down only by a chemical change (1 mark).
- Any other correct difference, for example that **heat is given out** when the compound is formed but not when the two are merely stirred (1 mark, maximum 3).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 3 marks. A difference must be written as a comparison; a statement about only one of the two dishes scores nothing.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Test:** pass a magnet, wrapped in a piece of paper or cling film, over the material in the dish (1 mark).
- **Result:** the grey **iron filings are attracted** and are lifted away, leaving the yellow sulphur behind, showing that the two substances are only mixed and not chemically combined (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept adding carbon disulphide or warm water as alternative separation tests only where the expected result is correctly stated. The magnet test is the expected answer.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- A **binary compound is a compound made up of two different elements** chemically combined (1 mark).
- Any correct household example: **water**, **table salt (common salt)**, **quicklime**, **magnesium oxide**, **hydrogen chloride** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Do not award the example mark for marble, baking soda or a fertiliser, because each of these contains more than two elements.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Table salt - chemical name **sodium chloride** (1 mark).
- Table salt - one use: **seasoning food**, **preserving fish or meat**, or **making oral rehydration solution** (1 mark).
- Quicklime - chemical name **calcium oxide** (1 mark).
- Quicklime - one use: **making mortar or whitewash for building**, **treating acidic soil on a farm**, or **treating water** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The use must be a real use of that material. Do not award a mark for 'used in the laboratory' without saying what it is used for.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Iron filings and powdered sulphur are mixed** (in the correct proportion by mass) and placed in a hard-glass test tube or on a tin lid (1 mark).
- The mixture is **heated strongly** until the reaction starts (1 mark).
- **Observation:** the mixture **glows red hot** and continues to glow after the heat is removed, and a **black solid, iron(II) sulphide**, is left (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept the word equation iron + sulphur -> iron(II) sulphide in place of one of the first two points. A candidate who mentions that the reaction gives out heat has the third mark.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Na2O** (1 mark).
- (ii) **MgCl2** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Al2O3** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept the figures written as subscripts. Award no mark where the symbols are wrongly written, even if the figures are correct.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- P: **pH 1** (1 mark).
- R: **pH 7** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept the figure alone; the words 'pH' need not be repeated.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- P (pH 1) - **strong acid** (1 mark).
- Q (pH 5) - **weak acid** (1 mark).
- S (pH 13) - **strong alkali** (strong base) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Do not award the mark for 'acid' alone where the question asks for the strength as well.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) Blue litmus in **Q turns red**, because Q is acidic (1 mark).
- (i) Red litmus in **S turns blue**, because S is alkaline (1 mark).
- (ii) The solution may be a **strong acid or strong alkali that is corrosive or poisonous** and would burn the mouth or make the pupil ill (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) accept any answer that names harm to the body. Do not award the mark for 'it is against the rules' alone.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Universal indicator gives a **different colour at each pH**, which is matched against a chart to read a **pH value** (1 mark).
- It therefore shows **how strong or how weak** the acid or alkali is, while litmus shows only **whether** the solution is acidic or alkaline (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The second mark depends on the comparison with litmus being stated.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- They have a **bitter taste** (1 mark).
- They **feel soapy or slippery** between the fingers (1 mark).
- They **turn red litmus paper blue** (1 mark).
- They **neutralise acids** to form a salt and water (1 mark).
- The soluble ones (alkalis) give solutions with a **pH greater than 7** (1 mark, maximum 3).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 3 marks, one for each correct property.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Acid:** ethanoic acid (in vinegar) used in cooking and for preserving food, **or** citric acid (in lime, lemon or orange) used in drinks; the name and the use together earn 1 mark.
- **Salt:** sodium chloride (table salt) used to season food, to preserve fish or meat, or to make oral rehydration solution; the name and the use together earn 1 mark.
  - *Marking note: A name without a use, or a use without a name, scores nothing for that half of the question.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Neutralisation** (1 mark).
- (ii) **acid + base -> salt + water** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Shake a sample of the soil with water and test it with universal indicator** (or a soil-testing kit) and find that the pH has risen towards 7 (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) accept 'alkali' for 'base'. In (iii) accept improved crop growth only where the pupil also mentions testing the soil.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- The burning feeling is caused by **too much acid (hydrochloric acid) in the stomach** (1 mark).
- The tablet contains a **base (for example magnesium hydroxide or a carbonate), which neutralises the excess acid**, forming a salt and water and so reducing the acidity (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The second mark requires the word neutralise or a clear statement that the base cancels the acid.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- X - **2, 8, 1** (1 mark).
- Y - **2, 8, 7** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 2.8.1 and 2.8.7. Award no mark where the shells are written in the wrong order.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- X has **1 electron** in its outermost shell; Y has **7 electrons** in its outermost shell (1 mark for both).
- **X loses its one outer electron** and is left with a complete outer shell, becoming a **positively charged ion** (1 mark).
- **Y gains one electron** to complete its outer shell of eight, becoming a **negatively charged ion** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept the ions written as X+ and Y-. The idea of a complete or stable outer shell must appear for the second and third marks.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Ionic bond** (electrovalent bond) (1 mark).
- (ii) **XY** (1 mark).
- (iii) One electron is **transferred from X to Y**, giving X+ and Y- ions, and the **opposite charges attract each other strongly**, holding the ions together (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) do not accept X2Y or XY2. In (iii) the words transfer and attraction (or their clear equivalents) are both needed.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- It is a **crystalline solid at room temperature** (1 mark).
- It has a **high melting point and boiling point** (1 mark).
- It **dissolves in water** (1 mark).
- It **conducts electricity when molten or dissolved in water, but not when solid** (1 mark, maximum 2).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 2 marks, one for each correct property.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Ionic:** formed when **electrons are transferred** from a metal atom to a non-metal atom; example **sodium chloride** (magnesium oxide, calcium chloride) (1 mark).
- **Covalent:** formed when **electrons are shared** between non-metal atoms; example **water** (carbon(IV) oxide, hydrogen chloride) (1 mark).
- **Metallic:** formed by the **attraction between the positive metal ions and the free (mobile) electrons** around them; example **copper** (iron, aluminium) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Each row earns its mark only when both the formation and a correct example are given.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Dry cells or a battery, connecting wires, a bulb in a holder (or an ammeter), two carbon electrodes and a beaker or dish** (1 mark for a workable list).
- (ii) **Connect the cell, the bulb and the two electrodes in series, leaving a gap between the electrodes**; place the dry salt in the dish and press the two electrodes into it, and observe the bulb (1 mark).
- (ii) **Clean the electrodes, dissolve the salt in water in the beaker, dip the two electrodes into the solution without letting them touch each other**, and again observe the bulb (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept an ammeter or a torch bulb as the detector. A plan that does not keep everything else the same in the two tests earns at most 1 mark in (ii).*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- In the **dry solid the ions are held firmly in fixed positions** in the crystal and cannot move, so no current flows (1 mark).
- When the salt **dissolves, the ions become free to move** and carry the charge through the solution, completing the circuit and lighting the bulb (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Do not award a mark for 'water conducts electricity'; the moving ions must be mentioned.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 1: Diversity of Matter | **Sub-strand:** 1: Materials | **Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)

**Content Standard:** **B9/JHS3.1.1.1** - Show an understanding of formation of binary chemical compounds and their uses (Acids, Bases and Salts). **B9/JHS3.1.1.2** - Demonstrate knowledge of atomic bonding in the formation of chemical compounds.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 1: Diversity of Matter, Sub-Strand 1: Materials, Basic 9, pages 87 to 89. Two content standards are examined. Under B9/JHS3.1.1.1 the indicators are B9/JHS3.1.1.1.1 (exemplars: identify and name chemical compounds from a collection of materials commonly found at home, school and in the community such as table salt, water, vinegar, fuel, soap, detergents, marble and fertilisers; write the chemical symbols of the elements identified in the chemical compounds), B9/JHS3.1.1.1.2 (exemplars: distinguish among elements, molecules, ions and compounds; write molecular formulae of binary compounds and describe their formation; compare and contrast different binary chemical compounds based on their composition and properties; form models to represent chemical compounds such as water, carbon(IV) oxide, iron(II) sulphide and magnesium oxide) and B9/JHS3.1.1.1.3 (exemplars: identify acids, bases and salts by their characteristics; create a model of a pH scale and use it to determine the strength of common acids and alkali solutions using indicators). Under B9/JHS3.1.1.2 the indicator is B9/JHS3.1.1.2.1 (exemplars: identify types of inter-atomic bonds; describe the formation of inter-atomic bonds; identify examples of substances that exhibit ionic, covalent and metallic bonding).

> Note: This paper opens the Basic 9 series and examines the whole of Sub-Strand 1: Materials, which the syllabus writes as two content standards. The blueprint separates the four indicators: I1 (B9/JHS3.1.1.1.1) carries topics 1.1 and 1.2 and Questions 1 and 2(a) to 2(b); I2 (B9/JHS3.1.1.1.2) carries topic 1.3 and Questions 2(c) and 2(d); I3 (B9/JHS3.1.1.1.3) carries topic 1.4 and Questions 3 and 4; I4 (B9/JHS3.1.1.2.1) carries topic 1.5 and Questions 5 and 6. The school's sheets use the shorter coded forms (B9.1.1.1 and B9.1.1.2); both forms refer to the same standards.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This is the first paper of the Basic 9 series and it covers the whole of Strand 1, Sub-Strand 1: Materials, which the syllabus writes as two content standards - B9/JHS3.1.1.1 (binary compounds, acids, bases and salts) and B9/JHS3.1.1.2 (atomic bonding).
- Candidates should be reminded before the examination that a chemical symbol begins with a capital letter and that any second letter is small. Many marks are lost each year on NA, CU and MG.
- Question 2(d) is the most demanding item in Section B. Candidates who cross the valencies mechanically without checking the result will write NaO or MgCl; insist on the correct formula.
- In Question 3, Fig. 1 carries no words such as 'acid' or 'alkali', so candidates must read the pH numbers and apply what they know about the scale.
- In Question 5, the letters X and Y are not chemical symbols. Candidates who answer in terms of sodium and chlorine have reasoned correctly, but the formula asked for is XY; award the marks where the chemistry is right and the letters are used consistently.
- Question 6(b) is a design task. Reward a workable plan rather than a textbook description; a candidate who tests the dry salt and the solution with the same circuit has met the requirement.
- Teachers should follow up this paper with practical work: making a pH scale model with universal indicator and testing lime juice, soap solution, rainwater and well water from the pupils' own community.

### Section B - Theory (summary answers; full detail in the Marking Scheme)

| Question | Expected Answer | Curriculum Area | Cognitive Level |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (a) | Specialised cell: a cell with a particular shape and structure that suit it to one special job. Tissue: a group of similar cells working together to carry out the same job. | Cells, Tissues and the Meaning of Specialised Cells | Remember |
| 1 (b) | (i) Cell, tissue, organ, organ system (organism). (ii) Tissue: muscle tissue, blood or nervous tissue; organ: heart, lung, stomach, kidney or eye. | Cells, Tissues and the Meaning of Specialised Cells | Understand |
| 1 (c) | Unspecialised cells divide to make new cells; the new cells then differentiate, changing their shape and structure to suit one job, and similar cells group together as tissues. In the plant the dividing regions are the meristems (root and shoot tips and the cambium); in humans the dividing cells are stem cells. | How Specialised Cells Are Formed in Plants and Humans | Understand |
| 1 (d) | Each job is carried out efficiently by cells built for it; the work of the body is shared out, so the organism can grow larger and carry out many different activities at the same time. | Cells, Tissues and the Meaning of Specialised Cells | Understand |
| 2 (a) | A - epidermal cell; B - guard cells (a pair, with a stoma between them); C - xylem vessel. | Specialised Cells of Dicotyledonous Plants | Apply |
| 2 (b) | A protects the inner tissues and reduces water loss; B opens and closes the stoma to control gas exchange and water loss; C carries water and dissolved mineral salts up the plant and supports it. | Specialised Cells of Dicotyledonous Plants | Understand |
| 2 (c) | It is a long hollow tube; its end walls have broken down so there are no cross walls; it is made of dead, empty cells; and its walls are thickened and strengthened with lignin. | Specialised Cells of Dicotyledonous Plants | Analyse |
| 2 (d) | Water enters the guard cells by osmosis; they become turgid and, because the inner wall is thicker than the outer wall, they curve apart and the stoma opens. When the plant is short of water the guard cells lose water, become flaccid and close the stoma, reducing further water loss. | Specialised Cells of Dicotyledonous Plants | Understand |
| 3 (a) | The cambium is a layer of actively dividing (meristematic) cells; it lies between the xylem and the phloem in the vascular bundles of the stem. | Specialised Cells of Dicotyledonous Plants | Remember |
| 3 (b) | Epidermal cell - covers and protects the plant and cuts down water loss; cambium cell - divides to form new xylem and phloem so that the stem grows thicker; xylem vessel - carries water and mineral salts and supports the plant. | Specialised Cells of Dicotyledonous Plants | Understand |
| 3 (c) | Water and mineral salts cannot reach the leaves, so the leaves wilt and may dry up; photosynthesis falls and growth is poor; the plant loses support and may finally die. | Specialised Cells of Dicotyledonous Plants | Apply |
| 3 (d) | The cocoa tree is a dicotyledonous plant and has a cambium which keeps dividing to add new xylem and phloem, so the stem thickens; the maize plant is a monocotyledon and has no cambium in its vascular bundles, so no new xylem and phloem are added. | Specialised Cells of Dicotyledonous Plants | Analyse |
| 4 (a) | P - nerve cell (neurone); Q - red blood cell; R - muscle cell (muscle fibre); S - sperm cell. | Specialised Cells of the Human Body | Apply |
| 4 (b) | P carries messages (nerve impulses) from one part of the body to another; Q carries oxygen from the lungs to the body cells; S fertilises the egg cell of the female. | Specialised Cells of the Human Body | Understand |
| 4 (c) | (i) Q has no nucleus, leaving more room for haemoglobin, and its biconcave disc shape gives a large surface area; it is also small and flexible enough to squeeze through capillaries. (ii) P is very long, so it can carry a message over a long distance, and it has branched ends for passing the message on. | Adaptation of Specialised Cells to Their Functions | Analyse |
| 5 (a) | The red cell has no nucleus while the white cell has one; the red cell contains haemoglobin and is red while the white cell has none and is colourless; the red cell is a biconcave disc of fixed shape while the white cell can change its shape; red cells are far more numerous; their functions differ. | Specialised Cells of the Human Body | Understand |
| 5 (b) | (i) Fewer red cells means less haemoglobin, so less oxygen reaches the body cells; less energy is then released in respiration and she feels weak and tired. (ii) Kontomire, liver, beans, dark green leafy vegetables or fish - the mineral is iron. | Adaptation of Specialised Cells to Their Functions | Apply |
| 5 (c) | Muscle cells shorten (contract) to bring about movement of parts of the body; nerve cells carry messages from one part of the body to another. | Specialised Cells of the Human Body | Remember |
| 5 (d) | Mitochondria are the sites of respiration, where energy is released; a muscle cell needs a great deal of energy in order to contract, so it has many of them. | Adaptation of Specialised Cells to Their Functions | Analyse |
| 6 (a) | A large pencil drawing showing an oval head containing the nucleus, a short mid-piece behind the head and a long whip-like tail, with the four parts correctly labelled. | Adaptation of Specialised Cells to Their Functions | Create |
| 6 (b) | Its long tail allows it to swim to the egg; its mid-piece is packed with mitochondria to release the energy needed for swimming; it is small and streamlined; its head carries enzymes that help it to enter the egg. | Adaptation of Specialised Cells to Their Functions | Analyse |
| 6 (c) | No. The cells differ in shape and structure because each is built for a different job; for example a red blood cell has no nucleus and is a biconcave disc for carrying oxygen, while a nerve cell is long and branched for carrying messages. | Adaptation of Specialised Cells to Their Functions | Evaluate |

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) In a diagram, award the marks for the correct shape and for each correct label with a straight label line that touches the part named. (3) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed, but 'xylem' and 'phloem' must be clearly distinguishable. (6) Where a candidate uses a local example of a plant or a food that the scheme does not list, award the mark if the biology is correct.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Specialised cell** - a cell whose shape and structure have changed so that it can carry out one particular job very well (1 mark).
- **Tissue** - a group of similar cells that work together to carry out the same job (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'a cell adapted to perform a special function'. Do not award the tissue mark for 'a part of the body' alone.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Cell -> tissue -> organ -> organ system (-> organism)** (1 mark; the order must be correct).
- (ii) Tissue: **muscle tissue**, **blood**, **nervous tissue** or **bone** (1 mark).
- (ii) Organ: **heart**, **lung**, **stomach**, **kidney**, **eye** or **brain** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) do not accept 'skin cell' as a tissue or 'blood cell' as an organ.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Unspecialised cells divide** (by cell division) to produce new cells (1 mark).
- The new cells then **differentiate**, that is they change their shape, size and contents so that each can carry out one particular job (1 mark).
- In the plant this happens in the **meristems - the tips of roots and shoots and the cambium**; in the human being the dividing cells are the **stem cells**, and similar specialised cells then group together to form tissues (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The word differentiation, or a clear description of it, is needed for the second mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Each kind of cell carries out its own job **more efficiently**, because its structure suits that job (1 mark).
- The **work of the body is shared out (division of labour)**, so many different activities go on at the same time (1 mark).
- It allows the organism to **grow larger and more complex** and to survive in its surroundings (1 mark, maximum 2).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 2 marks.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- A - **epidermal cell** (1 mark).
- B - **guard cells** (a pair of guard cells with a stoma between them) (1 mark).
- C - **xylem vessel** (xylem) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In B accept 'guard cell'. Do not award the mark for 'stoma' alone, since the stoma is the opening and not the cell.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- A - **protects the tissues beneath and reduces the loss of water** from the leaf (1 mark).
- B - **opens and closes the stoma**, controlling the movement of gases into and out of the leaf and the loss of water vapour (1 mark).
- C - **carries water and dissolved mineral salts from the root to the rest of the plant** (and helps to support the plant) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Only one function is required for each cell; mark the first one given.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- It is a **long, narrow, hollow tube**, so water flows through it easily (1 mark).
- It has **no cross walls**, since the end walls have broken down, so the water column is not interrupted (1 mark).
- It is made of **dead, empty cells with no cytoplasm or nucleus**, leaving the whole space for water (1 mark).
- Its **walls are thickened with lignin**, which strengthens the tube and supports the plant (1 mark, maximum 3).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 3 marks, one for each correct feature.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- **Water passes into the guard cells by osmosis** and they become **turgid** (1 mark).
- Because the **inner wall is thicker and less elastic than the outer wall**, the turgid cells **curve away from each other** and the stoma opens (1 mark).
- On a hot afternoon when water is short, the guard cells **lose water, become flaccid and close the stoma**, so that less water vapour is lost from the leaf (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The second mark depends on the idea of the cells curving apart; a candidate who writes only 'they open' does not earn it.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- The cambium is a **layer of thin-walled cells that keep dividing** (a meristem) (1 mark).
- It lies **between the xylem and the phloem** in the vascular bundle of the stem and the root (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'inside the bark, between the wood and the phloem'.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Epidermal cell - **forms a protective covering over the plant and reduces the loss of water** (1 mark).
- Cambium cell - **divides to produce new xylem and phloem cells, so that the stem grows thicker** (1 mark).
- Xylem vessel - **carries water and dissolved mineral salts upwards and gives support to the plant** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Mark each row on its own. A function given for the wrong cell scores nothing.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Water (and dissolved mineral salts) cannot reach the leaves**, so the leaves **wilt** and later dry up (1 mark).
- **Photosynthesis is reduced**, because water and minerals are short, so the tree makes less food and **grows poorly** (1 mark).
- The tree **loses support and may die** if the blockage is not cleared (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'the pods or fruits are small or do not form' as an alternative third point.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- The cocoa tree, a **dicotyledonous plant, has a cambium** whose cells keep dividing and add **new xylem and phloem** each season, so the stem becomes thicker (1 mark).
- The maize plant, a **monocotyledon, has no cambium** in its vascular bundles, so no new xylem and phloem are formed and the stem does not thicken in the same way (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Both halves of the comparison are needed for full marks; one correct half earns 1 mark.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- P - **nerve cell** (neurone) (1 mark).
- Q - **red blood cell** (erythrocyte) (1 mark).
- R - **muscle cell** (muscle fibre) (1 mark).
- S - **sperm cell** (spermatozoon) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'neurone' for P and 'muscle fibre' for R. Do not accept 'blood' alone for Q.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- P - **carries messages (nerve impulses)** from one part of the body to another, for example from the brain to a muscle (1 mark).
- Q - **carries oxygen** from the lungs to all the cells of the body (1 mark).
- S - **fertilises the egg cell (ovum)** of the female (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'carries carbon dioxide away' as part of the answer for Q.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) It has **no nucleus**, so there is more room for the **haemoglobin** that carries the oxygen (1 mark).
- (i) Its **biconcave disc shape gives a large surface area** for taking in and giving out oxygen; it is also small and flexible enough to pass through narrow capillaries (1 mark).
- (ii) It is **very long**, so one cell can carry a message a long way, and it has **fine branched endings** for passing the message to the next cell (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (i) award one mark for each distinct feature with its reason. A feature without a reason earns the mark only where the reason is obvious.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- The red blood cell has **no nucleus** when mature; the white blood cell **has a nucleus** (1 mark).
- The red blood cell contains **haemoglobin and is red**; the white blood cell has **no haemoglobin and is colourless** (1 mark).
- The red blood cell is a **biconcave disc of fixed shape**; the white blood cell can **change its shape** to engulf germs (1 mark).
- Red blood cells are **far more numerous** than white blood cells, and they carry oxygen while white cells defend the body (1 mark, maximum 3).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 3 marks. Each difference must compare the two cells.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) With **fewer red blood cells there is less haemoglobin**, so **less oxygen is carried** to the cells of her body (1 mark).
- (i) With less oxygen, **less energy is released during respiration** in the cells, so she feels weak and tired (1 mark).
- (ii) A named iron-rich food - **kontomire (cocoyam leaves), liver, beans, dark green leafy vegetables, fish or meat** - together with the mineral **iron** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) the food and the mineral are both needed for the mark. Accept any locally sold iron-rich food.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Muscle cells **contract (shorten) and so bring about movement** of the parts of the body (1 mark).
- Nerve cells **carry messages (impulses)** from the sense organs to the brain and from the brain to the muscles (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'cause movement' for the muscle cell.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- The **mitochondria are the parts of the cell where respiration takes place and energy is released** (1 mark).
- A muscle cell **needs a large supply of energy in order to contract again and again**, so it contains many mitochondria (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The link between respiration, energy and contraction must be clear for the second mark.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Correct outline: an **oval or pear-shaped head, a short mid-piece and a long tail**, drawn large and in clear pencil lines (1 mark).
- **Head** correctly labelled (1 mark; the label line must touch the head).
- **Nucleus** shown inside the head and labelled (1 mark).
- **Mid-piece** and **tail** correctly labelled (1 mark for both).
  - *Marking note: Do not award marks for a small, sketchy or shaded drawing. Labels written without label lines may still earn the marks where the part meant is clear.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- It has a **long tail that lashes from side to side**, so that the cell can swim towards the egg (1 mark).
- Its **mid-piece contains many mitochondria**, which release the energy needed for swimming (1 mark).
- It is **small and streamlined**, and the **tip of its head carries enzymes** that help it to enter the egg (1 mark, maximum 2).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 2 marks.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **No, the pupil is wrong** (1 mark).
- A reason supported by an example: the cells **differ in shape and structure because each is suited to a different job** - for example, a **red blood cell has no nucleus and is a biconcave disc so that it can carry oxygen**, while a **nerve cell is long and branched so that it can carry messages** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The first mark is for taking a clear position; it is lost where the candidate agrees with the statement. The second mark requires a named cell and the job it does.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 1: Diversity of Matter | **Sub-strand:** 2: Living Cells | **Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)

**Content Standard:** **B9/JHS3.1.2.1** - Demonstrate knowledge of specialist cells of dicotyledonous plants and humans, their formation and functions for the existence of the plants and humans.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 1: Diversity of Matter, Sub-Strand 2: Living Cells, Basic 9, pages 90 and 91. One content standard, B9/JHS3.1.2.1, is examined through its three indicators: B9/JHS3.1.2.1.1 (exemplars: brainstorm to bring out the meaning of specialised cells; discuss how specialised cells are formed in dicotyledonous plants and humans), B9/JHS3.1.2.1.2 (exemplars: observe specialised dicotyledonous plant cells such as epidermal cells, guard cells, cambium and xylem from videos and charts and identify them by their names and shapes; search books and the internet for the functions of these cells and how they relate to the existence of the plants) and B9/JHS3.1.2.1.3 (exemplars: observe specialised animal cells such as nerve cells, blood cells, muscle cells and sperm cells from pictures, videos and charts, identify them by their names and make models to represent their shapes; search books, journals and the internet for information on these cells and how they relate to the existence of humans).

> Note: The blueprint separates the three indicators: I1 (B9/JHS3.1.2.1.1) carries topics 2.1 and 2.2 and Question 1; I2 (B9/JHS3.1.2.1.2) carries topic 2.3 and Questions 2 and 3; I3 (B9/JHS3.1.2.1.3) carries topics 2.4 and 2.5 and Questions 4, 5 and 6. Only the cells named in the exemplars - epidermal cells, guard cells, cambium and xylem in the plant, and nerve, blood, muscle and sperm cells in the human being - are examined. The school's sheets use the shorter coded form (B9.1.2.1); both forms refer to the same standard.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This paper covers the whole of Sub-Strand 2: Living Cells for Basic 9. The syllabus names the cells to be studied, and only those cells are examined: epidermal cells, guard cells, cambium and xylem in the dicotyledonous plant, and nerve, blood, muscle and sperm cells in the human being.
- Candidates should be taught to write the function of a cell in terms of what the cell does for the whole organism. 'The xylem is in the stem' is a position, not a function, and earns nothing.
- In Question 2(a) many candidates will write 'stoma' for B. The stoma is the opening between the two guard cells; only the name of the cells earns the mark.
- Question 2(d) is the most demanding item in Section B. The marking scheme requires the thicker inner wall of the guard cell; teachers should demonstrate this with two long balloons stuck together along one side.
- Question 6(a) is a drawing task. Insist throughout the year on large, unshaded pencil drawings with ruled label lines that touch the part named; this is where marks are most often lost in the BECE.
- Question 6(c) asks the candidate to take a position and defend it. Reward a clear 'no' supported by one named cell and its job; do not expect a long essay.
- Follow-up practical work: prepare a leaf-peel slide from a hibiscus or waterleaf plant and let the pupils find the guard cells and stomata for themselves, and compare them with a prepared slide of human blood.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Accept the spellings 'denitrification' and 'de-nitrification'. (3) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed, but 'nitrification' and 'denitrification' must be clearly distinguishable. (6) Where a candidate names a crop or a farming practice of his or her own district that the scheme does not list, award the mark if the science is correct.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) About **78%** (accept 78 to 79 per cent, or 'about four-fifths') (1 mark).
- (ii) Nitrogen gas is **unreactive (inert)**, so the plant cannot take it in through its roots or leaves in that form; it must first be changed into nitrates (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Do not award (ii) for 'there is too little nitrogen in the air'.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) As **nitrates dissolved in the soil water** (accept ammonium compounds) (1 mark).
- (ii) For **making proteins**, which are needed for **growth and the repair of worn-out parts** (1 mark).
- (ii) For making other nitrogen compounds such as **chlorophyll, enzymes and the material of the nucleus** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Do not award a mark for 'to give the plant energy'.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Nitrogen passes **from the air into the soil** as compounds (fixation) and **from the soil into plants and then animals** (1 mark).
- It is **returned to the soil** when plants and animals die or pass out waste, and **returned to the air** by denitrifying bacteria (1 mark).
- The **same series of changes is then repeated**, so the nitrogen is used over and over again and the amount in nature stays roughly the same (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The idea of returning to the starting point and beginning again must be present for the third mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- (i) **Nitrogen** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Apply well-rotted manure or compost**, **apply a nitrogen fertiliser (sulphate of ammonia, urea, NPK)**, or **grow a leguminous crop such as cowpea or groundnut on the plot** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept any one correct remedy in (ii).*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- 1 - **nitrogen fixation** (1 mark).
- 2 - **assimilation** (accept 'absorption of nitrates by plants and their use in making protein') (1 mark).
- 5 - **nitrification** (1 mark).
- 6 - **denitrification** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'fixation' for 1. Do not accept 'nitrification' for 1 or 'nitrogen fixation' for 5.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Ammonification** (accept 'decay' or 'decomposition' with the formation of ammonium compounds) (1 mark).
- (ii) **Decomposers - bacteria and fungi** (1 mark).
- (iii) By the farmer **adding manure, compost or nitrogen fertiliser**, or by **rain washing in the nitrates formed by lightning** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'putrefying bacteria' in (ii).*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Nitrogen gas is fixed** into compounds and reaches the soil as **nitrates** (by nitrogen-fixing bacteria, by lightning, or after nitrification) (1 mark).
- The **grass absorbs the nitrates** through its roots and uses them to make **plant protein** (1 mark).
- The **cow feeds on the grass**, digests the plant protein and uses it to build **animal protein** in its own body (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The three stages must be in the right order. A candidate who leaves out the plant earns at most 1 mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Ammonium compounds would not be changed into nitrates**, so the nitrate in the soil would fall (1 mark).
- The plants would be **short of nitrogen**, so their leaves would **turn yellow, growth would be stunted and yields would fall** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who writes only 'the plants would die' without a reason earns 1 mark.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) **Root nodules** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Nitrogen-fixing bacteria** (accept Rhizobium) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Do not award (ii) for 'bacteria' alone without 'nitrogen-fixing'.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- The bacteria inside the nodules **fix nitrogen from the air into compounds (nitrates) that the plant can use** (1 mark).
- The plant in turn **supplies the bacteria with food and shelter**, so both gain from the relationship (1 mark).
- When the plant dies or its remains are ploughed in, the **nitrogen compounds are left in the soil**, making it more fertile for the next crop (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'symbiosis' or 'mutualism' as the name of the relationship, but the mark is for the explanation.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Mark out two similar plots** on the same soil, side by side (1 mark).
- **Grow a leguminous crop (cowpea or groundnut) on plot 1** and leave plot 2 without a legume; at the end of the season **dig the legume remains into plot 1**, then **plant maize on both plots and treat them in exactly the same way** (1 mark).
- **Expected result:** the maize on the plot that carried the legume grows **taller and greener and gives a better yield**, showing that the legume has enriched the soil with nitrogen (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A plan without a control plot earns at most 1 mark. Accept pots in place of plots where the pupil keeps the conditions the same.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Advice: he should not burn them**; he should **plough or dig the remains into the soil, or use them to make compost** (1 mark).
- **Reason:** burning **destroys the organic matter, drives off the nitrogen and kills the soil organisms**, while digging the remains in **returns nitrogen compounds and humus to the soil** for the next crop (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The advice must be clear; a candidate who merely lists the effects of burning without advising earns 1 mark.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Nitrogen fixation - **nitrogen gas is changed into nitrogen compounds that plants can use** - **nitrogen-fixing bacteria** (in root nodules or free in the soil) **or lightning** (1 mark).
- Nitrification - **ammonium compounds are changed into nitrates** - **nitrifying bacteria** (1 mark).
- Ammonification - **the protein in dead plants, dead animals and animal waste is broken down into ammonium compounds** - **decomposers: bacteria and fungi** (1 mark).
- Denitrification - **nitrates in the soil are changed back into nitrogen gas, which escapes into the air** - **denitrifying bacteria** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Each row earns its mark only when both the change and the agent are correct.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- The **energy of the lightning flash makes nitrogen and oxygen of the air combine**, forming oxides of nitrogen (1 mark).
- These oxides **dissolve in the rain water** (forming weak acids) (1 mark).
- The rain **carries them into the soil, where they form nitrates** that the plants can absorb (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'nitric acid' for the dissolved product.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Denitrification** (1 mark).
- (ii) In the **waterlogged soil there is little air**, so **denitrifying bacteria change the nitrates into nitrogen gas**, which escapes; the crop is therefore short of nitrogen (1 mark).
- (iii) **Drain the field** (dig channels or make ridges and furrows) so that air can enter the soil, and apply the fertiliser after draining (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) the loss of nitrate as nitrogen gas must be stated for the mark.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Grow leguminous crops** (cowpea, groundnut, soya bean) or include them in a crop rotation (1 mark).
- **Apply well-rotted farmyard manure or compost** (1 mark).
- **Plough in crop remains or green manure** (1 mark).
- **Apply a nitrogen fertiliser** such as sulphate of ammonia, urea or NPK (1 mark, maximum 3).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 3 marks.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Different crops **take different nutrients, and in different amounts**, so changing the crop prevents one nutrient from being used up (1 mark).
- The **leguminous crop carries nitrogen-fixing bacteria in its root nodules**, which add nitrogen compounds to the soil (1 mark).
- When the **legume remains are ploughed in**, the nitrogen compounds and humus are left in the soil for the crop that follows (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'it also helps to control pests and diseases' as an extra point only after the three above.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Water plants and algae grow very quickly and cover the surface** of the water (1 mark).
- When they die and decay, the **oxygen dissolved in the water is used up, so fish and other water animals die** and the water becomes unfit for domestic use (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'the river becomes green and smells bad' as the first point.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Organic manure:** it is **cheap and available on the farm**, and it **adds humus**, which improves the structure, the water-holding and the life of the soil (1 mark).
- **Inorganic fertiliser:** it supplies a **known, concentrated amount of nitrogen that acts quickly**, and it is easy to carry and to apply (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: One advantage of each is required; two advantages of only one kind earn 1 mark.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) Burning **destroys the plant cover, the humus and the decomposers and nitrifying bacteria in the topsoil**, and the nitrogen in the burnt material escapes into the air (1 mark).
- (ii) Heavy rain **washes the dissolved nitrates down through the soil, beyond the reach of the roots**, so less nitrogen is available to the crop (1 mark).
- (iii) Clearing the legumes **removes the nitrogen-fixing bacteria of the root nodules**, so less nitrogen from the air is fixed into the soil (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Mark each of the three parts on its own.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Yields will fall season after season**, because the humus and the nitrogen compounds in the topsoil are destroyed by the fire and are not replaced (1 mark).
- The **bare soil will be eroded by rain and wind and its nitrates leached away**, so the topsoil becomes thin and poor (1 mark).
- The **soil organisms (decomposers and nitrifying bacteria) will die out**, so decay and nitrification slow down and the farmer must spend more on fertiliser, or abandon the land (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Each prediction earns its mark only when a reason is given with it.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- A clear, correct message on **not burning the bush**, for example 'Do not burn the bush - fire burns away the food in your soil' (1 mark).
- A clear, correct message on a **good practice**, for example 'Plant cowpea and groundnut - they feed your soil with nitrogen' or 'Cover your land after harvest; bare soil loses its riches to the rain' (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The message must be short, addressed to the community and scientifically correct. Do not award a mark for a message that merely repeats the question.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 2: Cycles | **Sub-strand:** 1: Earth Sciences | **Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)

**Content Standard:** **B9/JHS3.2.1.1** - Demonstrate an understanding of the Nitrogen cycle as a repeated pattern of change in nature, and how it relates to the environment.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 2: Cycles, Sub-Strand 1: Earth Sciences, Basic 9, pages 92 and 93. One content standard, B9/JHS3.2.1.1, is examined through its two indicators: B9/JHS3.2.1.1.1 (exemplars: identify the nitrogen cycle from the internet, charts or pictures; explain the nitrogen cycle depicting processes such as nitrogen fixation, nitrification, assimilation, ammonification and de-nitrification; explain the relationship between the nitrogen cycle and the environment; explain why the nitrogen cycle is a repeated pattern in nature) and B9/JHS3.2.1.1.2 (exemplars: describe the importance of nitrogen to the environment; carry out a project to show how certain plants such as leguminous crops can replenish nitrogen in the soil; predict what will happen if the nitrogen cycle is interrupted by actions such as leaching, bush burning and destruction of leguminous plants).

> Note: The blueprint separates the two indicators: I1 (B9/JHS3.2.1.1.1) carries topics 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 and Questions 1(a) to 1(b), 2 and 4; I2 (B9/JHS3.2.1.1.2) carries topics 3.4 and 3.5 and Questions 1(c) to 1(d), 3, 5 and 6. The five processes named in the exemplars - fixation, nitrification, assimilation, ammonification and denitrification - are all examined, and so are the three named interruptions: leaching, bush burning and the destruction of leguminous plants. The school's sheets use the shorter coded form (B9.2.1.1); both forms refer to the same standard.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This paper covers Sub-Strand 1: Earth Sciences for Basic 9, whose single content standard is the nitrogen cycle. Both indicators are examined: the process of the cycle itself and its importance to the environment.
- Candidates commonly confuse nitrification with nitrogen fixation. Teach the two side by side: fixation starts from nitrogen gas in the air; nitrification starts from ammonium compounds already in the soil.
- In Question 2(a) the arrows must be named with the scientific name of the process. 'Plants take in nitrates' is accepted for arrow 2 only because the syllabus exemplar uses the word assimilation in that sense.
- Question 3(c) is a project task taken directly from the syllabus exemplar. The control plot is the heart of the answer; candidates who grow cowpea on one plot and compare nothing with it cannot score full marks.
- Question 4(c) rewards candidates who connect waterlogging with the absence of air and the activity of denitrifying bacteria. Many will write 'the fertiliser was washed away', which is leaching, not denitrification; award no mark for that in (i).
- Question 6(c) asks for poster messages. Reward brevity and accuracy, as in a real community campaign; a long paragraph is not a poster message.
- Follow-up work: let the pupils uproot a cowpea or groundnut plant from the school farm, wash the roots and look at the nodules with a hand lens, then set up the two-plot project described in Question 3(c) and record the maize heights weekly.

| 3 (c) | (i) Jar 1 - complete metamorphosis; Jar 2 - incomplete metamorphosis. (ii) The young was worm-like and unlike the adult, and it passed through a still, resting stage inside a case, which is the pupa. | Incomplete and Complete Metamorphosis Compared | Apply |

| 4 (b) | They eat the leaves and young shoots of crops, so yields fall; a swarm can destroy a whole field in a short time, causing hunger and loss of income; they damage pasture needed by livestock; farmers must spend money on control measures. | Activities of the Grasshopper and Their Effects on Humans | Understand |
| 4 (c) | They are collected, fried and eaten as a food rich in protein and are sold for income; they are food for birds, lizards and other animals in the food chain; they help to break down plant material and return nutrients to the soil. | Activities of the Grasshopper and Their Effects on Humans | Understand |

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) In a diagram, award the marks for the correct stages and for each correct label with a label line that touches the part named. (3) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed, but 'nymph' and 'larva' must be clearly distinguishable. (6) Where a candidate describes a control measure used in his or her own district that the scheme does not list, award the mark if the science is correct.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- P - **head** (1 mark).
- Q - **thorax** (1 mark).
- R - **abdomen** (1 mark).
- S - **wing** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'fore wing' for S.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- T (the **hind leg**) is used for **jumping** (and for pushing the insect into the air before flight) (1 mark).
- The **antennae** are used for **feeling and smelling** - for finding food and sensing danger (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'for walking as well as jumping' for the hind leg.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The body is divided into **three parts - head, thorax and abdomen** (1 mark).
- It has **three pairs of legs (six legs) joined to the thorax** (1 mark).
- It has **one pair of antennae on the head** and **wings on the thorax** (1 mark, maximum 2).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 2 marks.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Biting and chewing** mouth parts (1 mark).
- With them the insect **bites off and chews the leaves and young shoots**, leaving ragged holes, so that the plants cannot make enough food and the yield falls (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Do not accept 'piercing and sucking'.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- J - **eggs** (an egg pod in the soil) (1 mark).
- K - **young nymph** (a nymph without wings) (1 mark).
- L - **older nymph**, with wing buds (1 mark).
- M - **adult** (the fully winged insect) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'nymph' for both K and L only where the candidate shows the difference, for example 'young nymph' and 'late nymph with wing buds'. Do not accept 'larva' or 'pupa'.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- (i) **In a pod in moist soil**, below the surface (1 mark).
- (ii) The soil and the pod **protect the eggs from drying up and from enemies** (and keep them moist until they hatch) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'so that the young have food and cover when they hatch'.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Moulting** (casting off the outer covering) (1 mark).
- (ii) The **hard outer covering (cuticle) cannot stretch as the insect grows**, so it must be cast off and a larger one formed (1 mark).
- (iii) **L is larger than K and has wing buds**, while K has no wings at all (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'ecdysis' in (i).*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Incomplete metamorphosis** (1 mark).
- (ii) Because there is **no pupal stage**: the young stage (nymph) **looks like the adult** and only grows larger and develops wings at each moult (1 mark).
- (iii) The **housefly**, the **mosquito** or the **butterfly** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) either the absence of the pupa or the resemblance of the nymph to the adult earns the mark; both together are not required.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Number of stages - **three** / **four** (1 mark for both).
- Name of the young stage - **nymph** / **larva** (1 mark for both).
- Resting (pupal) stage - **no** / **yes** (1 mark for both).
- Example - **grasshopper** (or cockroach) / **housefly** (or mosquito or butterfly) (1 mark for both).
  - *Marking note: Each row earns its mark only when both columns are correct.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- The **nymph looks like the adult**, while the **larva is quite unlike the adult** in shape (1 mark).
- The nymph usually **feeds on the same food and lives in the same place as the adult**; the larva often feeds on different food and lives elsewhere (1 mark).
- The nymph **changes gradually into the adult by moulting**, while the larva must first change into a **pupa** (1 mark).
- The nymph **develops wing buds that grow into wings**, while the larva has no wing buds at all (1 mark, maximum 3).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 3 marks; each point must compare the two.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) Jar 1 - **complete metamorphosis** (1 mark).
- (i) Jar 2 - **incomplete metamorphosis** (1 mark).
- (ii) In Jar 1 the young was **worm-like and quite unlike the adult**, and it passed through a **still, resting stage inside a case (a pupa)** before the adult came out (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) either the pupal stage or the difference between the young and the adult earns the mark.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- It **feeds on grasses, weeds and the leaves of crops** (1 mark).
- It **jumps and flies from plant to plant** in the field (1 mark).
- The female **lays her eggs in a pod in the soil** (1 mark).
- The nymph **moults several times as it grows**, and in large numbers the insects **move together in swarms** (1 mark, maximum 3).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 3 marks.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- They **eat the leaves, shoots and even the grain of crops**, so the yield falls (1 mark).
- A **swarm can clear a whole field in a short time**, causing food shortage and loss of income for the family (1 mark).
- They **destroy the grass on which cattle, sheep and goats feed**, and farmers must **spend money on insecticides and labour** to control them (1 mark, maximum 3).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 3 marks.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- They are **eaten as food rich in protein** in some communities, and are sold for income (1 mark).
- They serve as **food for birds, lizards, frogs and other animals** in the food chain (1 mark).
- Their droppings and dead bodies **return nutrients to the soil**, and they help to keep weeds down (1 mark, maximum 2).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 2 marks.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **No** - a clear position is taken (1 mark).
- **Reason:** grasshoppers are **part of the food chain** - birds, lizards and even people feed on them - so destroying them completely would **upset the balance of nature**; the aim should be to **keep their numbers low** at the time the crops are young (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who answers 'yes' can still earn the second mark only with a well-argued reason; the expected answer is 'no'.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Cultural control** - for example **ploughing the land to expose and destroy the egg pods**, clean weeding or early planting (1 mark).
- **Biological control** - for example **protecting the birds, lizards and frogs** that feed on grasshoppers (1 mark).
- **Chemical control** - for example **spraying carefully with an approved insecticide**; or **manual control** - hand-picking the insects (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The method and its example must agree; a correct example with the wrong method name earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Ploughing **turns up the egg pods buried in the soil** (1 mark).
- The exposed eggs are **dried by the sun or eaten by birds and ants**, so **fewer nymphs hatch** (1 mark).
- Clean weeding **removes the grasses and weeds on which the nymphs and adults feed, hide and lay their eggs**, so fewer insects survive near the crop (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who writes only 'it kills them' without linking to the eggs or the feeding plants earns at most 1 mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- They **kill useful insects as well**, such as bees and the birds' and insects' natural enemies of the pest (1 mark).
- They **pollute the soil, water and crop and may harm the farmer or the person who eats the food**; they are also **costly**, and the pests may become **resistant** to them in time (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 2 marks.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- One clear, correct piece of advice, for example **'Plough your land early; the sun will destroy the eggs hidden in the soil'** (1 mark).
- A second clear, correct piece of advice, for example **'Keep the farm free of tall weeds'** or **'Protect the birds and lizards; they eat the pests for you'** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The advice must be short, addressed to farmers and scientifically correct.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Three stages drawn, in pencil and large enough to be seen: **egg (or egg pod), nymph and adult** (1 mark).
- **Egg** and **nymph** correctly labelled (1 mark).
- **Adult** correctly labelled (1 mark).
- **Arrows showing the correct order**, egg -> nymph -> adult and back to egg (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who inserts a pupa loses the mark for the stages. Accept a straight line of stages with an arrow returning to the egg.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **Plot B** (1 mark).
- (i) Rise = **31 - 14 = 17 grasshoppers** (1 mark; the working or the figure 17 is enough).
- (ii) Plot B **kept its weeds, which provided food, shelter and places to lay eggs**, while plot A was weeded clean and offered none of these (1 mark).
- (iii) **Keeping a farm free of weeds reduces the number of grasshoppers on it** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (i) award the second mark for 17 even where the candidate does not show the subtraction.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 2: Cycles | **Sub-strand:** 2: Life Cycle of Organisms | **Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)

**Content Standard:** **B9/JHS3.2.2.1** - Demonstrate an understanding of the life cycle of grasshopper and assess how their activities affect humans.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 2: Cycles, Sub-Strand 2: Life Cycle of Organisms, Basic 9, pages 94 and 95. One content standard, B9/JHS3.2.2.1, is examined through its two indicators: B9/JHS3.2.2.1.1 (exemplars: draw the stages of the life cycle of a grasshopper from egg through nymph to adult; identify the behaviour of each stage of the life cycle; explain why the life cycle of the grasshopper is described as incomplete metamorphosis as compared with complete metamorphosis in the housefly and the mosquito studied in B7/JHS1.2.2.1.1 and B8/JHS2.2.2.1.1) and B9/JHS3.2.2.1.2 (exemplars: outline the activities of the grasshopper in everyday life, for example feeding on grasses and weeds; search for information on activities of the grasshopper that are harmful or beneficial to humans; generate activities to promote or reduce the effect of the activities of grasshoppers on humans).

> Note: The blueprint separates the two indicators: I1 (B9/JHS3.2.2.1.1) carries topics 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3 and Questions 1(a) to 1(c), 2, 3 and 6(a); I2 (B9/JHS3.2.2.1.2) carries topics 4.4 and 4.5 and Questions 1(d), 4, 5 and 6(b). The comparison with the housefly and the mosquito is examined because the syllabus exemplar directs the teacher back to those two insects, which the pupils met in Basic 7 and Basic 8; no new insect is introduced. The school's sheets use the shorter coded form (B9.2.2.1); both forms refer to the same standard.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This paper covers Sub-Strand 2: Life Cycle of Organisms for Basic 9, whose single content standard is the life cycle of the grasshopper and the effect of its activities on humans.
- The captions of both figures say 'an insect' and not 'a grasshopper', because Question 2(d) asks the candidate to work out the kind of metamorphosis shown. Invigilators should not name the insect for the candidates.
- Nymph and larva are the two words most often confused. Insist on the test: a nymph looks like its parent, a larva does not.
- In Question 2(a) candidates must distinguish K from L. 'Nymph' written twice without any difference earns only one of the two marks.
- Question 6(a) is the drawing exemplar of the syllabus. A candidate who draws four stages, inserting a pupa, has misunderstood the whole sub-strand and loses the first mark, even if the drawing is neat.
- Question 6(b) is a data-handling task. Candidates should be taught to quote figures from a table when explaining a trend; 'plot B had more' without the figures earns only the first mark.
- Follow-up work: let the pupils dig in a grassy corner of the school farm at the beginning of the rains to look for egg pods, and keep a few nymphs in a ventilated jar with fresh grass to watch them moult.
