## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Readings taken from the graph are accepted within one small square of the value in the scheme, and the unit cm must be given. (3) Award marks for correct points, not for repeating the question. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed. (6) Where a candidate names a crop, a dish or a seed bed used in his or her own district that the scheme does not list, award the mark if the farming is correct.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) The **stage at which the crop, or the part of it that is wanted, is fully developed and ready to be harvested** (1 mark).
- (ii) The **husks and silk are dry and brown**, the leaves have turned yellow, and the **grains are hard** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'the grain is hard and dry' alone in (ii).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Germination -> seedling -> vegetative growth -> flowering -> maturity** (2 marks for the whole order correct; 1 mark where only one pair is out of place).
- (ii) The plant **produces leaves, stems and roots and grows larger**, making and storing food, but it does not yet flower (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: No mark in (i) where two or more pairs are out of order.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Early maturing - **okro, cowpea, garden egg, lettuce or other leafy vegetable** (1 mark).
- Medium maturing - **maize, rice, groundnut or tomato** (1 mark).
- Late maturing - **cassava, yam, plantain, oil palm or cocoa** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept any locally grown crop placed in the right group; the grouping, not the particular crop, earns the mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- She should **count back the ten weeks from the date she needs the maize** and sow at that time - about the **first or second week of October** (1 mark).
- She should also make sure the crop will have **enough water (rain or irrigation) during those ten weeks**, and may sow in batches so that some maize is ready even if the weather changes (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'early October' or 'about the beginning of October' for the first mark.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- A - **flat bed** (1 mark).
- B - **ridges** (1 mark).
- C - **mounds** (heaps) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'level bed' for A and 'heaps' for C.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- A (flat bed) - **easy and quick to prepare** and suitable for small seeds sown close together on well-drained land (1 mark).
- B (ridges) - **give a deeper layer of loose soil and allow excess water to drain away**, and make weeding and earthing up easier (1 mark).
- C (mounds) - **give the deepest loose soil for large tubers such as yam** and drain very well on heavy or wet land (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: One advantage only for each bed; mark the first given.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **C, the mounds** (accept B, the ridges, where the reason is correct) (1 mark).
- (i) **Reason:** the crop is **raised above the wet soil, so excess water drains away and air can reach the roots** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Yam** (accept cassava or sweet potato) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The reason must mention drainage or air for the roots.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- A bed of **deep, loose, well-drained soil lets the roots spread quickly** and take in water, air and nutrients, so the crop grows fast and **matures earlier** (1 mark).
- A **hard, compacted or waterlogged bed keeps air from the roots**, growth is slowed and the crop **matures late** or gives a poor yield (1 mark).
- A well-prepared bed gives **even germination and even moisture**, so the plants grow at the same rate and the whole crop is ready at about the same time (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Award the third mark for any other correct point, such as the effect of the manure worked into the bed.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **About 41 cm** (accept 40 to 42 cm) (1 mark).
- (ii) **Soil Q** (1 mark).
- (iii) **60 cm - 27 cm = 33 cm** (accept 32 to 34 cm) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The unit cm is required in (i) and (iii).*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Soil Q probably contains **more plant nutrients and humus** than soil R (1 mark).
- Soil Q **holds enough water while still letting air reach the roots**, while soil R may be sandy and lose water and nutrients quickly, or be hard and airless (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'soil Q was loam and soil R was sandy' with a reason.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Soil Q** (1 mark).
- (i) **Reason:** its plants are **growing fastest and are already much taller**, so they will reach flowering and grain filling before the others (1 mark).
- (ii) The **date of flowering** (or the date of harvest, the number of cobs per plant, or the weight of grain harvested) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'number of leaves' in (ii) only with the date recorded.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- The **same variety of maize, sown on the same day, at the same spacing and depth** (1 mark).
- The **same amount of water, the same weeding and the same exposure to sunlight** on all three plots (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Any two distinct factors earn the marks; 'everything' without examples earns nothing.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Mark out two plots of the same size on the same soil, side by side**, preparing ridges on one and a flat bed on the other (1 mark).
- **Sow the same variety of okro on the same day, at the same spacing and the same depth** on both plots (1 mark).
- **Water, weed and treat both plots in exactly the same way** throughout the study (1 mark).
- **Record the date of sowing and the date on which the plants on each plot flower** (and measure several plants, taking the average) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A plan with only one plot cannot earn more than 2 marks, since there is nothing to compare.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) The **height of the plants** each week (1 mark).
- (i) The **number of leaves, the date of flowering, the rainfall or watering, or any pest damage** (1 mark).
- (ii) Plants **vary from one to another**, so the **average of ten gives a more reliable result** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'to avoid being misled by one unusual plant' in (ii).*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **42 - 35 = 7 days** (1 mark).
- (ii) The **ridges gave deeper, looser and better-drained soil**, so the roots spread quickly, the plants took in more water, air and nutrients and grew faster (1 mark).
- (iii) **Farmers should sow okro on ridges**, especially on heavy or wet land, if they want an earlier crop (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (iii) accept any sensible advice that follows from the result.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Green maize cob - **roasted or boiled and eaten on the cob** (1 mark).
- Dry maize grain - **milled into flour for kenkey, banku, tuo zaafi or porridge**, used as poultry feed or kept as seed (1 mark).
- Green plantain - **boiled for ampesi, pounded for fufu or sliced for plantain chips** (1 mark).
- Ripe plantain - **fried for kelewele or for 'red red', or eaten raw** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Any one correct use for each row earns the mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) Green pods - **cooked and eaten as a fresh vegetable** (1 mark).
- (i) Dry seeds - **stored and cooked as beans (waakye, red red, koose)**, or kept as seed for the next season (1 mark).
- (ii) **Protein** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Do not accept 'vitamins' in (ii).*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) The **two stages are used for different dishes** and customers ask for each, so the **stage of maturity decides the use** to which the crop is put (1 mark).
- (ii) The **mature tuber has stored much more starch**, so it gives a **larger and better quality yield of gari** (1 mark).
- (iii) The grains are **still soft and watery, so they shrivel and break during milling** and both the quantity and the quality of the rice are poor (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'he gets less money for the crop' in (iii) with a reason.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- It helps him to **choose crops that will mature within his growing season** and suit his soil (1 mark).
- It helps him to **decide when to sow and when to harvest**, so that the crop is ready for the market, the festival or the family's needs (1 mark).
- It helps him to **harvest each crop at the stage that suits the use intended**, and to **plan labour, storage and the use of the land (intercropping and rotation)** so that food is available at different times (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 3 marks.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **No, the advice should not be followed** (1 mark).
- **Reason 1:** the crop would **still be in the field when the rains stopped**, so it would suffer drought at the very time the grain is filling, and the yield would be poor or fail altogether (1 mark).
- **Reason 2:** he would **lose the seed, money and labour** put into the crop; an **early maturing variety that ripens within four months** would be the right choice (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The first mark is for taking a clear position. A candidate who agrees with the advice cannot earn the reason marks.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- A **short duration crop with its time**, for example **cowpea or okro, ready about 2 to 3 months after sowing** (1 mark).
- A **longer duration crop with its time**, for example **maize ready in about 3 to 4 months**, or **cassava, which can be harvested from about 12 months and left in the ground until needed** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The crop must be named together with a reasonable time; a crop without a time earns nothing.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 2: Cycles | **Sub-strand:** 3: Crop Production | **Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)

**Content Standard:** **B9/JHS3.2.3.1** - Show an understanding of differences in maturities of different crops grown in different soils and different seed beds. **B9/JHS3.2.3.2** - Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of uses of different crops at different maturity stages.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 2: Cycles, Sub-Strand 3: Crop Production, Basic 9, pages 96 to 98. Two content standards are examined. Under B9/JHS3.2.3.1 the indicator is B9/JHS3.2.3.1.1 (exemplars: observe and record the maturity stages of different crops grown in different soils and seed beds; discuss the differences in maturity stages among the different crops on the different soils and seed beds; compare and contrast the maturity stages of crops and seedlings in the community or school garden with others grown elsewhere). Under B9/JHS3.2.3.2 the indicators are B9/JHS3.2.3.2.1 (exemplars: discuss and write the uses of each maturity stage of each crop identified; categorise crops by their different maturity stages and uses) and B9/JHS3.2.3.2.2 (exemplars: explain the specific uses of each maturity stage of different crops to humans, other crops, animals and the environment; explain how the knowledge of the maturity stages of different crops helps a farmer in crop selection, time of harvest and others; compare different stages of maturity of crops identified in the community with those used in other places).

> Note: The blueprint separates the three indicators: I1 (B9/JHS3.2.3.1.1) carries topics 5.1, 5.2 and 5.3 and Questions 1 to 4; I2 (B9/JHS3.2.3.2.1) carries topic 5.4 and Question 5; I3 (B9/JHS3.2.3.2.2) carries topic 5.5 and Question 6. Only crops grown and sold in Ghanaian communities are used, as the exemplars require the comparison to be made with the school or community garden. The school's sheets use the shorter coded forms (B9.2.3.1 and B9.2.3.2); both forms refer to the same standards.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This paper covers Sub-Strand 3: Crop Production for Basic 9, which the syllabus writes as two content standards: differences in the maturity of crops on different soils and seed beds, and the uses of crops at the different maturity stages.
- The syllabus expects the work to be done in the school or community garden. Questions 3 and 4 are therefore built around a class investigation rather than recall, and teachers should run such a study with the class before the examination.
- In Question 3(a) the unit cm must be written. Readings within one small square of the scheme are accepted, so 40 to 42 cm is correct for week 4 on soil Q.
- Question 4(a) is the design task. The three things that must appear are two comparable plots, identical treatment apart from the seed bed, and a record of the date of flowering. Neatness of expression is not marked.
- Question 5 draws on dishes the pupils know. Accept any local dish that fits the stage named; a candidate from the north may write tuo zaafi where the scheme says banku.
- Question 6(b) asks for a judgement. Candidates who agree with the advice have misread the length of the rains and cannot earn the reason marks; teach pupils to compare the length of the growing period with the length of the rains before choosing a variety.
- Follow-up work: keep a planting calendar on the classroom wall for the school farm, with the sowing date, the expected date of flowering and the expected date of harvest for every crop the class plants.

### Section B - Theory (summary answers; full detail in the Marking Scheme)

| Question | Expected Answer | Curriculum Area | Cognitive Level |

| 1 (a) | (i) A ration is the mixture of feed given to an animal to meet its needs for one day. (ii) The animal grows well, stays healthy and produces more meat, milk or eggs, and no feed is wasted. | Feed Ingredients and the Preparation of Feed | Remember |
| 1 (b) | Maize - carbohydrate (energy); fish meal - protein; oyster shell - mineral salts, chiefly calcium; premix - vitamins and trace minerals. | Feed Ingredients and the Preparation of Feed | Understand |
| 1 (c) | Weigh out each ingredient in the correct proportion; sweep a clean, dry concrete floor and spread the largest ingredient (the maize meal) first; mix the premix and salt with a small quantity of maize meal before adding them, and spread the other ingredients on top; turn the heap over with a shovel several times until the colour is even throughout; then bag the feed, label it with the date and store it on pallets in a cool, dry room. | Feed Ingredients and the Preparation of Feed | Create |
| 2 (a) | (i) P. (ii) W - rumen; Z - abomasum (the true stomach). | Ruminants, Monogastrics, Poultry and the Feed They Take | Apply |
| 2 (b) | (i) The feed is stored and softened, and micro-organisms (bacteria) in it break down the cellulose of the grass by fermentation; the coarse material is also returned to the mouth to be chewed again as cud. (ii) Pig (also fowl, rabbit or dog). | Ruminants, Monogastrics, Poultry and the Feed They Take | Understand |
| 2 (c) | (i) P can use bulky, fibrous roughage such as grass, hay, silage and crop residues, while Q needs feed low in fibre; Q needs a concentrate rich in nutrients, often in small, frequent feeds, while P can be left to graze. (ii) Elephant grass, guinea grass, hay, silage, maize stover, groundnut haulms or cassava peels. | Ruminants, Monogastrics, Poultry and the Feed They Take | Understand |
| 2 (d) | The pig has a simple stomach without the micro-organisms of a rumen, so it cannot break down the cellulose in the grass; most of the grass passes out undigested and the pig gets very little energy and protein from it, so it stays thin. He should feed a concentrate ration of maize, bran and a protein source, using the grass or greens only as a small part of the feed. | Ruminants, Monogastrics, Poultry and the Feed They Take | Analyse |

| 3 (b) | (i) The higher the protein content of the ration, the heavier the birds became. ## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Readings taken from the bar chart are accepted within one small square of the value in the scheme, and the unit kg must be given. (3) In calculations award the method mark even where the final figure is wrong, provided the working is shown. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed. (6) Accept the name of any feed ingredient or farm animal common in the candidate's own district.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) The **quantity of feed, made up of different ingredients, given to an animal in one day to meet its needs** (1 mark).
- (ii) The animal **grows fast and stays healthy and produces more meat, milk or eggs**; feed is not wasted and disease is reduced (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'the daily feed allowance of an animal' in (i).*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Maize - **carbohydrate (energy)** (1 mark).
- Fish meal - **protein** (1 mark).
- Oyster shell - **minerals, chiefly calcium** (1 mark).
- Premix - **vitamins and trace minerals** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'energy food' for maize and 'body-building food' for fish meal.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- **Weigh out each ingredient** in the correct proportion for 100 kg (1 mark).
- On a **clean, dry floor spread the ingredient of the largest quantity (the maize meal) first** and the smaller ones on top (1 mark).
- **Mix the premix and the salt with a little maize meal first** so that the small quantity spreads evenly through the heap (1 mark).
- **Turn the heap over with a shovel several times until the mixture is uniform**, then bag it, label it with the date and store it in a cool dry place on pallets (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Marks are for the steps, not for the order alone; a candidate who mixes the premix directly into the whole heap loses the third mark.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **P** (1 mark).
- (ii) W - **rumen** (1 mark).
- (ii) Z - **abomasum** (true stomach) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Do not accept 'stomach' alone for Z.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) The feed is **stored and softened**, and is later **returned to the mouth to be chewed again as cud** (1 mark).
- (i) **Micro-organisms (bacteria) break down the cellulose (fibre)** of the feed by fermentation (1 mark).
- (ii) **Pig** (accept fowl, rabbit or dog) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Either of the two points in (i) may be given in any order.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) P can feed on **bulky, fibrous roughage (grass, hay, silage, crop residues)**, while Q needs feed that is **low in fibre** (1 mark).
- (i) Q must be given a **concentrate rich in nutrients, in small regular feeds**, while P can be allowed to graze over a long period (1 mark).
- (ii) **Elephant grass, guinea grass, hay, silage, maize stover, groundnut haulms or cassava peels** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Any named local roughage is accepted in (ii).*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- The pig has a **simple (one-chambered) stomach and no rumen with micro-organisms**, so it **cannot digest the cellulose** in the grass (1 mark).
- Most of the grass therefore **passes out undigested** and the animal gets too little energy and protein, so it remains thin (1 mark).
- He should feed a **concentrate ration of maize, bran and a protein source such as fish meal or soya bean meal** (with clean water), using greens only as a small part of the feed (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The first mark requires the idea of cellulose or fibre.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **2.4 kg** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Ration M** (1 mark).
- (iii) **2.4 kg - 1.2 kg = 1.2 kg** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The unit kg is required in (i) and (iii).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **The higher the protein content of the ration, the greater the average weight of the birds** (1 mark).
- (ii) Ration M supplied **too little protein, which is needed to build muscle and other body tissue**, so the birds grew slowly (1 mark).
- (iii) **Broilers should be fed a ration high in protein (about 20%) if they are to grow well** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (i) accept 'weight increases as protein increases'.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Whether the **extra weight gained is worth more than the extra money spent on the feed** - that is, the profit per bird (1 mark).
- The **price the market pays for heavier birds**, the **quantity of feed needed per kilogramme of meat**, or whether he can **mix a ration of the same quality more cheaply from local ingredients** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct considerations are needed.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- The **same breed, age and number of chicks** in each group (1 mark).
- The **same housing, space, water, vaccination and length of time** for all three groups (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Any two distinct factors earn the marks.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Young, growing and mature (adult)** animals (1 mark for all three).
- (ii) **Colostrum** (1 mark).
- (ii) It contains **antibodies that protect the young animal against disease** (accept: it is rich in protein and vitamins) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: No mark in (i) unless all three stages are given.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Day-old to four weeks - **chick (starter) mash** (1 mark).
- Nutrient - **protein** (accept vitamins) for rapid growth (1 mark).
- Laying hen - **layer mash** (1 mark).
- Nutrient - **calcium** for the shells of the eggs (accept protein) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'chick starter' and 'layers' mash' as written.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) The eggs will have **thin, soft shells that break easily**, because the ration is **low in calcium** (1 mark).
- (i) The **number of eggs laid will fall**, and the birds may peck the shells or become weak in the legs (1 mark).
- (ii) He should **change the birds to a layer ration** and may also offer **oyster shell or limestone grit** separately (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'he is wasting money' as an extra point only, not for the mark.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Wash the feeders and drinkers and provide clean, fresh water** first thing in the morning (1 mark).
- **Weigh out the day's ration (a grower or finisher mash) and share it among enough feeders** so that every bird can reach one (1 mark).
- **Observe the birds while they feed and remove any sick or weak bird**; remove wet, stale or soiled feed (1 mark).
- **Top up feed and water in the evening and record the quantity of feed given** in the farm record book (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who only writes 'give them feed and water' earns 1 mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Wash the feeders and drinkers regularly** and keep the area around them clean (1 mark).
- **Give clean, fresh drinking water at all times** (1 mark).
- **Never feed mouldy, stale or soiled feed**, and store feed in a cool, dry, rat-proof store (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 3 marks; accept any three correct hygiene rules.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **No, the suggestion should not be accepted** (the position must be clear) (1 mark).
- **Reason 1:** growing broilers must be **fed every day (feed available for most of the day)**, otherwise growth stops, the birds lose weight and the flock becomes uneven (1 mark).
- **Reason 2:** feed that has been wet **grows mould, which produces poisons that can make the birds sick or kill them**, so it must be thrown away (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who agrees with the suggestion cannot earn the reason marks.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **50 x 0.12 kg = 6 kg** per day (1 mark).
- (ii) **6 kg x 7 = 42 kg** per week (1 mark).
- (iii) **42 x GH¢ 6.50 = GH¢ 273.00** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Award the later marks on a wrong figure carried forward, provided the working is correct.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- To **know how much feed is used, work out the cost of production and see whether the farm is making a profit** (1 mark).
- To **notice at once when the animals eat less (an early sign of disease)**, to order feed in good time and to compare one ration or batch with another (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct reasons are required.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Mix their own ration from local ingredients** (maize, bran, palm kernel cake, fish meal) instead of buying ready-made feed (1 mark).
- **Buy ingredients in bulk at harvest time, when prices are low, and store them dry and rat-proof** so that none is lost (1 mark).
- **Reduce wastage: use well-designed feeders, fill them only part full and raise them to the level of the birds' backs**, and control rats and wild birds (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'add safe greens or farm by-products while keeping the ration balanced'; do not accept 'feed the birds less'.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 2: Cycles | **Sub-strand:** 4: Animal Production | **Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)

**Content Standard:** **B9/JHS3.2.4.1** - Demonstrate understanding of the preparation of feed for domestic and commercial animals. **B9/JHS3.2.4.2** - Demonstrate skills and knowledge of feeding domestic and commercial animals.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 2: Cycles, Sub-Strand 4: Animal Production, Basic 9, pages 99 to 101. Under B9/JHS3.2.4.1 the indicator is B9/JHS3.2.4.1.1 (exemplars: demonstrate how farmers prepare feed for different domestic and commercial animals with ingredients; write down the process of preparing feed; compile a table matching feed, ingredients and method of preparation; formulate and prepare feed). Under B9/JHS3.2.4.2 the indicators are B9/JHS3.2.4.2.1 (exemplars: compile a list of feed commonly consumed by the different animals in the environment; compare and contrast the characteristics of the feed taken by ruminants, monogastrics and poultry; record feed used on farms over a period of time; identify named samples of feed for the three categories), B9/JHS3.2.4.2.2 (exemplars: categorise animals according to their stages of growth - young, growing and matured; list the types of feed used for the various stages of growth; compare the major functions of feed in each growth stage; discuss types of feed used at different stages of growth) and B9/JHS3.2.4.2.3 (exemplar: demonstrate how to feed domestic and commercial animals at different stages of growth and production, with appropriate feed, on the school farm or a farm in the community).

> Note: Four indicators are examined. I1 (B9/JHS3.2.4.1.1) carries topic 6.1 and Question 1; I2 (B9/JHS3.2.4.2.1) carries topics 6.2 and 6.3 and Question 2; I3 (B9/JHS3.2.4.2.2) carries topic 6.4 and Questions 3 and 4; I4 (B9/JHS3.2.4.2.3) carries topic 6.5 and Questions 5 and 6. The indicators are practical ones, so the paper uses feed ingredients, animals and prices found in Ghanaian communities. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find these standards written as B9.2.4.1 and B9.2.4.2.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- Sub-Strand 4 for Basic 9 is a practical sub-strand: the four indicators ask pupils to prepare feed, to select feed for ruminants, monogastrics and poultry, to match feed to the stage of growth, and actually to feed animals on a farm. Questions 1, 5 and 6 should therefore follow real work on the school farm.
- In Question 2 the examiner is looking for the link between the structure of the stomach and the kind of feed the animal can use. Candidates who name the four compartments but cannot say why a ruminant copes with grass have missed the point of the indicator.
- In Question 3 the unit kg must be written. Readings within one small square are accepted, so 2.3 to 2.5 kg is correct for ration L.
- Question 4(b) is a table item. A ration name without the nutrient (or the nutrient without the ration) earns only the mark for the part given.
- In Question 6(a) the method marks stand even where a candidate makes an arithmetic slip, provided the working is shown. The prices used are illustrative; teachers should replace them with current local prices when re-using the question.
- Feed names vary from district to district. Accept 'chick starter', 'chick mash' or 'broiler starter' for the first four weeks, and 'layers' mash' or 'layer ration' for hens in lay.
- Follow-up work: let the class formulate and mix a small quantity of feed (about 10 kg) for the school's birds, weigh it out, record what the birds eat for two weeks and work out the cost per kilogramme of weight gained.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Accept the alternative names used in textbooks, for example auricle for atrium and alveolus for air sac. (3) A spelling that clearly means another structure, such as 'artery' written for 'atrium', earns no mark. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Award the mark for a correct idea expressed in the candidate's own words. (6) In the word equation for respiration both the correct reactants and the correct products are required for full marks.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- **Plasma** and **red blood cells** (1 mark for both).
- **White blood cells** and **platelets** (1 mark for both).
  - *Marking note: Award 1 mark where only two or three components are correct.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Red blood cells - **carry oxygen from the lungs to the body cells** by means of haemoglobin (1 mark).
- White blood cells - **defend the body against disease-causing organisms** (1 mark).
- Platelets - **help the blood to clot when a vessel is cut** (1 mark).
- Plasma - **transports digested food, hormones, carbon dioxide and other wastes** (and distributes heat) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: One correct function for each row earns the mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- (i) **Anaemia** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Kontomire or other dark green leafy vegetable, liver, meat, fish or beans** - foods rich in iron (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Do not accept 'plenty of water' in (ii).*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- There is **little haemoglobin, so the blood carries too little oxygen** to the cells (1 mark).
- The cells therefore **cannot respire fast enough to release the energy needed**, so the person tires quickly and breathes faster to try to take in more oxygen (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The idea of oxygen shortage must be clear for the first mark.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- A - **right atrium** (accept right auricle) (1 mark).
- B - **right ventricle** (1 mark).
- E - **vena cava** (accept superior vena cava) (1 mark).
- G - **aorta** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'auricle' for atrium throughout the paper.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) It is a **valve**: it **allows blood to flow in one direction only (from the atrium into the ventricle) and prevents it from flowing back** (1 mark).
- (ii) **D pumps blood to the whole body, while B pumps blood only to the lungs**, which are close to the heart (1 mark).
- (ii) **D must therefore develop a much greater pressure**, so it has a thicker layer of muscle (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Both reasons in (ii) must refer to the work done by the chamber.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- From **E (vena cava) into A, the right atrium** (1 mark).
- Through the **valve into B, the right ventricle** (1 mark).
- Out through **F, the pulmonary artery, to the lungs** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The order must be correct; a correct list in the wrong order earns 1 mark only.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- K is the **septum**; a hole allows **oxygenated and deoxygenated blood to mix** (1 mark).
- The blood sent to the body therefore **carries less oxygen**, the heart has to work harder and the child tires easily and is breathless (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The idea of mixing of the two kinds of blood is essential.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Arteries, veins and capillaries** (1 mark for all three).
- (ii) So that **materials can pass quickly and easily between the blood and the body cells** (1 mark).
- (iii) The **wrist** (accept the neck, the temple or the ankle) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: No mark in (i) unless all three are named.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Direction - artery: **carries blood away from the heart** (1 mark).
- Direction - vein: **carries blood towards the heart** (1 mark).
- Wall - artery: **thick, muscular and elastic**, to stand the high pressure (1 mark).
- Wall - vein: **thinner, with a wider space inside and with valves** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Marks are for the paired comparison; an answer that describes only one vessel earns half of the available marks.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) The blood **passes through the heart twice in one complete round of the body** (1 mark).
- (i) Once on the **short journey to the lungs and back** and once on the **journey to the rest of the body and back** (1 mark).
- (ii) The blood is **pumped again after the lungs, so it reaches the body at high pressure and travels quickly**, and the two kinds of blood are kept separate (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'pulmonary circulation and systemic circulation' for the second mark in (i).*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- K - the **wall of the air sac (alveolus)** (1 mark).
- L - the **blood capillary** (1 mark).
- M - a **red blood cell** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'alveolus wall' for K and 'capillary' alone for L.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) Arrow 1 - **oxygen** (from the air sac into the blood) (1 mark).
- (i) Arrow 2 - **carbon dioxide** (from the blood into the air sac) (1 mark).
- (ii) **Diffusion** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'gaseous exchange by diffusion' in (ii); 'breathing' earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The wall is **very thin (one cell thick) and moist**, so gases cross easily (1 mark).
- The sacs are **very many, giving a large surface area**, and each is **richly supplied with capillaries** carrying blood away all the time (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Any two distinct features earn the marks.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- The **oxygenated blood is carried to the heart and pumped through the arteries and capillaries to every cell**, where the oxygen is used in respiration (1 mark).
- The blood then **collects the carbon dioxide made in the cells and carries it back through the veins and the heart to the lungs** to be breathed out (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Both the outward and the return journey are needed for full marks.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) The **chemical breakdown of glucose in the cells, using oxygen, to release energy** (1 mark).
- (ii) **glucose + oxygen** on the left of the arrow (1 mark).
- (ii) **carbon dioxide + water + energy** on the right of the arrow (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'food' for glucose in (i) but not in the equation.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) Breathing is the **physical movement of air into and out of the lungs**; respiration is a **chemical reaction that releases energy** (1 mark).
- (i) Breathing takes place in the **breathing organs only**, while respiration takes place in **every living cell** (1 mark).
- (ii) For **movement of the muscles** (accept growth and repair, keeping the body warm, or the working of the organs) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct differences are needed in (i).*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- The **muscles were working hard and needed much more energy, so they respired faster** (1 mark).
- **Breathing became faster and deeper to take in more oxygen** (and to remove carbon dioxide at the lungs) (1 mark).
- The **heart beat faster to carry oxygen and glucose to the muscles and to carry carbon dioxide away** more quickly (1 mark).
- After the race the **muscles needed less energy and the extra carbon dioxide was removed**, so breathing and heart beat slowly returned to normal (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who writes only 'he was tired' earns no mark.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) The **force with which the blood presses on the walls of the blood vessels** as the heart pumps (1 mark).
- (ii) A **sphygmomanometer** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Hypertension (high blood pressure)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'BP apparatus' only where the candidate also writes sphygmomanometer.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Stroke** or bursting of a blood vessel in the brain (1 mark).
- **Heart attack, heart failure, kidney damage or damage to the eyes** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct problems are required; 'death' alone earns no mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Use less salt in food** - too much salt **raises the blood pressure** (1 mark).
- **Eat less fried and fatty food and more fruit and vegetables** - fat is **deposited in the arteries and narrows them** (1 mark).
- **Exercise regularly (about thirty minutes on most days), avoid smoking and heavy drinking, and check the blood pressure at the clinic** - this **strengthens the heart and finds trouble early** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Each mark requires both a piece of advice and a reason; advice without a reason earns no mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 3: Systems | **Sub-strand:** 1: The Human Body System | **Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)

**Content Standard:** **B9/JHS3.3.1.1** - Demonstrate understanding of the blood circulatory system, health problems associated with the system and its relationship with the respiratory system in humans.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 3: Systems, Sub-Strand 1: The Human Body System, Basic 9, page 102. The indicator B9/JHS3.3.1.1.1 carries the exemplars: discuss the blood circulatory system in humans and the composition and functions of blood; explain the functions of the parts of the circulatory system; draw and label the longitudinal section of a mammalian heart; describe the causes and prevention of diseases of the circulatory system; and describe what blood pressure is and ways of managing it. The indicator B9/JHS3.3.1.1.2 carries the exemplars: explain the concept of respiration, and explain how deoxygenated blood from circulation is oxygenated through inhalation for respiration to take place. The curriculum notes that respiration is a chemical reaction that releases carbon dioxide, water and energy from glucose and oxygen.

> Note: I1 (B9/JHS3.3.1.1.1) carries topics 7.1 to 7.4 and Questions 1, 2, 3 and 6; I2 (B9/JHS3.3.1.1.2) carries topic 7.5 and Questions 4 and 5. The curriculum exemplar that pupils should draw and label a longitudinal section of the mammalian heart is examined in Question 2, which uses a lettered section so that no answer is given away by the figure. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find this standard written as B9.3.1.1.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This paper examines the whole of Sub-Strand 1 for Basic 9: the composition and functions of blood, the parts of the circulatory system, the diseases of the system, blood pressure, and the way the respiratory and circulatory systems complement each other.
- Question 2 is built on the curriculum exemplar that pupils should draw and label a longitudinal section of the mammalian heart. Teachers should let pupils draw the section themselves, in pencil, before the examination; a candidate who has drawn it finds the lettering easy.
- The letters on Fig. 1 follow the convention that the section is seen from the front, so the right side of the heart appears on the left of the drawing. Candidates who reverse A and C have not read the caption.
- In Question 4 the two gas arrows are numbered, not named, so that the figure does not give away the answer. Accept 'alveolus' or 'air sac' interchangeably.
- Question 5(a)(ii) is marked in two halves: one mark for the reactants and one for the products. An equation written with chemical formulae in place of words is accepted if correct.
- Question 6 deals with hypertension, which is common in Ghanaian communities. Marks in 6(c) are given only where advice is supported by a reason; this is what the curriculum means by describing ways of managing blood pressure.
- Follow-up work: invite a nurse from the nearest clinic to take the blood pressure and pulse rate of volunteers in the class, and let the pupils record and discuss the readings, taking care not to alarm or label any pupil.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Accept 'asteroid belt' and 'belt of small rocky bodies' as the same answer, and 'air' for 'atmosphere'. (3) The words meteoroid, meteor and meteorite must be used correctly; one written for another earns no mark. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Award the mark for a correct idea expressed in the candidate's own words. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) The **Sun together with all the bodies that move round it** (planets, satellites, asteroids, comets and meteoroids) (1 mark).
- (ii) The **gravitational pull (gravity) of the Sun** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'gravity' alone in (ii).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Asteroids** (1 mark).
- **Comets** (1 mark).
- **Meteoroids** (accept natural satellites or moons, or dwarf planets) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Do not accept 'stars' or the name of a planet.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) A **planet moves round the Sun**, while a **natural satellite moves round a planet** (1 mark).
- (ii) Planet - **the Earth** (accept any of the eight planets) (1 mark).
- (ii) Natural satellite - **the Moon** (accept a named moon of another planet) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A difference in size alone earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- A planet must **move in its own orbit round the Sun**; the Moon **moves round the Earth** (1 mark).
- The Moon goes round the Sun **only because it is carried along by the Earth**, so it is classed as a **natural satellite** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The idea that the Moon orbits a planet is essential.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- A - the **Sun** (1 mark).
- C - the **asteroid belt** (a belt of asteroids, small rocky bodies) (1 mark).
- D - a **comet** (1 mark).
- E - the **orbit (path) of the comet** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'asteroid' for C where the candidate shows it is the belt.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **E is a long, narrow ellipse, while F is nearly circular** (1 mark).
- (i) The **distance of D from the Sun changes greatly along E**, and one journey round E takes far longer than one journey round F (1 mark).
- (ii) At the **part of the path nearest to the Sun** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'at perihelion' or 'when closest to the Sun' in (ii).*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) Between the orbits of **Mars and Jupiter** (1 mark).
- (ii) They are **small, rocky (or metallic) bodies of irregular shape**, much smaller than a planet (1 mark).
- (ii) They **move round the Sun in the same direction as the planets, in nearly circular orbits in about the same plane** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Either of the last two points earns the second mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- It would travel in towards the inner solar system; a **small body would burn up in the atmosphere and be seen as a meteor** (1 mark).
- A **large one could strike the ground as a meteorite, forming a crater, destroying life around it and throwing dust into the air** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Either outcome, correctly explained, earns both marks only where the two cases are distinguished.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- P - the **nucleus** (1 mark).
- Q - the **coma** (1 mark).
- R - the **tail** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'head' for Q only where the candidate writes 'coma (head)'.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Position 3** (1 mark).
- (ii) There the comet is **heated most strongly, so much more of its ice turns into gas and dust is released** (1 mark).
- (ii) The gas and dust are **pushed far out by the radiation and the stream of particles coming from the Sun**, giving a long, bright tail (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'solar wind' for the stream of particles.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The tail points **away from the Sun** (1 mark).
- **Reason:** the gas and dust are **pushed outwards by the Sun's radiation and solar wind**, so the tail always lies on the side away from the Sun, whatever the direction of travel (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Behind the comet' earns no mark; the tail is not controlled by the direction of travel.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- The orbit is a **very long ellipse, so the comet is close to the Sun, with a bright tail, for only a short part of the journey** (1 mark).
- For the rest of the time it is **far from the Sun, with no tail and too faint to be seen**, and one complete orbit takes many years (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept a reference to Halley's comet returning after about 76 years as supporting detail.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) A **small piece of rock or metal moving through space** (1 mark).
- (ii) The **streak of light seen when such a body burns up in the Earth's atmosphere** (1 mark).
- (iii) A **piece that survives the burning and lands on the surface of the Earth** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The three terms must be distinguished; two identical definitions earn one mark only.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Friction between the fast-moving body and the air** heats it until it glows (1 mark).
- (ii) They are **small and burn up completely** in the atmosphere before reaching the ground (1 mark).
- (iii) **Many meteors seen in a short time**, when the Earth passes through the **trail of dust left by a comet** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'air resistance' for friction in (i).*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- (i) It lies in a **fresh crater or hollow with soil thrown out around it** (1 mark).
- (i) It is **unusually heavy, rich in iron (a magnet may stick to it) and has a dark melted crust**, unlike the rocks of the district (1 mark).
- (ii) A **large crater is formed and buildings, farms and living things nearby are destroyed** by the shock and heat (1 mark).
- (ii) **Dust is thrown high into the air, cutting off sunlight and affecting the weather and climate** (accept an earth tremor) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (i) 'people said so' is not an observation and earns no mark.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Asteroid - made of **rock and metal** (1 mark).
- Comet - made of **ice, frozen gases and dust** (1 mark).
- Asteroid - orbit **nearly circular**, mostly within the belt (1 mark).
- Comet - orbit a **long, narrow ellipse** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Marks are for the paired comparison; one column alone earns the marks in that column only.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- They **all move round the Sun** in closed orbits, returning to the same part of the path (1 mark).
- They are **all held in their paths by the gravitational pull of the Sun** (1 mark).
- Each **moves faster when nearer to the Sun**, and most travel round the Sun in the same direction (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 3 marks.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **No, the claim is not correct** (1 mark).
- **Reason 1:** a comet is a **natural body moving on a fixed orbit round the Sun, and its return can be predicted** years ahead, so it is not caused by, and does not cause, events on the Earth (1 mark).
- **Reason 2:** **records of many past comets show that no disaster followed them**; the belief is a superstition that observation and record keeping disprove (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who agrees with the claim cannot earn the reason marks. This part examines the competence of identifying and disproving misconceptions.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Find out the date, the time and the part of the sky** from a reliable source such as an astronomy website or the Ghana Astronomy Centre (1 mark).
- **Choose a dark, open place away from street lights**, with permission and adult supervision, on a clear night (1 mark).
- **Record the observation**: sketch the comet and write down the date, the time, the direction and anything used, such as binoculars (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'use a sky map or phone application' for the first mark.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Who published it** - whether the author or organisation is a recognised scientific body, and **how recent the page is** (1 mark).
- **Whether the same information is given by other reliable sources**, and whether the page offers evidence rather than advertisements or rumours (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct checks are required.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- They **carry material left from the formation of the solar system**, so they tell us how the Sun, the Earth and the planets began (1 mark).
- **Watching the bodies that come near the Earth gives warning of a possible collision** in good time (1 mark).
- The study **replaces superstition with evidence** and **interests young people in science, mathematics and careers in technology** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'comets may have brought water to the early Earth' for any one mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 3: Systems | **Sub-strand:** 2: The Solar System | **Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)

**Content Standard:** **B9/JHS3.3.2.1** - Demonstrate knowledge of other non-planetary bodies such as comets, asteroids, and their relationship with the solar system.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 3: Systems, Sub-Strand 2: The Solar System, Basic 9, page 103. The content standard B9/JHS3.3.2.1 has one indicator, B9/JHS3.3.2.1.1, with the exemplars: research for information on the movement of non-planetary bodies in the solar system, for example asteroids and comets; and compare and contrast the movement of the non-planetary bodies in the solar system. The core competences named are Communication and Collaboration and Digital Literacy (DL 5.6, CC 8.2).

> Note: This sub-strand carries a single indicator, B9/JHS3.3.2.1.1, so every item in the paper is traced to it; the five topics 8.1 to 8.5 show how the indicator has been spread over the paper. Because the exemplars ask pupils to research and then to compare and contrast, Question 5 is a comparison question and Question 6 is built on the research and digital literacy competence. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find this standard written as B9.3.2.1.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- The sub-strand has only one indicator, so the paper spreads that indicator over five topics: the members of the solar system, asteroids, comets, meteoroids and a final comparison. Teachers should note that the emphasis of the indicator is on MOVEMENT, which is why several items ask about orbits, speed and direction rather than about names alone.
- The words meteoroid, meteor and meteorite are the commonest source of lost marks. Drill them as a sequence: in space, in the air, on the ground.
- Question 3(c) tests the common misconception that a comet's tail trails behind it like smoke from a lorry. The tail always points away from the Sun, so when the comet is moving away from the Sun the tail goes in front of it.
- Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 are not drawn to scale, and candidates must not be asked to measure distances on them. In reality the asteroid belt is far wider and the bodies in it are very far apart.
- Question 5(c) examines the core competence of identifying and disproving a misconception. Treat beliefs raised by candidates with respect, but mark only the scientific reasoning.
- Question 6 reflects the digital literacy competence named in the curriculum. Where the school has no internet, the same marks can be earned for checking a library book, a newspaper or a radio announcement against a second source.
- Follow-up work: keep a sky diary for one term. Pupils record the date, time and direction of anything unusual they see at night, and the class discusses the records at the end of the term.

# PAPER 9 - ECOSYSTEM: INTERDEPENDENCE OF ORGANISMS

**Strand 3: Systems | Sub-Strand 3: Ecosystem | B9/JHS3.3.3.1**

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) In a food chain the arrows must point in the correct direction; a chain written with the arrows reversed earns no mark. (3) Readings taken from the graph are accepted within one small square of the value in the scheme, and the unit kg must be given. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Award the mark for a correct idea expressed in the candidate's own words. (6) Accept the name of any ecosystem, organism or local practice known in the candidate's district.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) A **community of living organisms together with the non-living surroundings in which they live and with which they interact** (1 mark).
- (ii) The **particular place in which an organism lives** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'the home of an organism' for (ii).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) Any **two living things**, for example **water lilies and tilapia** (or grass, frogs, birds, bacteria) (1 mark).
- (ii) Any **two non-living things**, for example **water and sunlight** (or soil, air, dissolved oxygen, temperature) (1 mark).
- (iii) **All the organisms of the same kind living in one area at the same time** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Both examples are needed in (i) and in (ii) for the mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- A habitat is the **place where an organism lives**, while an ecosystem is the **whole community of organisms together with the non-living surroundings** (1 mark).
- A **habitat is part of an ecosystem and is smaller**; one ecosystem contains many habitats (1 mark).
- Example - habitat: **the mud at the bottom of the pond** (or the bark of a tree); ecosystem: **the whole pond** (or the grassland) (1 mark for both examples).
  - *Marking note: The third mark requires one example of each.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- (i) A **population** (1 mark).
- (ii) An **ecosystem** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: No mark where two answers are given for one part.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Grass and the maize plant** (1 mark for both).
- (ii) A chain of **four organisms taken correctly from the web**, for example **grass -> mouse -> snake -> hawk** (1 mark).
- (ii) The **arrows point from the organism eaten to the organism that eats it** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A chain containing a link that is not in the web earns no mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Grasshopper, mouse or weaver bird** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Lizard or snake** (1 mark).
- (iii) The **hawk** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) accept the hawk only where the candidate states that it is feeding on the weaver bird.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) The number of snakes would **fall (decrease)** (1 mark).
- (i) **Reason:** they would lose one of their main foods and would have to depend on lizards alone, so some would **starve or move away** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Less maize would be eaten, so the harvest would improve** for a time (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'the number of lizards would also fall as snakes eat more of them' as an additional correct point.*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- Prediction: the **maize harvest would fall** (1 mark).
- **The predators that controlled the mice and the weaver birds would be gone, so their numbers would increase rapidly** (1 mark).
- The larger numbers of mice and birds would **eat more maize in the field and in store**, so the balance of the ecosystem is upset and the farmers lose more than they gain (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A prediction without justification earns 1 mark only.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Green plants make their own food by photosynthesis** and so bring the Sun's energy into the ecosystem (1 mark).
- (ii) Consumers **feed on plants or on other animals**, passing energy and materials along the food chain (1 mark).
- (iii) Decomposers **break down dead organisms and waste and release nutrients back into the soil and water** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'recycle nutrients' for (iii).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) The **Sun** (1 mark).
- (ii) It means **'is eaten by'** and shows the direction in which food and energy pass (1 mark).
- (iii) **Bacteria** (accept fungi, mushrooms or moulds) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Do not accept 'earthworm' alone in (iii) unless described as feeding on dead matter.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- Much of the energy is **used for the life processes of the organism (movement, growth, keeping warm)** (1 mark).
- This energy is finally **lost to the surroundings as heat**, and some is lost in **waste and in parts that are not eaten** (1 mark).
- Only the energy **stored in the body can pass to the next level**, so there is **less energy at every step** (1 mark).
- Therefore **food chains are short, and there must be far more producers than primary consumers, and more primary consumers than predators** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The fourth mark requires the link to numbers of organisms.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **About 520 kg** (accept 510 to 530 kg) (1 mark).
- (ii) **About 95 kg** (accept 90 to 100 kg) (1 mark).
- (iii) **520 kg - 95 kg = 425 kg** (accept 410 to 440 kg) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The unit kg is required in all three parts.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) Before 2022 the catch **fell only slowly** (from about 520 kg to about 465 kg) (1 mark).
- (i) After 2022 it **fell steeply and steadily** to about 95 kg (1 mark).
- (ii) The **mining appears to have damaged the river, so that the fish population has collapsed** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (i) a candidate must distinguish the two periods.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The water is **filled with mud, which cuts off light from water plants and clogs the gills of fish** (1 mark).
- **Poisonous chemicals such as mercury enter the water**, killing organisms and passing along the food chain; breeding grounds on the banks are destroyed (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct ways are required.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **No (not completely)** - the graph only shows that the two things **happened at the same time**, which does not by itself prove cause (1 mark).
- Other evidence: **tests of the mud and chemicals in the water before and after 2022**, records of the number of fishermen and the nets used, or the catch from a **similar river with no mining** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who simply agrees with the pupil earns no mark.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Bush burning - **destroys humus, soil organisms and the homes of animals, and leaves the soil bare to erosion** (1 mark).
- Cutting down a forest - **removes habitats, causes soil erosion and reduces rainfall in the area** (1 mark).
- Overhunting - **the species may disappear from the area, affecting all the organisms that depend on it** (1 mark).
- Heavy use of pesticide - **kills useful organisms as well as pests and builds up in the bodies of animals along the food chain** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: One correct effect for each row earns the mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- The pesticide **washes into the lagoon and is taken in by the small plants and animals**, and is **not broken down or passed out** of their bodies (1 mark).
- Each fish **eats many of these small organisms and keeps all their pesticide**, and each bird eats many fish (1 mark).
- So the quantity **becomes greater at every step of the food chain**, until the birds at the top are harmed (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The idea of building up along the chain must be clear.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Prediction 1 with justification: the **grass dies because there is too little water for photosynthesis and growth**, so the producers and the food supply of the ecosystem are reduced (1 mark).
- Prediction 2 with justification: the **plant-eating animals starve, die or move away**, and their **predators decline too**, because each level depends on the one below (1 mark).
- A further correct prediction with justification - for example **water holes dry up so animals crowd together and disease spreads**, or **the bare soil is eroded when the rains return** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A prediction without a justification earns no mark.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- **Stop all mining in and along the river** and report illegal mining to the authorities (1 mark).
- **Replant trees and grass along the banks** to hold the soil and shade the water (1 mark).
- **Ban poisons, chemicals and small-mesh nets in fishing, agree on a closed season, and keep refuse out of the river** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 3 marks; any three sensible measures are accepted.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Every organism depends on others, so damage to one part upsets the whole system**, including the human beings in it (1 mark).
- People **depend on the ecosystem for food, water, fuel, medicines and income**, and a lost species cannot be brought back (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct reasons are required.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Reason 1:** the work is **short lived** - when the river and the land are destroyed the mining ends and nothing is left for the community (1 mark).
- **Reason 2:** the damage **costs far more than the wages earned**: farming, fishing and clean drinking water are lost and mercury harms health (1 mark).
- A better way: **licensed and regulated mining with reclamation of the land**, or **farming, fish farming, tree planting, agro-processing or ecotourism** supported by the district assembly (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Candidates may argue for regulated mining; award the marks where the reasoning deals with the damage to the ecosystem.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 3: Systems | **Sub-strand:** 3: Ecosystem | **Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)

**Content Standard:** **B9/JHS3.3.3.1** - Recognise the interdependence of organisms in an ecosystem and appreciate their interaction to maintain balance in the system.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 3: Systems, Sub-Strand 3: Ecosystem, Basic 9, page 104. The content standard B9/JHS3.3.3.1 has one indicator, B9/JHS3.3.3.1.1, with the exemplars: describe how organisms depend on each other in different ecosystems (pictures, charts and videos may be used); state the differences between an ecosystem and a habitat; construct a food chain and a food web found in an ecosystem; and predict and justify your predictions on how interferences such as earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, hunting, farming, mining, galamsey, pollution, pesticides and bush burning will affect the balance in an ecosystem.

> Note: This sub-strand carries a single indicator, B9/JHS3.3.3.1.1, so every item traces to it; topics 9.1 to 9.5 show how the four exemplars have been spread over the paper. Exemplar 2 (ecosystem and habitat) is examined in Question 1, exemplar 3 (food chain and food web) in Questions 2 and 3, and exemplar 4 (predicting the effect of interference) in Questions 4, 5 and 6. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find this standard written as B9.3.3.1.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- The single indicator of this sub-strand is wide, so the paper is organised round the four exemplars: interdependence, ecosystem against habitat, food chains and webs, and the effect of interference on the balance of the system.
- The commonest error in Section B is to draw a food chain with the arrows pointing the wrong way. Teach the arrow as the words 'is eaten by', and insist on it in every exercise.
- In Question 2 the web is deliberately drawn with named organisms, since the task is to read relationships, not to recall names. Candidates must take their chains from the web as drawn and may not add links of their own.
- Question 4(d) is a reasoning item about evidence. Candidates should learn that two things happening at the same time do not by themselves prove that one caused the other, and that a comparison river acts as a control.
- Galamsey appears by name in the curriculum exemplar, and the subject is sensitive in many districts. Mark the science, not the opinion: the marks in 6(c) are for reasoning about the ecosystem and about livelihoods, not for the side the candidate takes.
- Where a candidate names an ecosystem, organism or practice from his or her own district that the scheme does not list, award the mark if it is correct.
- Follow-up work: let the class choose a small area - a school garden plot, a drain, a patch of bush or a pond - and record for one term the organisms found there, the non-living conditions, and any human interference; then build a food web from the records.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Accept the name of any waste material or manure used in the candidate's own district, for example cocoa pod husks, rice husk, groundnut shells or brewery waste. (3) Readings taken from the bar chart are accepted within one small square of the value in the scheme, and the unit kg must be given. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) In a practical description the marks are for the steps, not for neat English. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) **Material of plant or animal origin added to the soil to supply nutrients and improve it** (1 mark).
- (ii) Manure is made from **plant and animal waste and adds humus, improving the structure and the water-holding of the soil**, while fertiliser is manufactured and supplies nutrients only (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'manure acts slowly, fertiliser acts quickly' in (ii).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Farmyard manure** (1 mark).
- **Compost** (1 mark).
- **Green manure** (accept poultry manure, liquid manure or treated night soil) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Do not accept the names of inorganic fertilisers.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) Two plant wastes, for example **dry leaves and kitchen vegetable peelings** (accept weeds, maize stalks, cocoa pod husks, rice husk) (1 mark).
- (i) Two animal wastes, for example **poultry droppings and cow dung** (accept pig dung, goat droppings, bone meal) (1 mark).
- (ii) **Nitrogen** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Both examples are needed in each half of (i).*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- A sandy soil **loses water and nutrients quickly**, since the particles are large and the soil is poor in humus (1 mark).
- The **humus in the manure holds water and nutrients in the topsoil** where the roots can reach them, and feeds the soil organisms (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A general answer such as 'manure is good for soil' earns 1 mark only.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- A - **coarse woody material: twigs, chopped maize stalks or stems** (1 mark).
- B - **green plant waste: leaves, weeds, grass or kitchen peelings** (1 mark).
- C - **animal waste: cow dung or poultry droppings** (1 mark).
- E - **a cover of grass, palm fronds or old sacks** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept any sensible material for each layer, provided it is placed correctly.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) It **introduces the micro-organisms (bacteria and fungi) that cause the waste to decay** (1 mark).
- (ii) So that the **different materials are well mixed and rot evenly** (1 mark).
- (iii) It **keeps the heap moist and warm and protects it from heavy rain and the hot Sun** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'to keep flies away' as a second use in (iii).*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) To **test the condition inside the heap** from time to time (1 mark).
- (ii) The heap is **working well: the organisms are active (it is warm) and there is enough moisture** (1 mark).
- (iii) To **add water when the heap becomes dry**, since the organisms of decay need moisture (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) accept 'decomposition is going on well'.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- The **micro-organisms respire as they break down the waste and release heat**, which is trapped inside the covered heap (1 mark).
- The heat **destroys many weed seeds, insect eggs and disease-causing organisms** (accept: it speeds up the rotting) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'The Sun heats the heap' earns no mark.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Collect and sort the waste**, removing plastics, glass, metal and stones, and **chop large materials into small pieces** (1 mark).
- **Choose a shady site away from classrooms and from any well or stream** and prepare the heap or pit (1 mark).
- **Build the heap in layers** - coarse material, green plant waste, animal dung, a thin layer of topsoil - **watering each layer** (1 mark).
- **Cover the heap and turn it every two or three weeks, watering when dry**, until the compost is ready (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Steps given out of order lose one mark overall.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **Plastics such as water sachets and bags** (1 mark).
- **Broken glass or metal (tins, nails)** (1 mark).
- **Stones, rubber, batteries or chemicals** (accept badly diseased plants) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 3 marks.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) It is **dark brown or black and crumbly, and the original materials can no longer be recognised** (1 mark).
- (i) It **smells like fresh earth, not foul, and the heap has cooled and shrunk** (1 mark).
- (ii) About **two to three months** (accept 6 to 12 weeks) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'about three months' in (ii).*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **18 kg** (1 mark).
- (ii) **7 kg** (1 mark).
- (iii) **18 kg - 7 kg = 11 kg** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The unit kg is required in all three parts.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Well-rotted poultry manure (plot Y)** (1 mark).
- (ii) Plot W **received no manure, so the soil could not supply enough nutrients**, especially nitrogen (1 mark).
- (iii) **Adding organic manure raises the yield of maize**, and in this trial poultry manure gave the biggest increase (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (iii) a conclusion that goes beyond the data earns no mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The **same variety of maize, sown on the same day at the same spacing, on plots of the same size and soil** (1 mark).
- The **same weeding, watering, pest control and time of harvest** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct factors are required.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Advise him to **compost the stalks, weeds and kitchen waste and use the compost on his field** (1 mark).
- **Reason:** plot Z shows that **compost gave almost as good a yield as the bought manure**, the materials cost nothing, and the compost improves the soil for later seasons (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The reason must refer to the data or to the benefit to the soil.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Sandy soil - **work in plenty of well-rotted manure or compost, because the humus holds water and nutrients** (1 mark).
- Heavy clay - **work in manure to open up the soil so that air and water move through it** and the soil is easier to work (1 mark).
- Heavy rains - **work the manure into the soil rather than leave it on the surface, where it would be washed away** (1 mark).
- Fresh poultry droppings - **rot or compost them first, because fresh droppings are strong enough to scorch young plants** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Each mark needs both the action and the reason.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) So that it has time to **mix with the soil and break down, releasing its nutrients when the crop needs them** (1 mark).
- (ii) It is **too strong and may scorch the plants, and it may carry weed seeds and disease-causing organisms** (1 mark).
- (iii) The **humus added each year makes the soil crumbly and open, so it holds water and is easier to dig** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'it attracts flies' as part of the answer in (ii).*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- The practice is **poor**: burning **destroys the organic matter that would have formed humus and sends the nitrogen into the air** (1 mark).
- The fire also **kills useful soil organisms and leaves the soil bare to erosion**; the ash gives some potash but **no humus** (1 mark).
- Advice: he should **compost the residues or plough them into the soil** and apply the compost to the field (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who defends burning cannot earn the first two marks.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- A **suitable shaded site away from classrooms, the kitchen and any well or stream** (1 mark).
- **Separate containers or a sorting point** so that waste that rots is kept apart from plastics, glass and metal (1 mark).
- **Tools (cutlass, hoe, fork, watering can, gloves) and a duty roster with a record book** for turning and watering (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Maximum 3 marks; any three sensible arrangements are accepted.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Wear gloves or use a tool, and wash the hands with soap and water afterwards and before eating** (1 mark).
- **Do not handle broken glass, sharp metal or chemicals; keep the heap away from drinking water and keep it covered** (accept: never use untreated night soil on vegetables eaten raw) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct rules are required.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **The waste becomes free manure that raises yields and saves the money spent on fertiliser** (1 mark).
- **The compound and gutters are kept clean**, so there are fewer flies, mosquitoes, smells and blocked drains (1 mark).
- **Burning pollutes the air and destroys humus, and dumping pollutes soil and water**, while compost improves the soil season after season (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Three distinct points are needed; repetition of one idea earns 1 mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 3: Systems | **Sub-strand:** 4: Farming Systems | **Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)

**Content Standard:** **B9/JHS3.3.4.1** - Demonstrate knowledge and skills in the preparation of different types of manure from animal and plant waste.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 3: Systems, Sub-Strand 4: Farming Systems, Basic 9, pages 105 and 106. Indicator B9/JHS3.3.4.1.1 carries the exemplars: list some types of manure used by farmers; identify and write down the materials used in preparing manure and their sources; categorise manure into those from plant wastes and animal wastes; compile a list of plant parts or wastes and animal parts or wastes used to prepare manure; and justify the use of different animal and plant manures (poultry droppings, cow dung, animal parts and carcases, pig dung, human excreta, domestic refuse, leaves, waste fruits, plant parts and shavings) under different soil and climatic conditions. Indicator B9/JHS3.3.4.1.2 carries the exemplars: prepare manure from the different plant and animal wastes, and discuss the preparation of manure using the wastes available in a community. Indicator B9/JHS3.3.4.1.3 carries the exemplar: treat various plant and animal wastes to generate manure (cleaning or sorting, curing or composting) in the field or school garden.

> Note: I1 (B9/JHS3.3.4.1.1) carries topics 10.1 to 10.3 and Questions 1, 4 and 5; I2 (B9/JHS3.3.4.1.2) carries topic 10.4 and Question 2; I3 (B9/JHS3.3.4.1.3) carries topic 10.5 and Questions 3 and 6. The three indicators move from listing, through describing the method, to doing the work, so Questions 3 and 6 are written as practical tasks on the school garden. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find this standard written as B9.3.4.1.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- The three indicators of this sub-strand rise from listing the wastes, through describing the preparation, to actually preparing manure. A written paper can only sample the practical work, so Questions 2, 3 and 6 are built round a heap the class should have made before the examination.
- In Question 2(a) candidates are asked to SUGGEST materials for the layers. Any sensible material placed in the right position earns the mark: coarse and woody at the bottom, green waste next, animal waste above it and a cover on top.
- Candidates often confuse manure with fertiliser. Insist on the two differences that matter: the origin of the material, and the fact that manure adds humus and so improves the structure of the soil.
- In Question 4 the unit kg must be written. Readings within one small square are accepted, so 17 to 19 kg is correct for plot Y.
- Question 5(a) requires both an action and a reason in each row of the table. A row that gives only the action earns no mark.
- Night soil appears in the curriculum exemplar. Treat it factually: it may be used only after thorough composting or treatment, and never on vegetables that are eaten raw.
- Follow-up work: build two small heaps on the school garden, turn one every fortnight and leave the other untouched; record the temperature with a stick test and the appearance of each heap every two weeks, and compare the compost after three months.
