## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) In calculations, award the method mark for a correct formula or substitution even when the arithmetic that follows is wrong, and award the final mark only when the unit is given. (3) Accept kWh written as kilowatt-hour or as units of electricity. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) In a description of a practical activity the marks are for the steps and the observation, not for neat English. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Using energy carefully so that it is not wasted**, that is, doing the same work with less energy (1 mark).
- (ii) **Switch off the lamps, fan and television when they are not in use** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Iron all the clothes at one time (ironing in bulk)** or **fit energy-efficient lamps** or **use daylight during the day** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) the two ways must be different from each other.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) The iron is **heated up once instead of four times**, so less energy is used in heating it (1 mark).
- (ii) An LED **gives the same light for much less electrical energy**, while a filament bulb wastes most of its energy as heat (1 mark).
- (iii) The lid **keeps the heat and steam in the pot**, so the food cooks faster and less fuel is used (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A bare statement such as 'it saves energy' earns no mark; a reason is required.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **It reduces the electricity bill and the money spent on fuel** (accept: it makes the supply serve more people) (1 mark).
- **It makes non-renewable fuels last longer and reduces pollution and the release of carbon dioxide** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct reasons are required; two ways of saying 'saves money' earn 1 mark only.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **No / I do not agree** (1 mark).
- **Reason:** the food would warm up and spoil, and the motor must then work hard to cool the whole cabinet again, so little energy is saved; **it is better to keep the door shut, defrost it and keep it away from the cooker** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who agrees cannot gain the reason mark, because the reason must support a sound judgement.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- A - **the object (the lighted candle)** (1 mark).
- B - **the pinhole / small opening** (1 mark).
- C - **the light-proof box (body of the camera)** (1 mark).
- E - **the image of the candle** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'aperture' for B and 'inverted image' for E.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) It is **real** (it is caught on a screen) (1 mark).
- (i) It is **inverted (upside down)**; accept 'smaller than the object' or 'laterally inverted' (1 mark).
- (ii) **Light travels in straight lines**, so rays from the top of the flame cross at the hole and reach the lower part of the screen, and rays from the foot reach the upper part (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Clear' or 'bright' is not a property for the purpose of this question.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Correct relation: **height of image / height of object = length of box / distance of the object** (1 mark).
- Substitution: **height of image = 12 × 15 / 60** (1 mark).
- **Height of image = 3 cm** (unit required) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Award the first two marks for correct method even if the arithmetic is wrong; the final mark needs the unit cm.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- (i) The picture becomes **larger** (1 mark).
- (ii) The picture becomes **brighter but blurred (not sharp)**, because overlapping patches of light reach the screen (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (i) accept 'bigger and less sharp'; the key idea is the increase in size.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) **P = IV** (power = current × voltage) (1 mark).
- (ii) **I = P/V = 1 500/240 = 6.25 A** (unit required) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 6.3 A.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **0.24 kW × 5 h = 1.2 kWh** (1 mark).
- (ii) **0.1 kW × 4 h = 0.4 kWh** (1 mark).
- (iii) **1.5 kW × 1 h = 1.5 kWh** (1 mark).
- (iv) **0.15 kW × 24 h = 3.6 kWh** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who works in watt-hours and then divides by 1 000 gains full marks; the unit kWh must appear.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Energy in one day = **1.2 + 0.4 + 1.5 + 3.6 = 6.7 kWh**, so in 30 days = **201 kWh** (1 mark).
- Cost = **201 × GH¢1.50 = GH¢301.50** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Allow the candidate's own total from (b) to be carried forward; the second mark is for multiplying correctly by the tariff.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any one sensible change with a reason drawn from the table, for example **fit LED lamps in place of the filament lamps, because the lamps run for five hours a day** (1 mark).
- A second change with a reason, for example **keep the refrigerator door closed, defrost it and move it away from the cooker, because it runs for 24 hours and uses the most energy (3.6 kWh a day)** (accept: iron in bulk, since the iron has the highest power rating) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The reason must refer to the power rating or the hours of use shown in the table.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **The umbra (full or total shadow)** (1 mark).
- (ii) **The penumbra (partial shadow)** (1 mark).
- (iii) **A fully lit, bright part of the screen**, since light from the whole lamp reaches it (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Dark part' alone is not accepted for (i); the name is required.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Light travels in straight lines and the ball is opaque**, so it cuts off the light from every part of the lamp (1 mark).
- (ii) The **lamp is broad, so light comes from many points on it** (1 mark).
- (ii) At Q and R the ball **blocks the light from some parts of the lamp but not from others**, so these regions receive some light (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The idea of a broad source with many points is essential in (ii).*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The shadow becomes **larger (both the umbra and the penumbra widen)** (1 mark).
- Because the rays grazing the ball **travel a greater distance to the screen and so spread out more** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'the edges become less sharp' as part of the explanation.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **A sharp, completely dark shadow (umbra only), with no penumbra around it** (1 mark).
- Because a very small lamp is **a point source**: every point of the screen either sees the whole source or none of it (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who says the shadow disappears earns no mark.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) **The cutting off of the sun's light from one heavenly body by another**, so that it passes into a shadow (1 mark).
- (ii) **The moon is between the sun and the earth** (the three in a straight line), and the moon's shadow falls on the earth (1 mark).
- (iii) **The earth is between the sun and the moon**, and the earth's shadow falls on the moon (1 mark).
- (iv) Any one correct difference, for example **a solar eclipse is seen from only a small part of the earth and lasts a few minutes, while a lunar eclipse is seen from the whole night side and lasts much longer** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) and (iii) the order of the three bodies must be clearly stated.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) The **umbra of the moon's shadow covers only a small patch of the earth's surface** (1 mark).
- (i) **Only observers standing in that umbra see a total eclipse** (those in the penumbra see a partial one), and the patch moves quickly across the earth (1 mark).
- (ii) **Do not look at the sun directly; use a proper filter or view the image projected through a pinhole on to a card** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'the moon is much smaller than the earth' as part of the first mark in (i).*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- The three bodies drawn **in a straight line in the order sun, moon, earth** (1 mark).
- **Straight rays drawn from the sun grazing the edges of the moon** and continuing to the earth (1 mark).
- The **shadow on the earth shown and labelled (umbra, and penumbra around it)**, with all three bodies named (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Marks are for the physics, not for the quality of the drawing; the sizes and distances need not be to scale.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Apparatus and setting up** - a coin placed at the bottom of an opaque cup and the eye moved until the coin is just out of sight (or a straight stick stood slanting in a beaker) (1 mark).
- **What is done** - water is poured gently into the cup without moving the head or the coin (1 mark).
- **Observation** - the coin comes into view (or the stick appears bent at the water surface) (1 mark).
- **Conclusion** - **light changes its path (is refracted) when it passes from water into air**, so it does not travel in one straight line through the two media (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Any correct activity of the candidate's own is accepted, provided the method, the observation and the conclusion are all given.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- (i) **Refraction** (1 mark).
- (ii) **The speed of light changes in the new medium**, so a ray meeting the surface at an angle changes direction (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Do not accept 'reflection' in (i).*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Light from the fish **is refracted as it leaves the water, so the fish appears nearer the surface (shallower) than it really is** (1 mark).
- He should **aim below the image he sees** (accept: stand almost directly above the fish) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The idea that the apparent position is higher than the real position is essential for the first mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 4: Forces and Energy | **Sub-strand:** 1: Energy | **Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)

**Content Standard:** **B9/JHS3.4.1.1** - Show understanding of the concept of conservation of energy and ways of conserving energy. **B9/JHS3.4.1.2** - Demonstrate understanding in and the capability to do calculations involving energy. **B9/JHS3.4.1.3** - Evaluate the application of light energy in life.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 4: Forces and Energy, Sub-Strand 1: Energy, Basic 9, pages 107 and 108. Content standard B9/JHS3.4.1.1 carries indicator B9/JHS3.4.1.1.1, list the ways to conserve energy (examples: ironing in bulk, using energy-efficient appliances and switching off appliances when not in use), with the exemplar identify and discuss various strategies of conserving energy; and indicator B9/JHS3.4.1.1.2, explain the importance of energy conservation in daily life, with the exemplar research information about energy conservation and discuss its importance to life. Content standard B9/JHS3.4.1.2 carries indicator B9/JHS3.4.1.2.1, explain how to calculate energy consumed over a period of time, with the exemplar calculate electrical energy consumed by the use of electrical appliances in kilowatt-hour (kWh), P = IV, where P is power, I is current and V is voltage; indicator B9/JHS3.4.1.2.2, describe how images are formed in cameras, with the exemplar create a model of a camera and describe how it works to form an image; indicator B9/JHS3.4.1.2.3, describe the formation of shadows, with the exemplar discuss the terms umbra and penumbra in relation to the formation of shadows and explain how they are formed; and indicator B9/JHS3.4.1.2.4, demonstrate the formation of an eclipse, with the exemplar use a model to illustrate how an eclipse is formed. Content standard B9/JHS3.4.1.3 carries indicator B9/JHS3.4.1.3.1, demonstrate that light changes path when it travels from one medium to a different medium, with the exemplar carry out a practical activity to show that light bends as it travels from one medium to another, for example a rod appears bent in water and deep water appears shallower than its real depth.

> Note: I1 (B9/JHS3.4.1.1.1) carries topic 11.1 and Question 1(a) and (b); I2 (B9/JHS3.4.1.1.2) carries topic 11.2 and Question 1(c) and (d); I3 (B9/JHS3.4.1.2.1) carries topic 11.3 and Question 3; I4 (B9/JHS3.4.1.2.2) carries topic 11.4 and Question 2; I5 (B9/JHS3.4.1.2.3) carries topic 11.5 and Question 4; I6 (B9/JHS3.4.1.2.4) carries topic 11.6 and Question 5; and I7 (B9/JHS3.4.1.3.1) carries topic 11.7 and Question 6. This sub-strand places the conservation of energy, energy calculations and three applications of light energy under one heading, so the paper samples all seven indicators. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find these standards written as B9.4.1.1, B9.4.1.2 and B9.4.1.3.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This sub-strand is unusually wide: it joins the conservation of energy and energy calculations to three applications of light energy. The paper therefore samples all seven indicators rather than examining one of them deeply, and the weighting follows the number of indicators under each content standard.
- In Question 3 the marks are method marks. A candidate who writes energy = power × time and substitutes correctly keeps the first mark even if the arithmetic fails; the final mark is lost when the unit kWh is missing.
- Candidates commonly write that the pinhole camera gives a 'virtual' image. Insist on 'real', since the image is caught on a screen, and require the straight-line argument in Question 2(b)(ii).
- The words umbra and penumbra must be used in Question 4(a). 'Dark part' and 'light part' describe but do not name, and so earn no mark.
- In Question 5(c) credit the physics of the sketch, not the drawing: the straight line of the three bodies, the rays grazing the moon and the labelled shadow on the earth. Scale is not required and should not be rewarded or penalised.
- Question 6 rests on a practical activity. Candidates who have actually poured water over a hidden coin, or looked at a stick in a beaker, write the observation confidently; those who have only read about it usually omit the observation, which carries a mark of its own.
- Follow-up work: let each group build a pinhole camera from a shoe box and greaseproof paper, then read the meter at home for a week and work out the family's daily energy use in kWh and its cost, comparing the figure before and after the lamps are changed.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) In calculations, award the method mark for a correct formula or substitution even when the arithmetic that follows is wrong, and award the final mark only when the unit is given. (3) In circuit diagrams accept the standard symbols or clearly labelled drawings of the components; the circuit must be complete. (4) Accept 'bulb' for 'lamp' and 'battery' for 'cells'. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Electrical energy to light energy** (accept 'and heat') (1 mark).
- (ii) **Electrical energy to kinetic (mechanical) energy** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Electrical energy to heat energy** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The starting form, electrical energy, must be stated in at least one of the three answers for full credit.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- A **complete (closed) circuit** drawn as a single loop (1 mark).
- **Correct symbols for the cell and the switch** (1 mark).
- **Two lamps drawn one after the other in the same path (in series), all parts labelled** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept clearly labelled drawings of the components in place of the standard symbols; a circuit with a gap in it loses the first mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Arrangement or voltage:** in series the lamps are in one path and share the voltage; in parallel each lamp is across the supply and receives the full voltage (1 mark).
- **Effect of a break:** in series one broken lamp puts off all the lamps; in parallel the other lamps continue to work (accept the current comparison) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Each mark needs both sides of the comparison.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Each lamp **receives the full supply voltage and so lights normally, and each has its own switch** (1 mark).
- **A lamp that blows does not put out the other lamps**, since the other branches are still complete (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A bare statement 'parallel is better' earns no mark.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- W - **the battery (two cells)** (1 mark).
- Z - **the switch (open)** (1 mark).
- C - **the ammeter** (1 mark).
- D - **a lamp (bulb)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'cells' for W; do not accept 'voltmeter' for C.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **In parallel** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Lamp X continues to burn (stays on)** (1 mark).
- (ii) Because **its own branch is still a complete path from the battery**; only the branch carrying Y is broken (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It goes off' earns no mark, even with a good explanation.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Both X and Y go off** (1 mark).
- (i) Because **D is in series with the whole parallel section, so the only path from the battery is broken** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Electrical energy to light energy (and heat energy)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (i) the reason must mention that D is in the main line (in series).*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Correct formula and substitution: **V = IR = 1.5 × 6** (1 mark).
- **V = 9 V** (unit required) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Award the first mark for the correct substitution even if the arithmetic fails.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **V = IR** (1 mark).
- (ii) Current: **ampere (A)** (1 mark).
- (ii) Resistance: **ohm (Ω)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'amp' for ampere.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **I = V/R = 6/3 = 2 A** (1 mark).
- (ii) Total resistance = **3 + 3 = 6 Ω** (1 mark).
- (ii) **I = 6/6 = 1 A** (unit required) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who writes 1 A without showing the total resistance earns 1 mark only.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **R = V/I = 12/0.5** (1 mark).
- **R = 24 Ω** (unit required) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who writes 6 Ω (having multiplied) earns no marks.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **No / the pupil is wrong** (1 mark).
- **Reason:** I = V/R, so at the same voltage doubling the resistance **halves the current** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The reason mark requires the relation I = V/R or a clear statement of the inverse relationship.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- J - **a resistor** (1 mark).
- K - **a light-emitting diode (LED)** (1 mark).
- L - **the cells (battery)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'battery' for L; 'diode' alone for K earns the mark only if 'light-emitting' or LED is written.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Forward biased** (1 mark).
- (ii) The **positive terminal of the cells is connected to the anode of the LED** (the broad side of the triangle), so current flows in the direction in which the triangle points (1 mark).
- (ii) **The LED conducts and gives out light**, which happens only when it is forward biased (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept an answer argued from the observation (the LED lights, so it must be forward biased) for the second mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **The LED would not light (goes off)** (1 mark).
- Because it is now **reverse biased, and a diode conducts in one direction only**, so practically no current flows (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It will burn out' earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- (i) **To limit the current so that the LED is not damaged** (1 mark).
- (ii) **I = V/R = 1.2/60 = 0.02 A** (accept 20 mA; unit required) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (i) 'to increase the brightness' earns no mark.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **A component that allows current to flow in one direction only** (1 mark).
- (ii) **The positive of the supply is joined to the anode**, so the diode conducts (1 mark).
- (iii) **The positive of the supply is joined to the cathode**, so practically no current flows (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept answers written in terms of 'the way the cells are turned round' if the direction of conduction is clear.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Controls or limits the current** (opposes the flow of current) (1 mark).
- (ii) **Stores electric charge and releases it when needed** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Gives out light when current passes through it in the forward direction** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) 'stores electricity' is accepted.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **LED lamps give the same light for much less electrical energy** (a filament lamp wastes most of its energy as heat), so the bill falls (1 mark).
- **They last much longer** (accept: they run cool and are safer, or they suit a solar supply) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct reasons are required.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **The LED lights very brightly for a moment and is then damaged (burns out)**, because the current is not limited (1 mark).
- **A resistor should be connected in series with the LED** to limit the current to about 20 mA (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who says only 'it will spoil' without the idea of the large current earns 1 mark.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Set-up:** the cell, switch, lamp and diode joined in series in a complete circuit (1 mark).
- **Method:** close the switch and note the lamp; then turn the diode round (or turn the cell round), leaving everything else unchanged, and note the lamp again (1 mark).
- **Observation:** the lamp lights in one connection only and does not light in the other (1 mark).
- **Conclusion:** the diode **allows current in one direction only - it conducts when forward biased** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A group that turns the cell round instead of the diode gains the same marks.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Keep the switch open until the circuit has been checked, and never short-circuit the cell** (1 mark).
- **Use only the low-voltage cells supplied (never the mains), and disconnect the cell when the work is finished** (accept: include a series resistor with an LED; make clean tight connections) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct precautions are required.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **The circuit is not complete** - a loose or broken connection, or the switch left open (1 mark).
- **The cell is flat, the lamp's filament is broken, or the diode itself is damaged** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Two different reasons are required; 'the diode is reverse biased' cannot explain a failure in both connections and earns no mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 4: Forces and Energy | **Sub-strand:** 2: Electricity and Electronics | **Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)

**Content Standard:** **B9/JHS3.4.2.1** - Construct electrical circuits and illustrate how electrical energy is transformed into other forms of energy, and perform electrical calculations. **B9/JHS3.4.2.2** - Demonstrate an understanding of forward and reverse bias and explain the behaviour of LEDs, diodes, resistors and capacitors in electronic circuits.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 4: Forces and Energy, Sub-Strand 2: Electricity and Electronics, Basic 9, page 109. Content standard B9/JHS3.4.2.1 carries indicator B9/JHS3.4.2.1.1, demonstrate transformation of electrical energy to other forms of energy in both series and parallel circuits and perform simple calculations involving the flow of current in circuits, with the exemplars: predict the impact of changes in electrical circuits with regard to the output of bulbs and describe how electrical energy transformation occurs in series and parallel circuits; construct simple electrical circuits and measure the voltage, current and resistance; and calculate the potential difference in a circuit using the formula V = IR, where I is the current and R the resistance. Content standard B9/JHS3.4.2.2 carries indicator B9/JHS3.4.2.2.1, describe forward bias and reverse bias and explain the relationship among the components, such as LEDs, diodes, resistors and capacitors, in an electronic circuit, with the exemplars: explain forward bias and reverse bias in an electronic circuit; construct different electronic circuits (the forward and reverse bias) and observe what happens to the LED; and construct different electronic circuits involving resistors and capacitors, observe what happens to the LED and report on the findings.

> Note: I1 (B9/JHS3.4.2.1.1) carries topics 12.1 to 12.4 and Questions 1, 2 and 3; I2 (B9/JHS3.4.2.2.1) carries topics 12.5 and 12.6 and Questions 4, 5 and 6. Both indicators are written round practical construction of circuits, so Question 2 and Question 4 are set on circuit diagrams and Question 6 is a bench task. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find these standards written as B9.4.2.1 and B9.4.2.2.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- The curriculum limits the calculations in this sub-strand to the relation V = IR and to simple series and parallel reasoning. Nothing in this paper requires the formula for resistors in parallel, and candidates should not be expected to use it.
- In Question 1(b) the mark for a complete circuit is the one most often lost: many candidates draw the symbols correctly but leave a gap in the loop. Mark the loop first, then the symbols.
- Question 2 rewards reasoning rather than recall. In (b)(ii) and (c)(i) the statement and the reason carry separate marks, and a wrong statement cannot be rescued by a good reason.
- Candidates frequently reverse the relation in Question 3(c), writing R = VI. Award no marks for 6 ohms, but award the first mark wherever R = V/I is written, even if the division is then done wrongly.
- In Question 4(b) accept either line of argument: the physical one from the direction of the triangle and the positive terminal, or the observational one from the fact that the LED is alight. Both are sound at this level.
- The word 'bias' is new to many candidates. Encourage the plain form of words: forward bias is the way round that lets the current through, reverse bias is the way round that blocks it.
- Follow-up work: give each group an LED, a 100 ohm resistor, a switch and two cells, and let them build the circuit of Fig. 2, reverse the cells, and then add a large capacitor across the LED to see it fade slowly after the switch is opened. Each group should report its findings to the class, as the exemplar requires.

| 1 (a) | (i) Conversion of energy is the change of energy from one form into another form. (ii) Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be changed from one form into another, so the total energy remains the same. (iii) The joule (J). | The Law of Conservation of Energy | Remember |
| 1 (b) | (i) Light (solar) energy into electrical energy. (ii) Light energy into chemical energy stored in the food. (iii) Potential energy into kinetic energy. | Conversion of Energy from One Form to Another | Understand |
| 1 (c) | Chemical energy in the cells changes into electrical energy in the circuit, and the electrical energy changes into light energy (and some heat energy) in the lamp: chemical → electrical → light (and heat). | Conversion of Energy from One Form to Another | Apply |
| 1 (d) | Conversion is the change of energy from one form into another, for example the electrical energy supplied to a fan changing into kinetic energy. Conservation is the careful use of energy so that none is wasted, for example switching off the fan and the lights when the room is empty, or ironing all the clothes at one time. | Energy Conversion Compared with Energy Conservation | Understand |
| 2 (a) | A - the water stored in the reservoir (the lake behind the dam); B - the dam wall; C - the pipe (penstock) that carries the water down to the machines; E - the generator. | Application of Conversion and Conservation in Life | Remember |
| 2 (b) | (i) Potential energy, because the water is stored high above the machines. (ii) The potential energy changes into kinetic energy as the water falls and speeds up. (iii) The kinetic energy of the water is changed into the mechanical (rotational kinetic) energy of the turbine. (iv) The mechanical energy of the shaft is changed into electrical energy. | Application of Conversion and Conservation in Life | Understand |
| 2 (c) | No energy is created or destroyed anywhere in the station: the potential energy given up by the falling water is equal to the electrical energy sent out plus all the energy that is wasted as heat in the bearings and the wires, as sound in the power house and as the kinetic energy of the water that flows away. | The Law of Conservation of Energy | Understand |
| 2 (d) | The water is a renewable source that is not bought, so after the dam has been built the running cost is low, while diesel must be bought continually and its price rises; the station gives off no smoke and no carbon dioxide, so the air stays clean, while a diesel set pollutes the air and is noisy; the supply can be very large and steady; and the reservoir can also serve for fishing, water supply and transport. | Application of Conversion and Conservation in Life | Evaluate |
| 3 (a) | (i) The law of conservation of energy: the total energy leaving the motor must equal the energy supplied to it. (ii) Q = 1 000 - (600 + 50) = 1 000 - 650 = 350 J. | The Law of Conservation of Energy | Apply |
| 3 (b) | (i) The 600 J of kinetic energy, which lifts the load. (ii) The 50 J of sound energy and the 350 J of heat energy. (iii) 600/1 000 × 100 = 60 per cent. | The Law of Conservation of Energy | Analyse |
| 3 (c) | Oil and grease the bearings and the moving parts regularly so that there is less friction; tighten loose parts and fit the belt properly so that there is less rubbing and less noise; keep the motor clean and well ventilated so that it does not overheat; service it regularly; and replace a very old motor with a modern, more efficient one of the right size for the job. | The Law of Conservation of Energy | Apply |
| 3 (d) | Energy cannot be destroyed. The 400 J has not disappeared: it has been changed into 350 J of heat and 50 J of sound, which spread into the surroundings. The energy is wasted, not destroyed, because it is now in forms that cannot be used for lifting the load. | Energy Conversion Compared with Energy Conservation | Evaluate |
| 4 (a) | (i) Light (solar) energy is changed into electrical energy. (ii) Electrical energy is changed into chemical energy stored in the battery. (iii) The chemical energy is changed back into electrical energy and then into light energy (and a little heat). | Application of Conversion and Conservation in Life | Understand |
| 4 (b) | (i) Chemical energy in the petrol is changed into heat energy, then into the kinetic energy of the moving parts, and then into electrical energy. (ii) A great deal of the heat escapes with the exhaust gases and through the cooling of the engine; energy is lost in overcoming friction in the engine and the generator, and as sound and vibration; and more is lost as heat in the wires on the way to the lamps. | Application of Conversion and Conservation in Life | Understand |
| 4 (c) | Sunshine is plentiful all the year round and costs nothing once the system has been bought, while petrol and diesel must be bought and their prices rise; renewable sources will not run out, unlike crude oil; they give off no smoke, carbon dioxide or noise, so the air stays clean and climate change is slowed; and they can serve villages that are far from the national grid. | Application of Conversion and Conservation in Life | Understand |
| 4 (d) | Advise the solar home system: the sun shines strongly at Bolgatanga for most of the year and costs nothing, so after the first payment the lamps run almost free, the system is silent and gives off no fumes, and LED lamps need very little energy. The difficulty is that the panel gives no energy at night or on heavily clouded days, so the battery must be large enough and must be cared for and replaced in time; the first cost is also high. | Application of Conversion and Conservation in Life | Evaluate |
| 5 (a) | Walk through every room and list all the appliances, writing down the power rating of each and the number of hours it is used each day; read the electricity meter at the same time each day for a week to find how many units are used; note the places where energy is being wasted, such as lamps and fans left on in empty rooms, security lamps burning in the daytime, old filament bulbs and faulty switches; work out the energy used by each appliance in kWh and its cost; then write a short report with a table of the findings, the recommended changes and the saving expected, and present it to the headteacher. | Finding Opportunities to Conserve Energy and Reporting on Them | Create |
| 5 (b) | Lamps and fans left on in empty classrooms - fit a notice and make each class monitor responsible for switching off; security lamps burning in the daytime - fit a timer or a light-sensitive switch; old filament bulbs - replace them with LED lamps; air conditioners in the computer room left on at night - fit a timer and keep doors and windows closed while they run; a leaking hot water tap or a faulty kettle - repair it; and daytime lessons held with the lights on - open the curtains and use daylight. | Finding Opportunities to Conserve Energy and Reporting on Them | Apply |
| 5 (c) | (i) Filament lamps: 20 × 100 W = 2 000 W = 2 kW; energy = 2 × 5 = 10 kWh a day. LED lamps: 20 × 10 W = 200 W = 0.2 kW; energy = 0.2 × 5 = 1 kWh a day. Saving = 10 - 1 = 9 kWh a day. (ii) In 30 days = 9 × 30 = 270 kWh; money saved = 270 × GH¢1.50 = GH¢405.00. | Finding Opportunities to Conserve Energy and Reporting on Them | Evaluate |
| 6 (a) | For example, a bicycle dynamo demonstration: clamp the back wheel of a bicycle off the ground, press the dynamo against the tyre and connect it to a small lamp; turn the pedals faster and faster and the lamp lights more brightly. The kinetic (mechanical) energy of the turning wheel is changed into electrical energy in the dynamo and then into light energy in the lamp. (Accept any sound alternative: rubbing the palms together to show kinetic energy changing into heat; a dry cell, switch and lamp for chemical to electrical to light; a stone released from a height for potential to kinetic; or a toy windmill turned by a fan.) | Conversion of Energy from One Form to Another | Create |
| 6 (b) | Use only low-voltage cells or a dynamo and never the mains supply; keep water and wet hands away from the electrical parts; clamp the apparatus firmly and keep fingers, hair and clothing away from turning wheels and belts; do not touch hot parts and allow them to cool before handling; and keep the bench tidy, with visitors behind a line. | Finding Opportunities to Conserve Energy and Reporting on Them | Understand |

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) In an energy chain the forms must be written in the correct order; a chain in the wrong order earns no mark. (3) In calculations, award the method mark for a correct statement or substitution even when the arithmetic that follows is wrong, and award the final mark only when the unit is given. (4) Accept 'movement energy' for kinetic energy and 'stored energy of position' for gravitational potential energy. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **The change of energy from one form into another** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, but only changed from one form to another** (1 mark).
- (iii) **The joule (J)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) the words 'created' and 'destroyed' (or an equivalent statement that the total energy stays the same) are required.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Light (solar) energy to electrical energy** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Light energy to chemical energy** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Potential energy to kinetic energy** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Both the starting form and the final form are needed in each answer.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Chemical → electrical** (1 mark).
- **→ light energy (and some heat)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A chain written in the wrong order earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Conversion:** a change of energy from one form to another, with a correct example (for example electrical energy to kinetic energy in a fan) (1 mark).
- **Conservation:** using energy carefully so that none is wasted, with a correct example (for example switching off lamps in an empty room) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Each mark needs both the meaning and the example.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- A - **the water stored in the reservoir (lake)** (1 mark).
- B - **the dam (dam wall)** (1 mark).
- C - **the pipe that carries the water down (penstock)** (1 mark).
- E - **the generator** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'alternator' for E and 'water pipe' for C.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **Potential energy (stored energy of position)** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Potential energy changing into kinetic energy** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Kinetic energy of the water changed into mechanical (turning) energy of the wheel** (1 mark).
- (iv) **Mechanical energy changed into electrical energy** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'movement energy' for kinetic energy throughout.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **No energy is created or destroyed; it is only changed in form** (1 mark).
- The energy given up by the falling water **equals the electrical energy sent out plus the energy wasted as heat, sound and the motion of the water leaving** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The second mark requires the idea that the wasted energy must be included in the account.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **The water is free and renewable, so the running cost is low**, while diesel must be bought and its price keeps rising (1 mark).
- **It gives off no smoke or carbon dioxide and little noise**, so it does not pollute the air (accept: the reservoir also serves for fishing, water supply and transport) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct reasons are required.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **The law of conservation of energy** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Q = 1 000 - (600 + 50)** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Q = 350 J** (unit required) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Award the method mark for the correct subtraction even if the arithmetic fails.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **The 600 J of kinetic energy** (1 mark).
- (ii) **The sound energy (50 J) and the heat energy (350 J)** (1 mark).
- (iii) **600/1 000 × 100 = 60%** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) both wasted outputs are needed for the mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Oil or grease the bearings and moving parts to reduce friction** (1 mark).
- **Tighten and service the machine regularly, keep it clean and cool, or fit a modern motor of the right size** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct practical suggestions are required.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Energy cannot be destroyed** - the law of conservation of energy (1 mark).
- The 400 J has been **changed into heat and sound that spread into the surroundings; it is wasted, not destroyed** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who merely repeats the law without applying it to the 400 J earns 1 mark.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Light energy to electrical energy** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Electrical energy to chemical energy** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Chemical (then electrical) energy to light energy** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (iii) accept 'electrical energy to light energy'.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Chemical → heat → kinetic → electrical energy** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Much of the heat escapes in the exhaust gases and in cooling the engine** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Energy is lost to friction, sound and vibration, and as heat in the wires** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (i) accept the shorter chain 'chemical to electrical' only if heat or motion is mentioned somewhere in the answer.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **The sun is free and will not run out**, while fuels must be bought and are non-renewable (1 mark).
- **No smoke, carbon dioxide or noise is produced**, so the air stays clean (accept: it can serve places far from the grid) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct reasons are required.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **The solar home system**, because the energy from the sun is free and plentiful, there is no fuel to buy, and LED lamps need very little energy (1 mark).
- Difficulty: **the panel gives no energy at night or on cloudy days, so a battery must be bought, cared for and replaced** (accept: the first cost is high) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who chooses the generating set may earn both marks if the reason and the difficulty are sound and based on energy.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **List the appliances room by room with their power ratings and the hours they are used** (1 mark).
- **Read the meter regularly (for example at the same time each day for a week) to find the units used** (1 mark).
- **Note where energy is wasted** - lamps and fans left on in empty rooms, security lamps burning by day, old filament bulbs, faulty switches (1 mark).
- **Work out the energy and cost and write a report with a table of findings and recommendations** for the headteacher (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Marks are for the steps of the survey; the order need not be exactly as in the scheme.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Any one opportunity with its action, for example **lamps and fans left on in empty rooms - appoint a monitor to switch them off** (1 mark).
- A second, for example **security lamps burning by day - fit a timer or a light-sensitive switch** (1 mark).
- A third, for example **old filament bulbs - replace them with LED lamps** (accept: use daylight, service the air conditioners, repair faults) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Each mark needs both the opportunity and the action; a bare list of places earns no mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) Filament lamps use **2 kW × 5 h = 10 kWh** and the LED lamps **0.2 kW × 5 h = 1 kWh** (1 mark).
- (i) Saving = **10 - 1 = 9 kWh each day** (1 mark).
- (ii) **9 × 30 × GH¢1.50 = GH¢405.00** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Allow the candidate's own daily saving to be carried forward into (ii).*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Apparatus** clearly named, for example a bicycle with a dynamo, a small lamp and connecting wires (1 mark).
- **What is done** - the wheel is turned (the pedals are worked) so that the dynamo is driven (1 mark).
- **Observation** - the lamp lights, and more brightly as the wheel turns faster (1 mark).
- **Energy conversion shown** - **kinetic (mechanical) energy → electrical energy → light energy** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Any correct demonstration of the candidate's own is accepted provided all four points are given.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Use only low-voltage cells or a dynamo, never the mains, and keep water away from the electrical parts** (1 mark).
- **Clamp the apparatus firmly and keep fingers, hair and clothing away from turning parts** (accept: do not touch hot parts; keep visitors behind a line) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct rules are required.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Wasted energy is changed into heat and sound that spread out and cannot easily be used again** (1 mark).
- **The energy supplied must be paid for and comes largely from limited sources**, so waste costs money, uses up fuel and adds to pollution (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A simple restatement of the law of conservation of energy, without the idea of usefulness or cost, earns no mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 4: Forces and Energy | **Sub-strand:** 3: Conversion and Conservation of Energy | **Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)

**Content Standard:** **B9/JHS3.4.3.1** - Show an understanding of conversion and conservation of energy and their application to life.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 4: Forces and Energy, Sub-Strand 3: Conversion and Conservation of Energy, Basic 9, page 110. Content standard B9/JHS3.4.3.1 carries indicator B9/JHS3.4.3.1.1, describe how energy can be converted from one form to another and show how conservation of energy occurs, with the exemplar differentiate between conversion of energy and conservation of energy and show their application to life; and indicator B9/JHS3.4.3.1.2, describe how conversion and conservation of energy are applied in life, with the exemplars distinguish between energy conversion and conservation using everyday examples, and identify opportunities to conserve energy and produce a report of your work.

> Note: I1 (B9/JHS3.4.3.1.1) carries topics 13.1 to 13.4 and Questions 1, 2 and 3; I2 (B9/JHS3.4.3.1.2) carries topics 13.5 and 13.6 and Questions 4, 5 and 6. The two indicators of this sub-strand turn on one distinction - conversion is a change of form, conservation is the avoidance of waste - so that distinction is examined directly in Question 1(d) and again through examples in Questions 4 and 5. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find this standard written as B9.4.3.1.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- The whole sub-strand turns on one distinction, and it is the distinction candidates most often miss: conversion is a change of form, conservation is the avoidance of waste. Questions 1(d), 3(d) and 6(c) each test it from a different side, and a candidate who confuses the two words will lose marks in all three.
- Energy chains must be written in the right order. 'Chemical, light, electrical' for a torch earns nothing, however well the forms are named.
- In Question 3 the arithmetic is easy; the marks are really for applying the law of conservation of energy. Insist that candidates account for every joule that enters the motor.
- Question 5(c) is the only extended calculation. Watch for candidates who find the energy used by one lamp and forget that there are twenty, and for those who forget to subtract the energy still used by the LED lamps.
- Several Section A items use situations from everyday Ghanaian life - the clay stove, drying clothes in the sun, the biogas plant. Candidates should be encouraged to answer from what they see at home rather than from memorised lists.
- In Question 6(a) credit a demonstration of the candidate's own design. The four marks are for the apparatus, the action, the observation and the named conversion, and the last of these is the one most often left out.
- Follow-up work: let each class read the school meter at the same hour for two weeks, introduce one change in the second week, and then plot the daily units for the two weeks on the same graph. The report required by the indicator should carry that graph and the money saved.

| 4 (c) | A swimmer pushes the water backwards with her hands and feet and the water pushes her forwards; a gun pushes the bullet forward and the bullet pushes the gun backwards, so it recoils; a person stepping out of a canoe pushes the canoe backwards and the canoe pushes the person forwards; a rocket pushes the hot gases downwards and the gases push the rocket upwards; a person walking pushes backwards on the ground and the ground pushes them forwards. | Newton's Third Law: Action and Reaction | Apply |

Whatever the size of the pull, the two readings are always the same, although the pulls are in opposite directions - even when only one pupil pulls and the other merely holds. The conclusion is that the force exerted by the first body on the second is equal in size and opposite in direction to the force exerted by the second on the first, which is Newton's third law. (Accept equally: two pupils on trolleys or skateboards pushing each other apart and moving in opposite directions; or the balloon rocket of Fig. 2.) | Newton's Third Law: Action and Reaction | Create |
| 6 (b) | Check that each spring balance reads zero before the pull begins and that both are of the same range; take both readings at the same moment, while the pull is steady, and read them at eye level to avoid parallax; keep the balances in a straight line along the direction of the pull; do not pull beyond the range of the balances; and repeat the activity with different pulls to be sure the result always holds. | Newton's Third Law: Action and Reaction | Understand |
| 6 (c) | The prediction was wrong. The two balances always show the same reading, because the force the first pupil exerts on the second is matched by an equal and opposite force exerted by the second on the first. Being stronger does not make the pair of forces unequal; it only decides how hard the pull can become, and both readings rise together. What the stronger pupil can do is move the other one, because the forces act on different bodies and the other pupil's footing gives way first. | Newton's Third Law: Action and Reaction | Evaluate |

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) In calculations, award the method mark for a correct formula or substitution even when the arithmetic that follows is wrong, and award the final mark only when the unit is given. (3) Accept Pa or N/m² for the unit of pressure. (4) In explanations about pressure the idea of the AREA of contact must appear; an answer that speaks only of force earns half the available marks at most. (5) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **The force acting at right angles on each unit area of a surface** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Pressure = force ÷ area** (accept P = F/A) (1 mark).
- (iii) **The pascal (Pa)** (accept N/m²) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (i) 'force per unit area' is sufficient.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) The sharp edge has a **very small area**, so the same force gives a **large pressure** and cuts easily (1 mark).
- (ii) Wide tyres **spread the weight over a large area**, so the pressure on the soil is small and the tractor does not sink (1 mark).
- (iii) The wide foundation **spreads the load over a greater area of soil**, reducing the pressure on it (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Each mark requires the area of contact to be mentioned.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Sucking **lowers the air pressure inside the straw** (1 mark).
- The **greater atmospheric pressure on the surface of the drink pushes the drink up the straw** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: An answer that says the straw 'pulls' or 'sucks' the drink up, with no mention of pressure, earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Activity clearly described**, for example pressing a drawing pin between the thumb and the finger, or pressing a nail and a coin into clay with the same force (1 mark).
- **Observation given**, for example the point hurts (or sinks in) far more than the head, showing that the smaller area gives the greater pressure (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The observation mark is lost if the candidate only names an activity.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) **Area = 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.24 m²** (1 mark).
- (i) **Pressure = 480 ÷ 0.24 = 2 000 Pa** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Area = 0.4 × 0.2 = 0.08 m²** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Pressure = 480 ÷ 0.08 = 6 000 Pa** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The units m² and Pa are required; accept N/m².*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Position Q** (1 mark).
- (ii) The **force (weight) is the same in both positions** (1 mark).
- (ii) But in Q the **area of contact is smaller (0.08 m² against 0.24 m²)**, and pressure = force ÷ area, so the pressure is three times as great (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who says the block 'is heavier' in Q loses both explanation marks.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **The block will sink into the ground** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Lay it on its largest face (position P)** - the larger area lowers the pressure (1 mark).
- (ii) **Stand it on a wide flat board or slab** - this spreads the weight over a greater area and lowers the pressure (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Each suggestion must be accompanied by the reason in terms of area.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **4 000 Pa** (1 mark).
- Because **the area is unchanged and the force is doubled, so the pressure is doubled** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A correct long calculation (960 ÷ 0.24) also earns both marks.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Pressure = 600 ÷ 0.3** (1 mark).
- (i) **= 2 000 Pa** (unit required) (1 mark).
- (ii) **Force = 5 000 × 0.2 = 1 000 N** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Award the first mark for the correct substitution even if the division fails.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Pressure = 500 ÷ 0.05** (1 mark).
- (i) **= 10 000 Pa** (1 mark).
- (ii) **It doubles (to 20 000 Pa)**, because the area is halved while the weight is unchanged (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) 'it increases' alone earns the mark only if the reason or the value is given.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The water leaves through a **much smaller area** and so moves faster (1 mark).
- The force of the jet acting on that **small area gives a much greater pressure**, which drives the mud off (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The idea of the smaller area is essential.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **Yes - letting out a little air makes the tyre flatten and touch the sand over a larger area**, so the pressure on the sand is lower (1 mark).
- **But only a little, and the tyres must be pumped up again before he returns to the road**, since very soft tyres wear quickly and are unsafe (accept: he could reduce the load) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who answers 'no' may earn the second mark for a sound safety argument, but not the first.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction** (1 mark).
- (ii) P - **the action: the balloon pushes the air backwards** (1 mark).
- (ii) Q - **the reaction: the air pushes the balloon forwards with an equal and opposite force** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept the naming the other way round if the candidate makes clear which force acts on which body.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) The **balloon pushes the air backwards and the air pushes the balloon forwards with an equal and opposite force** (1 mark).
- (i) The forward force **acts on the balloon**, and friction on the string is small, so the balloon moves forward (1 mark).
- (ii) **It would move faster** (and empty sooner), since the forward force is greater (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (i) the second mark depends on the candidate noting that the two forces act on different bodies.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- One correct example with both forces named, for example **a swimmer pushes the water back; the water pushes the swimmer forward** (1 mark).
- A second correct example with both forces named, for example **a gun pushes the bullet forward; the bullet pushes the gun back (recoil)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: An example named without its pair of forces earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Forces **cancel only when they act on the same body** (1 mark).
- Here **the action acts on the air and the reaction on the balloon**, so the balloon has an unbalanced forward force and moves (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The idea of two different bodies is essential for the first mark.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **A body stays at rest or moves with uniform velocity in a straight line unless an external force acts on it** (1 mark).
- (ii) **The rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of the force** (accept: the acceleration produced is proportional to the force and inversely proportional to the mass) (1 mark).
- (iii) **f = ma** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept the second law stated in the acceleration form at this level.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) **a = f/m = 120/40** (1 mark).
- (i) **a = 3 m/s²** (unit required) (1 mark).
- (ii) **f = 40 × 5 = 200 N** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Award the method mark wherever f = ma is correctly rearranged.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- (i) The passengers **were moving forward and, by their inertia, continued to move forward when the vehicle stopped** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Wearing a seat belt** (accept head rests, air bags, securing loads, driving at a moderate speed) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The word inertia is not required if the idea is clear.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- (i) **Momentum = mass × velocity** (1 mark).
- (ii) The loaded vehicle has **greater mass and so greater momentum, needing a larger force (or a longer time and distance) to stop** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'It is heavier' alone, without momentum or force, earns no mark in (ii).*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- **Apparatus** named, for example two spring balances hooked together (or two trolleys and two pupils) (1 mark).
- **Method** - the two pupils pull in opposite directions and both balances are read at the same moment (1 mark).
- **Observation** - the two readings are always equal, however hard they pull (the trolleys move apart in opposite directions) (1 mark).
- **Conclusion** - **the two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction**, which justifies Newton's third law (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Any sound activity of the candidate's own design is accepted if all four points are given.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Check the zero of each balance and read both at the same moment at eye level** (1 mark).
- **Keep the balances in line with the pull, do not exceed their range, and repeat with different pulls** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct precautions are required.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **The prediction was wrong - both balances read the same** (1 mark).
- Because **the force of the first pupil on the second is equal and opposite to the force of the second on the first**; being stronger only decides how large that pair of forces becomes (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A candidate who says the prediction was right earns no mark, however the answer is argued.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 4: Forces and Energy | **Sub-strand:** 4: Force and Motion | **Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)

**Content Standard:** **B9/JHS3.4.4.1** - Demonstrate understanding of the concept of pressure and explain how pressure acts in everyday life. **B9/JHS3.4.4.2** - Demonstrate understanding of Newton's laws of motion and ability to apply the laws to solve problems in everyday life.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 4: Forces and Energy, Sub-Strand 4: Force and Motion, Basic 9, pages 111 and 112. Content standard B9/JHS3.4.4.1 carries indicator B9/JHS3.4.4.1.1, explain the concept of pressure and show how pressure relates to force and perform activities that work on the principle of pressure in the daily lives of humans, with the exemplars: demonstrate the action of pressure through a number of activities such as using a drinking straw, pumping car tyres, filling of balloons and water jets at washing bays; and describe the relationship between pressure and force and discuss the application of pressure in everyday life. The same content standard carries indicator B9/JHS3.4.4.1.2, demonstrate the application of Newton's third law of motion in life, with the exemplars: predict what happens when (a) a force is exerted on an object, (b) there is a reaction from the object, and (c) the force exerted is the same as the reaction of the object; and perform an activity to justify your predictions. Content standard B9/JHS3.4.4.2 carries indicator B9/JHS3.4.4.2.1, explain Newton's laws of motion and their applications to daily life, with the exemplars: explain Newton's laws of motion and relate them to momentum; demonstrate the application of Newton's laws of motion in everyday life; and derive the formula f = ma, where f is the force, m the mass of the object and a the acceleration, from Newton's three laws of motion, and use the formula to calculate the force that a moving mass of a body exerts when moving with known acceleration.

> Note: I1 (B9/JHS3.4.4.1.1) carries topics 14.1 to 14.3 and Questions 1, 2 and 3; I2 (B9/JHS3.4.4.1.2) carries topic 14.4 and Questions 4 and 6; I3 (B9/JHS3.4.4.2.1) carries topics 14.5 and 14.6 and Question 5. The published curriculum places the indicator on Newton's third law (B9/JHS3.4.4.1.2) under the pressure content standard and states the importance of the third law under B9/JHS3.4.4.2.1 as well; this paper therefore examines pressure and all three laws of motion, which together make up the sub-strand. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find these standards written as B9.4.4.1 and B9.4.4.2.

| Diagrams supplied as hand-drawn (pencil) figures | Yes - Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 |
| Figure labels do not reveal the answers | Yes - the two positions are lettered P and Q, and the forces in Fig. 2 are lettered P and Q without being named |
| Original items, no reproduction of official BECE or WAEC questions | Yes |
| British spellings and NaCCA terminology | Yes |

### EXAMINER NOTES

- The published curriculum numbers the indicator on Newton's third law (B9/JHS3.4.4.1.2) under the pressure content standard, and states the third law again under B9/JHS3.4.4.2.1. The paper therefore covers pressure and all three laws of motion; teachers should not be surprised to meet both topics in one sub-strand.
- In every explanation about pressure the area of contact must be mentioned. Answers such as 'the knife has more force' are the commonest way of losing marks in Question 1(b) and Question 2(b).
- Question 2 is the heart of the paper: the same block, the same weight, two different areas. Candidates who divide by the wrong area usually have not read the dimensions from the figure, so remind classes to write down the face they are using before they calculate.
- Units are part of the answer. A pressure written as '2 000' without Pa or N/m² loses the final mark, as does an acceleration without m/s².
- In Question 4(d) and Question 6(c) the same misconception is tested from two sides: that action and reaction cancel. The answer always turns on the two forces acting on different bodies, and nothing less earns the mark.
- The second law may be stated in the momentum form or in the acceleration form. Basic 9 candidates usually give the acceleration form, and this is accepted; the relation f = ma must, however, be written correctly.
- Follow-up work: let each group press a drawing pin and then a coin into a block of clay with the same force and measure the depth of each mark; then hook two spring balances together and tabulate the pairs of readings for five different pulls. The two sets of results cover both halves of this sub-strand.

| 1 (a) | (i) The hoe is used for weeding and for making mounds, ridges and seedbeds. (ii) The hand trowel is used for lifting and transplanting seedlings and for digging small holes. (iii) The rake is used for levelling the seedbed and for gathering dry leaves and rubbish. (iv) The wheelbarrow is used for carrying manure, soil, seedlings and harvested produce about the garden. | Simple Agricultural Tools and Their Uses | Remember |
| 1 (b) | A pair of secateurs (pruning shears). Its short, strong, curved blades cut a branch cleanly in one movement without tearing the bark, and it can be used with one hand close to the trunk. | Simple Agricultural Tools and Their Uses | Understand |
| 1 (c) | Cutlass: the blade is made of steel (hardened iron) and the handle of wood (or hard plastic or rubber). Hoe: the blade is made of steel or iron and the handle of wood (or bamboo). | Materials Used in Making Simple Tools | Understand |
| 2 (a) | A is the handle; B is a rivet; C is the tang; D is the blade; E is the cutting edge. | Connecting the Parts of a Tool | Remember |
| 2 (b) | (i) Part D is made of steel. Steel is hard and strong, so it can be sharpened and will keep its cutting edge without breaking. (ii) A handle of steel would be heavy, slippery and would become hot or cold and tiring to hold; wood is lighter, warmer to the hand and gives a firmer grip. | Connecting the Parts of a Tool | Understand |
| 2 (c) | The tang, which is the narrow part of the blade, is passed between (or into) the two pieces of the handle, and holes are drilled through the handle and the tang. Rivets are then driven through the holes and hammered flat so that the handle is gripped tightly on the tang and cannot come off. | Connecting the Parts of a Tool | Understand |
| 2 (d) | The rivets holding the handle to the tang have worked loose (or the wood has dried and shrunk away from the tang), so the handle is no longer gripped tightly. It can be corrected by hammering the rivets tight again, or by fitting new rivets, or by replacing the worn handle with a new, well-seasoned one that fits the tang closely. | Connecting the Parts of a Tool | Analyse |
| 3 (a) | L is the head (the cross bar) of the rake. J, the handle, is made of wood (or bamboo); K is made of wire; M, the teeth, are made of iron nails. | Materials Used in Making Simple Tools | Remember |
| 3 (b) | K binds the handle tightly to the head so that the two parts do not separate or twist when the rake is pulled through the soil. In its place the handle could have been nailed or screwed to the head, bolted to it, or fitted into a socket and wedged. | Connecting the Parts of a Tool | Understand |
| 3 (c) | Let a pupil pull the rake through a loose bed of soil and over a heap of dry leaves several times. If the teeth stay straight and firmly fixed, the joint between the handle and the head stays tight, and the leaves and loose soil are gathered easily, the tool is well made. | Making, Testing and Caring for Tools | Apply |
| 3 (d) | Use thicker and harder nails (or short lengths of steel rod) for the teeth; drive the teeth deeper into the head and set them closer together so that each tooth carries less load; shorten the teeth so that they bend less; and use a harder wood for the head so that the teeth are held more firmly. | Making, Testing and Caring for Tools | Evaluate |
| 4 (a) | The correct order is R, Q, T, S, P: measure and mark out, heat the metal, beat it to shape, sharpen and smooth it, then fit the handle. The process described in T is forging. | Processes Involved in Making a Tool | Understand |
| 4 (b) | (i) Heating makes the metal soft so that it can be beaten into shape without breaking. (ii) Cooling it quickly (quenching) makes the blade hard so that it keeps its edge, and warming it again gently (tempering) takes away some of the brittleness so that the blade does not snap. (iii) Seasoned wood has already lost its moisture, so the handle will not shrink, crack or become loose in the eye of the blade. | Processes Involved in Making a Tool | Understand |
| 4 (c) | The springs are cheap and easily obtained as scrap in the town, so the hoe costs less to make; they are made of good steel that hardens well and gives a strong blade; and using them turns waste metal into something useful instead of leaving it to litter the environment. | Processes Involved in Making a Tool | Understand |

Keep the workshop tidy and well ventilated, and carry sharp tools with the edge pointing down and away from the body. Work only under the teacher's supervision and report every injury at once. | Constraints and Precautions in Making Tools | Understand |

The class could look for scrap steel instead, such as old vehicle springs, a worn hoe blade or a piece of drum sheet; they could ask a local blacksmith or the nearby technical school for a piece of mild steel or for help in forging; they could make fewer trowels with the steel they can obtain; or they could strengthen the aluminium by folding and riveting it over a steel strip. | Constraints and Precautions in Making Tools | Evaluate |

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Accept the local name of a tool (for example matchet or machete for cutlass) provided the tool meant is clear. (3) In questions on materials, a mark is earned only when the material is named AND a property or reason is given, where the question asks for a reason. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Diagrams need not be works of art; marks are for correct shape, correct joining of the parts and correct labels. (6) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) **Weeding / making mounds, ridges or seedbeds** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Lifting and transplanting seedlings / digging small holes** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Levelling the seedbed / gathering dry leaves and rubbish** (1 mark).
- (iv) **Carrying manure, soil or produce about the garden** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: One correct use is enough in each case.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Tool: **a pair of secateurs** (accept pruning shears or pruning saw) (1 mark).
- Reason: it **cuts the small branches cleanly without tearing the bark**, and it can be worked with one hand (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept any sensible reason that fits the tool named.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- Cutlass - working part: **steel** (accept hardened iron) (1 mark); handle: **wood** (accept hard plastic or rubber) (1 mark).
- Hoe - working part: **steel or iron** (1 mark); handle: **wood** (accept bamboo) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The table must be copied; a list of four materials in the right order also earns the marks.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [5 marks]

- A - **handle** (1 mark).
- B - **rivet** (accept bolt or pin) (1 mark).
- C - **tang** (the part of the blade that runs inside the handle) (1 mark).
- D - **blade** (1 mark).
- E - **cutting edge** (accept sharpened edge) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: One mark for each correctly named part; no half marks.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) Material: **steel** (accept hardened iron) (1 mark); property: **hard and strong, takes and keeps a sharp edge** (1 mark).
- (ii) A steel handle would be **heavy, slippery and hot or cold to hold**, while wood is light, warm and easy to grip (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) any one clear comparison between the two materials earns the mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- The **tang of the blade is fitted into (or between) the handle** (1 mark).
- **Rivets (or bolts) are passed through holes in the handle and the tang and hammered tight** to hold the two parts firmly (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept a clear labelled sketch in place of words.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Cause: **the rivets have become loose / the wooden handle has shrunk or worn** so that it no longer grips the tang (1 mark).
- Correction: **tighten or replace the rivets, or fit a new well-seasoned handle** (accept adding a ferrule or wedge) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Do not award the second mark for 'buy a new cutlass'; the question asks for a repair.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- L - **the head (cross bar) of the rake** (1 mark).
- J - **wood** (accept bamboo) (1 mark).
- K - **wire** (accept binding wire or metal wire) (1 mark).
- M - **iron (nails)** (accept steel) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The name of the part and the three materials, one mark each.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Work: it **binds (lashes) the handle firmly to the head** so that the joint does not loosen or twist in use (1 mark).
- Other method: **nailing, screwing, bolting, or fitting the handle into a socket and wedging it** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Any one sensible alternative method earns the second mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Test: **pull the rake through loose soil or over dry leaves several times** (accept any reasonable trial on the work the tool is meant to do) (1 mark).
- Result: **the teeth remain straight and firm, the joint stays tight and the leaves or soil are gathered easily** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The test must be on the work the tool is meant to do.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **use thicker, harder nails or steel rods**; **drive the teeth deeper into the head**; **set the teeth closer together**; **make the teeth shorter**; **use a harder wood for the head** (1 mark each, maximum 2 marks).
  - *Marking note: The change must act on the strength or fixing of the teeth; 'be careful when using it' earns no mark.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [5 marks]

- Order: **R, Q, T, S, P** (4 marks; award 2 marks if only one pair of letters is out of place).
- Process in T: **forging** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Award the 4 marks only for the full correct order; a single transposition scores 2.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- (i) The hot metal is **soft and can be beaten into shape** (1 mark).
- (ii) Quenching **hardens** the blade and tempering **removes the brittleness** so that it does not snap (1 mark).
- (iii) Seasoned wood **will not shrink, crack or work loose** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) either hardening or tempering correctly explained earns the mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **cheap and easily available locally**; **made of good steel that hardens well**; **reduces the cost of the finished tool**; **recycles scrap and keeps the environment clean** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct advantages are required.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **shortage of money**; **lack of proper tools and equipment (forge, anvil, vice, files)**; **lack of skilled hands or trained supervision**; **limited time on the timetable**; **poor or uneven quality of the scrap materials**; **lack of safety equipment** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: The constraint must be one that affects the making of the tool.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Any FOUR of: **wear an apron, gloves, goggles and stout shoes**; **handle hot metal with tongs only**; **clamp the work in a vice and keep the hands behind the edge**; **keep the workshop tidy, well lit and ventilated**; **carry sharp tools with the edge downwards and away from the body**; **work under supervision and report injuries at once**; **keep a first aid box and water nearby** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Four distinct precautions; repeated ideas score once.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Reason: aluminium is **too soft - it bends in hard soil and cannot be hardened to keep an edge** (1 mark).
- Any TWO ways: **look for scrap steel (vehicle springs, old hoe blades, drum sheet)**; **ask a local blacksmith or technical school for material or help**; **make fewer trowels with the steel available**; **fold and rivet the aluminium over a steel strip to stiffen it** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Do not accept 'stop the project' as one of the two ways; the question asks how the work can be completed.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- Materials: any TWO of **a hardwood branch or broken handle**, **an old tyre or rubber strip**, **a metal pipe or cap**, **bamboo** (1 mark each).
- Tools: **a saw or cutlass, a knife or file or rasp, sandpaper, a hammer and nails** - any suitable set (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The tools named must match the materials chosen.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Recognisable shape of a dibber: a straight body with a tapered point (1 mark).
- A handle shown clearly at the top (1 mark).
- All three parts correctly labelled: **handle**, **body**, **point** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Marks are for shape and labels, not for artistic quality; a ruled pencil sketch is enough.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO actions with a reason: **smooth and oil the wood** - it does not splinter or take in water (1 mark); **clean, dry and store it under cover after use** - the wood does not rot and metal does not rust (1 mark); **cap or harden the point** - it does not wear away quickly (1 mark). Maximum 2 marks.
  - *Marking note: No mark for the action alone; the reason must be given.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 4: Forces and Energy | **Sub-strand:** 5: Agricultural Tools | **Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)

**Content Standard:** **B9/JHS3.4.5.1** - Demonstrate knowledge and skills in making simple agricultural tools for on-farm activities.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 4: Forces and Energy, Sub-Strand 5: Agricultural Tools, Basic 9, page 113. Content standard B9/JHS3.4.5.1 carries three indicators. Indicator B9/JHS3.4.5.1.1, identify materials used in making simple agricultural tools, with the exemplars: describe simple agricultural tools assembled from their environment; and identify the materials used to make the tools assembled and show how the parts are connected. Indicator B9/JHS3.4.5.1.2, discuss and write activities involved in making simple agricultural tools, with the exemplars: describe the activities and processes involved in making different agricultural tools; and explain the materials, processes, constraints and precautions involved in manufacturing simple agricultural tools. Indicator B9/JHS3.4.5.1.3, manufacture simple agricultural tools, with the exemplar: produce simple farm tools using materials from the environment.

> Note: I1 (B9/JHS3.4.5.1.1) carries topics 15.1 to 15.3 and Questions 1, 2 and 3; I2 (B9/JHS3.4.5.1.2) carries topics 15.4 and 15.5 and Questions 4 and 5; I3 (B9/JHS3.4.5.1.3) carries topic 15.6 and Question 6. Because the third indicator is a practical, manufacturing indicator, it is examined here through the planning, testing, improvement and maintenance of a tool actually made in school, which is the part of the work that can fairly be tested in a written paper. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find this content standard written as B9.4.5.1.
