### EXAMINER NOTES

- This sub-strand is practical. The written paper can test the knowledge behind the practical work - the tools, the materials, the joints, the processes and the precautions - but it cannot replace the workshop. Classes that have actually assembled and made tools answer Questions 3, 5 and 6 far better than classes that have only read about them.
- In Question 2 the lettering runs A to E on the cutlass and in Question 3 it runs J to M on the rake, so that no letter is used twice in the paper. Candidates should be reminded to answer with the letter given and not with a letter of their own.
- The commonest error in Question 2(a) is to call the tang the 'handle' because it lies inside the handle. The broken lines in the figure are the clue: they show a part that is hidden, and the question says so.
- Reasons must be tied to a property of the material. 'Steel is good' earns nothing; 'steel is hard and keeps a sharp edge' earns the mark. Teach the pairing of material and property throughout this sub-strand.
- Question 4(a) is an ordering item. Candidates who begin with heating rather than measuring have missed the first lesson of making anything: measure and mark out before you cut or heat.
- Safety answers must be specific. 'Be careful' and 'be serious' earn no marks, while 'hold hot metal with tongs' and 'clamp the work in a vice' do.
- Follow-up work: let each group assemble three tools from the school store, draw them, label the parts, name the material of each part and show on the drawing how the parts are joined. Then let the groups make one simple tool each - a dibber, a rake or a seed drill - and keep a written record of the materials, the steps, the difficulties met and the result of the test. This record is the evidence for the third indicator.

### Section B - Theory (summary answers; full detail in the Marking Scheme)

| Question | Expected Answer | Curriculum Area | Cognitive Level |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (a) | (i) Waste is any material that is no longer wanted or needed by the person, home or place that produced it. (ii) Biodegradable waste can be broken down (rotted) by micro-organisms into simple substances, while non-biodegradable waste cannot be broken down by them and stays in the environment for a very long time. | Types and Sources of Waste | Remember |
| 1 (b) | (i) Cassava or plantain peels (also used exercise books). (ii) Water sachets. (iii) Dirty water from the canteen. (iv) Old mobile phone batteries. | Types and Sources of Waste | Understand |
| 1 (c) | The gutter becomes choked, so rain water cannot flow away and the market floods. The standing water in the choked gutter breeds mosquitoes, which spread malaria. The rotting waste attracts flies, cockroaches and rats, which carry germs on to food and spread cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea. The heap gives off a foul smell that pollutes the air. The liquid draining from the waste pollutes the stream and the underground water, and plastics carried into the stream choke fish and remain there for many years. | Impact of Waste on the Environment | Understand |
| 2 (a) | P is the lining (liner) of the pit; Q is a layer of waste; R is the soil cover placed over each layer; S is the gas vent pipe; T is the pipe that collects the liquid (leachate) at the bottom. | Scientific Methods of Waste Management | Remember |
| 2 (b) | (i) P prevents the liquid from the waste from soaking through the soil into the underground water. (ii) R keeps away flies, rats and smell, stops the waste from being blown about and reduces the rain water entering the waste. (iii) S allows the gas formed as the waste decays without air to escape safely instead of building up and catching fire or exploding. (iv) T drains away the liquid that collects at the bottom so that it can be treated. | Scientific Principles Behind the Methods | Understand |
| 2 (c) | In a sanitary landfill the waste is covered daily, so flies, rats and vultures are kept away and there is little smell; the pit is lined and the liquid is collected, so the underground water and streams are not polluted; the gas is vented or collected instead of building up; the waste is not blown about or burnt in the open, so the air is cleaner; and when the site is full it can be covered and the land used again, for example as a park. | Scientific Methods of Waste Management | Analyse |
| 3 (a) | (i) A waste audit is an exercise in which the waste produced by a place is collected, sorted into types, weighed or measured and recorded, so that the school knows how much of each kind of waste it produces and how well it is being managed. (ii) 24 + 16 + 12 + 5 + 3 = 60 kg. | Waste Audits and Waste Management Practices in Ghana | Remember |
| 3 (b) | (i) Percentage of plastic = (12 ÷ 60) × 100 = 20%. (ii) Average per day = 60 kg ÷ 6 days = 10 kg per day. | Waste Audits and Waste Management Practices in Ghana | Apply |
| 3 (c) | The food and plant waste (24 kg). It is organic and biodegradable, so micro-organisms can break it down into manure, and it is also the largest single part of the school's waste. | Waste Audits and Waste Management Practices in Ghana | Analyse |
| 3 (d) | Because 24 kg of the 60 kg can be composted, the school should build a compost pit behind the garden and put the food and plant waste into it to make manure for the school farm. Because 36 kg is paper, plastic, metal and glass, separate labelled bins should be placed in every block and the sorted paper, plastics and tins sold or given to a recycling company. The school could also reduce the plastics by encouraging pupils to carry refillable bottles instead of buying sachet water. | Waste Audits and Waste Management Practices in Ghana | Evaluate |
| 4 (a) | (i) Composting is the controlled decay of plant and animal waste by micro-organisms to form a dark, crumbly manure called compost. (ii) Kitchen waste (food peels) and grass cuttings; dry leaves also decay, though more slowly. | Scientific Methods of Waste Management | Remember |
| 4 (b) | (i) Bacteria and fungi, helped by earthworms, termites and other small animals. (ii) Turning lets air (oxygen) into the heap so that the decomposers can respire and work faster, and it mixes the material. (iii) The micro-organisms need moisture to live and to break down the material; a dry heap stops working. (iv) The decomposers respire as they break down the waste and release energy as heat, which is trapped inside the heap. | Scientific Principles Behind the Methods | Understand |
| 4 (c) | (i) The water filled the air spaces and the tight packing kept air out, so there was no oxygen in the heap. Decay then went on without oxygen (anaerobic decay), and this produces foul-smelling gases such as hydrogen sulphide and methane instead of the sweet, earthy smell of good compost. (ii) Turn the heap to let air in and mix in dry material such as dry leaves or straw, and cover the heap so that rain does not soak it again. | Scientific Principles Behind the Methods | Analyse |
| 5 (a) | (i) Recycling. (ii) It removes plastics that do not rot from the gutters, streets and gutter-choked drains, so the town is cleaner and floods less; it provides jobs and income for the collectors and the workers; it produces a useful product (paving blocks) more cheaply; and it saves the raw materials and energy that would have been used to make new material. | Scientific Methods of Waste Management | Understand |
| 5 (b) | (i) Methane. (ii) Bacteria break down the kitchen waste and dung inside the closed digester, where there is no air; this anaerobic decay releases a mixture of gases of which methane is the chief one, and the gas collects at the top of the digester and is piped away. (iii) The slurry left behind is rich in plant nutrients and is used as manure on the school farm or garden. | Innovative Waste Management for Sustainable Development | Understand |
| 5 (c) | Both turn waste into something useful instead of leaving it to pollute the environment, so the needs of the people today are met without spoiling the land, water and air for those who come after. The recycling plant saves raw materials and reduces the plastic that would have stayed in the soil for hundreds of years, and it provides employment. The digester gives a clean fuel, so fewer trees are cut for firewood and charcoal and less smoke is released, while the slurry returns nutrients to the soil. | Innovative Waste Management for Sustainable Development | Evaluate |
| 6 (a) | Door-to-door collection by private companies removes waste regularly from homes; communal containers and transfer stations are provided in markets and lorry parks; some towns now use engineered landfill and treatment plants instead of open dumps; companies buy plastics, scrap metal and e-waste for recycling; monthly clean-up days and sanitation by-laws keep the public aware; and compost plants turn market waste into manure. | Waste Audits and Waste Management Practices in Ghana | Evaluate |
| 6 (b) | The waste is not separated at the house, so materials that could be recycled or composted are buried or burnt with the rest. Tipping everything at one site fills the site quickly and may pollute the water and air around it. Many households cannot pay the collection fee and so dump their waste in gutters, streams or open spaces. A clean-up day once a month is not enough, because waste is produced every day, and the waste gathered on such days is often left in heaps that are not carried away. There is also little enforcement of the sanitation by-laws. | Waste Audits and Waste Management Practices in Ghana | Evaluate |
| 6 (c) | Supply every household with two or three labelled bins and insist that waste is separated at home, so that paper, plastics, tins and glass can be sent for recycling instead of being buried. Set up a community compost site or a biogas digester for the food and market waste, so that the largest part of the waste becomes manure or fuel and the landfill lasts longer. Pay collectors for sorted plastics and scrap, so that people have a reason to separate their waste. Educate the people continuously through schools, churches, mosques and radio rather than once a month, and enforce the sanitation by-laws so that dumping in gutters stops. | Innovative Waste Management for Sustainable Development | Create |

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) In calculations, award the method mark for a correct working even when the arithmetic that follows is wrong, and award the final mark only when the unit or the percentage sign is given. (3) An effect on the environment must be stated as an effect, not simply as 'it is bad'. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) **Any material that is no longer wanted or needed by the person or place that produced it** (1 mark).
- (ii) Biodegradable waste **is broken down by micro-organisms**, non-biodegradable waste **is not and remains in the environment** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) the comparison must be made; one half earns no mark.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **Cassava or plantain peels** (accept used exercise books) (1 mark).
- (ii) **Water sachets** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Dirty water from the canteen** (1 mark).
- (iv) **Old mobile phone batteries** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The example must come from the list given in the scenario.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- Any FOUR of: **the gutter is choked and the area floods when it rains**; **stagnant water breeds mosquitoes which spread malaria**; **flies and rats are attracted and carry germs to food, spreading cholera and typhoid**; **a foul smell pollutes the air**; **liquid from the waste pollutes the stream and the underground water**; **plastics are carried into the water and choke fish and other animals** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Each mark requires a stated effect; 'it is dirty' alone earns nothing.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [5 marks]

- P - **the lining (liner) of the pit** (accept clay or plastic lining) (1 mark).
- Q - **a layer of waste (refuse)** (1 mark).
- R - **the soil cover over the layer of waste** (1 mark).
- S - **the gas vent pipe** (accept pipe that lets out the gas) (1 mark).
- T - **the pipe that collects the liquid (leachate) from the waste** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: One mark for each part; no half marks.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **Stops the liquid from the waste from reaching the underground water** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Keeps off flies, rats and smell and stops the waste being blown about** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Lets the gas produced by decay escape safely** (1 mark).
- (iv) **Carries away the liquid collected at the base for treatment** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Any one correct purpose earns the mark in each case.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **the waste is covered, so flies, rats and smell are controlled**; **the lining and drain keep the liquid out of the water supply**; **the gas is let out safely instead of building up**; **the waste is not blown about or burnt in the open, so the air is cleaner**; **the land can be used again when the site is full** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: The reason must contrast with the open dump.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) **Collecting, sorting, weighing and recording the waste produced by a place in order to find out its kinds and quantities** (1 mark).
- (ii) **60 kg** (24 + 16 + 12 + 5 + 3) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) the unit kg is required.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **(12 ÷ 60) × 100** (1 mark) **= 20%** (1 mark).
- (ii) **60 ÷ 6** (1 mark) **= 10 kg per day** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Award the method mark for correct working even if the arithmetic is wrong; the unit or % sign is needed for the final mark.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Food and plant waste** (1 mark).
- Reason: it is **organic (biodegradable) and so can be broken down by micro-organisms into manure** (accept: it forms the largest part of the waste) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The reason must refer to decay or biodegradability.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **start a compost pit for the food and plant waste and use the manure on the school garden**; **place separate labelled bins and send the paper, plastics, tins and glass for recycling**; **reduce plastics by using refillable bottles instead of sachets**; **repeat the audit later to check whether the changes have worked** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: The suggestion must be supported by the figures; 'keep the school clean' earns no mark.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **The controlled rotting of plant and animal waste by micro-organisms to form manure (compost)** (1 mark).
- (ii) Any TWO of **kitchen waste (peels)**, **grass cuttings**, **dry leaves**, **poultry manure** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: The materials must be taken from the list given.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **Bacteria and fungi** (accept micro-organisms, with earthworms and termites) (1 mark).
- (ii) **To let air (oxygen) in so that the decomposers work faster** (1 mark).
- (iii) **The micro-organisms need moisture to live and to break down the material** (1 mark).
- (iv) **Heat is released as the micro-organisms respire while breaking down the waste** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (iv) 'the sun heats it' is wrong and earns no mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Water and tight packing drove the air out, so there was no oxygen** (1 mark); **decay then took place without oxygen (anaerobic decay) and foul gases were produced** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Turn the heap and add dry material to let air in** (accept: cover the heap against rain, or make the heap less tightly packed) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The idea of lack of air (oxygen) must appear in (i).*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Recycling** (1 mark).
- (ii) Any TWO of: **removes plastic waste from the environment, so there is less choking of gutters and less flooding**; **creates jobs and income**; **provides a useful and cheaper product**; **saves raw materials and energy** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct benefits are required.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **Methane** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Bacteria break down the waste inside the closed digester where there is no air (anaerobic decay)** (1 mark), **and the gas released collects above the slurry and is piped off** (1 mark).
- (iii) **The slurry is used as manure (fertiliser) on the farm or garden** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'biogas' for methane in (i) only if methane is named.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Meets present needs **without damaging the environment for future generations** (1 mark).
- Recycling **saves raw materials, reduces lasting plastic waste and creates jobs** (1 mark).
- The digester **gives clean fuel so fewer trees are cut and less smoke is produced, and the slurry returns nutrients to the soil** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The idea of the future generation must appear for the first mark.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **regular door-to-door collection by waste companies**; **communal containers in markets and lorry parks**; **engineered landfill and treatment plants in some cities**; **companies that buy plastics, scrap metal and e-waste for recycling**; **compost plants that treat market waste**; **clean-up days and sanitation by-laws** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: The feature must be a practice, not a wish.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **the waste is not separated, so recyclable and compostable material is lost**; **one tipping site fills up quickly and may pollute water and air**; **households that cannot pay the fee dump waste in gutters, streams or open spaces**; **a monthly clean-up is too seldom for waste produced daily, and the heaps collected are often not carried away**; **the by-laws are not enforced** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Three distinct weaknesses; repeated ideas score once.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE improvements, each with a reason: **separate labelled bins in every home** - so recyclable material is not buried (1 mark); **a community compost site or biogas digester** - so food waste becomes manure or fuel and the landfill lasts longer (1 mark); **buying-back of sorted plastics and scrap** - so people gain by separating (1 mark); **continuous education and enforcement of the by-laws** - so that dumping in gutters stops (1 mark). Maximum 3 marks.
  - *Marking note: No mark for an improvement given without a reason.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 5: Humans and the Environment | **Sub-strand:** 1: Waste Management | **Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)

**Content Standard:** **B9/JHS3.5.1.1** - Demonstrate an understanding of the scientific ways of waste management. **B9/JHS3.5.1.2** - Demonstrate an understanding of the impact of waste on an environment, innovative waste management technologies for sustainable development and waste management practices in Ghana.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 5: Humans and the Environment, Sub-Strand 1: Waste Management, Basic 9, page 114. Content standard B9/JHS3.5.1.1 carries indicator B9/JHS3.5.1.1.1, investigate the scientific methods used in waste management, with the exemplars: identify scientific methods used in waste management such as recycling and composting; explain the scientific principles underlying the methods identified; and conduct an audit of waste management methods in schools and assess the effectiveness of each method. Content standard B9/JHS3.5.1.2 carries indicator B9/JHS3.5.1.2.1, describe innovative ways of waste management for sustainable development, with the exemplars: explain the impact of waste produced on the environment; identify innovative ways to manage waste for sustainable development; describe the types of waste produced within communities in Ghana; and examine and critique waste management practices in Ghana, identifying the positives, the negatives and the opportunities for improvement.

> Note: I1 (B9/JHS3.5.1.1.1) carries topics 16.3, 16.4 and 16.6 and Questions 2, 3 and 4; I2 (B9/JHS3.5.1.2.1) carries topics 16.1, 16.2 and 16.5 and Questions 1, 5 and 6. The waste audit exemplar belongs to the first indicator and is examined in Question 3, where candidates read and work on the results of a school audit. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find these standards written as B9.5.1.1 and B9.5.1.2.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- This sub-strand is easy to answer loosely. Marks are lost when candidates write 'it is bad' or 'it is dirty' instead of naming the effect - flooding, malaria, cholera, polluted water, dead fish. Train classes to finish every sentence with the consequence.
- Question 2 rewards careful reading of the figure. The lining, the daily soil cover, the gas vent and the leachate pipe are the four features that make a landfill 'sanitary', and each has a scientific reason behind it.
- In Question 3 the arithmetic is simple but the unit and the percentage sign are part of the answer. Candidates should also be reminded that the audit ran for six days, not seven, so the daily average is 10 kg and not about 8.6 kg.
- Question 4(c) tests the single most important principle in composting: decay with air is sweet and fast, decay without air is slow and foul. A class that has built and turned a heap answers this at once.
- Biogas is a mixture, but methane is the gas that burns and the one asked for. Accept 'biogas, which is mainly methane'; do not accept 'carbon dioxide'.
- Question 6 is a critique, and marks are given for balance. Candidates who can see both what works and what fails in their own town, and who then propose a practical improvement with a reason, are showing exactly the thinking the indicator asks for.
- Follow-up work: let the class run its own one-week waste audit, draw the bar chart, calculate the percentages, start a compost pit with the food waste and weigh the compost produced. Repeating the audit a term later gives a direct measure of how effective the school's new methods have been.

### Section B - Theory (summary answers; full detail in the Marking Scheme)

| Question | Expected Answer | Curriculum Area | Cognitive Level |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (a) | (i) The WHO defines health as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. (ii) A disease is any condition that upsets the normal working (functioning) of the body or the mind. | Health and Disease and Their Relationship | Remember |
| 1 (b) | Health and disease are opposite states of the same body. When a disease attacks a person, the normal working of the body or mind is upset and the level of health falls; the more serious the disease, the poorer the health. When disease is prevented or cured, health is restored. A person may, however, be free of disease and still not be completely healthy, because mental and social well-being are also part of health. | Health and Disease and Their Relationship | Understand |
| 1 (c) | The communicable diseases on the list are cholera, measles and tuberculosis. Cholera is passed on through water and food contaminated with the faeces of a patient; measles is passed on through droplets breathed out or coughed by a patient; tuberculosis is passed on through droplets coughed into the air by a patient. | Health and Disease and Their Relationship | Understand |
| 1 (d) | He is not completely healthy. Although he has no physical illness, his mental and social well-being is poor, and the WHO definition requires physical, mental and social well-being together. | Health and Disease and Their Relationship | Apply |
| 2 (a) | (i) A common disease is one that occurs in a large number of people in that community, that is, one reported much more often than others. (ii) Malaria, with 120 cases. | Common Diseases in a Community | Understand |
| 2 (b) | (i) (120 ÷ 300) × 100 = 40%. (ii) The non-communicable diseases shown are high blood pressure (40) and diabetes (20), giving 60 cases; (60 ÷ 300) × 100 = 20%. | Common Diseases in a Community | Apply |
| 2 (c) | (i) Malaria, spread by the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito. (ii) By drinking water or eating food contaminated with faeces, often because of poor toilets, unwashed hands or flies settling on food. | Common Diseases in a Community | Analyse |
| 2 (d) | Clear the bushes and drain or fill the pools and choked gutters around the houses, because the mosquito lays its eggs and breeds in stagnant water. Sleep under treated mosquito nets and screen the windows, because this prevents the mosquito from biting and passing on the parasite. Report fever early at the clinic for testing and treatment, because a treated patient is no longer a source of the parasite for other mosquitoes. | Common Diseases in a Community | Evaluate |
| 3 (a) | (i) Non-communicable diseases are diseases that are not passed from one person to another; they develop from the way a person lives, feeds or works, or from inherited and age-related changes. (ii) Kwashiorkor (accept marasmus, anaemia, rickets, goitre or night blindness). | Non-Communicable Diseases and Their Risk Factors | Remember |
| 3 (b) | Eating too much salt; eating fatty, fried food; drinking sugary soft drinks; sitting all day without exercise; and being overweight as a result. Age also plays a part, but the four habits above are the risk factors she can change. | Non-Communicable Diseases and Their Risk Factors | Analyse |
| 3 (c) | (i) Passing urine very often, great thirst, loss of weight although eating well, tiredness, blurred vision and sores that are slow to heal. (ii) It may cause a stroke, heart failure, kidney damage or damage to the eyes, and it may end in death. | Non-Communicable Diseases and Their Risk Factors | Understand |
| 3 (d) | Cut down the salt, fat and sugar in her food and eat more fruits, vegetables and fibre; take regular exercise, such as walking for thirty minutes on most days; reduce her weight; stop or avoid alcohol and tobacco; and attend the clinic regularly to have her blood pressure and blood sugar checked and to take her medicines as prescribed. | Non-Communicable Diseases and Their Risk Factors | Apply |
| 4 (a) | (i) Cancer is a disease in which certain cells of the body divide in an uncontrolled way, forming a growth (tumour) that may spread to other parts of the body and destroy healthy tissue. (ii) Lung cancer, breast cancer, cervical cancer, prostate cancer, liver cancer or skin cancer. | Cancer: Causes, Signs and Prevention | Remember |
| 4 (b) | A lump or swelling anywhere in the body; a sore or wound that refuses to heal; unusual bleeding or discharge, for example after the menopause; a change in a mole or in a long-standing wart; a cough or hoarseness that lasts for weeks; difficulty in swallowing or lasting indigestion; a change in bowel or bladder habits; and loss of weight that cannot be explained. | Cancer: Causes, Signs and Prevention | Understand |
| 4 (c) | (i) Tobacco smoke contains many chemicals that damage the cells lining the air passages and lungs, and the damaged cells may begin to divide uncontrollably, causing lung cancer. (ii) The ultraviolet rays in strong sunlight damage the cells of the skin, which may then grow out of control as skin cancer. (iii) Mouldy groundnuts and maize carry poisons (aflatoxins) produced by fungi, and these poisons damage the liver and can lead to liver cancer. | Cancer: Causes, Signs and Prevention | Analyse |
| 4 (d) | In the early stage the growth is still small and is confined to one place, so it can be removed by surgery or destroyed by treatment before it has spread. Once it has spread to other organs, treatment is much harder and less likely to succeed, so regular examination and early reporting of warning signs save lives. | Cancer: Causes, Signs and Prevention | Evaluate |
| 5 (a) | (i) Ringworm (tinea). (ii) Fungi. (iii) Candidiasis (thrush), fungal infection of the finger or toe nails, athlete's foot or fungal eye infection. | Fungal Diseases of Humans | Understand |
| 5 (b) | W, the comb, carries infected hairs and skin scales from one scalp to the next when it is shared. X, the shared towel, rubs the fungus and infected skin scales from the body of one pupil on to the damp skin of another. Y, the cap, holds the fungus from an infected head inside it and passes it to the head of the next wearer, and it also keeps the scalp warm and sweaty, which helps the fungus to grow. Z, the wet bathroom floor, holds skin scales containing the fungus, and pupils who walk barefoot on it pick them up between the toes, where the warm, damp skin favours growth. | Fungal Diseases of Humans | Apply |
| 5 (c) | Each pupil should have and use a personal comb, towel, cap and footwear, and these should never be shared. Infected pupils should be sent to the clinic at once for antifungal treatment and should complete the course. Bathrooms should be cleaned and disinfected daily and pupils should wear slippers in them. Clothing, towels and bedding should be washed and dried in the sun and ironed. The dormitory should be kept dry and airy and not overcrowded, and pupils should bathe daily and dry the skin, especially between the toes. | Fungal Diseases of Humans | Understand |
| 6 (a) | (i) The individual keeps the body, clothing and bedding clean and dry, avoids sharing personal articles and reports early for treatment. (ii) The community keeps the surroundings and public bathhouses clean, supports health education and clean-up exercises and encourages those affected to seek treatment instead of hiding the disease. (iii) The government provides clinics, trained health workers and antifungal medicines, carries out public education and screening in schools and makes and enforces public health rules. | Managing Disease: the Individual, the Community and Government | Understand |
| 6 (b) | A short, bold heading naming the disease; a clear drawing of the signs, such as the round scaly patch on the scalp; a few short points in simple language or the local language on how it is spread; the steps to avoid it, such as 'do not share combs and towels'; and a line telling people where to go for treatment, such as the name of the clinic. Large letters and few words make it readable from a distance. | Managing Disease: the Individual, the Community and Government | Create |
| 6 (c) | The belief is dangerous because the true cause, a fungus, is ignored, so the infection is not treated and continues to spread to other members of the family; rubbing with sand and hot leaves wounds the skin and may cause a further bacterial infection and lasting scars or bald patches. The club should explain that ringworm is caused by a fungus that is passed on by contact and shared articles, that it is cured by antifungal medicine from the clinic, and that cleanliness and avoiding shared articles prevent it. | Managing Disease: the Individual, the Community and Government | Evaluate |

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) A symptom must be written as something the patient feels or shows; a cause or a risk factor written in place of a symptom earns no mark. (3) In calculations, award the method mark for correct working even when the arithmetic that follows is wrong, and award the final mark only when the percentage sign or unit is given. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed, but names of diseases must be recognisable.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being** (1 mark), **and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Any condition that upsets the normal working of the body or mind** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (i) all three kinds of well-being are needed for the first mark.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- **Disease lowers the level of health, and the removal or prevention of disease restores health** (1 mark).
- **Freedom from disease alone is not full health, since mental and social well-being are also needed** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept any clear statement of the inverse relationship.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- **Cholera, measles and tuberculosis** (2 marks for all three; 1 mark for any two).
- Mode of spread of any one named: **cholera - contaminated water or food**; **measles or tuberculosis - droplets in the air from a patient** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A non-communicable disease named among the three loses the first mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **He is not completely healthy** (1 mark).
- Reason: **his mental and social well-being is poor, and health is more than the absence of disease** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: No mark for the judgement without the reason.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **A disease that occurs in a large number of people in the community** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Malaria** (1 mark), **120 cases** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Read the value from the bar; 120 only.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **(120 ÷ 300) × 100** (1 mark) **= 40%** (1 mark).
- (ii) **40 + 20 = 60 cases** (1 mark); **(60 ÷ 300) × 100 = 20%** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) the candidate must select high blood pressure and diabetes; selecting any communicable disease loses the first mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Malaria** (1 mark); **the female Anopheles mosquito** (accept mosquito) (1 mark).
- (ii) **Drinking or eating water or food contaminated with faeces** (accept dirty hands, flies on food, poor toilets) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'mosquito' alone for the insect.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO actions each with a reason: **drain stagnant water and clear bush and gutters** - removes the breeding places of the mosquito (1 mark); **sleep under treated nets and screen windows** - prevents biting (1 mark); **report and treat fever early** - removes the source of the parasite (1 mark). Maximum 2 marks.
  - *Marking note: No mark for the action without its reason.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) **Diseases that are not passed from one person to another** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Kwashiorkor** (accept marasmus, anaemia, rickets, goitre, night blindness) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Any named deficiency disease is acceptable in (ii).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **too much salt in the food**; **fatty or fried food**; **sugary drinks**; **lack of physical exercise (sitting all day)**; **being overweight** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: The risk factor must come from the passage.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) Any TWO of: **frequent passing of urine**, **great thirst**, **loss of weight in spite of eating**, **tiredness**, **blurred vision**, **sores that heal slowly** (1 mark each).
- (ii) **Stroke, heart failure, kidney damage or damage to the eyes** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A cause written in place of a symptom earns no mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **reduce salt, fat and sugar and eat more fruits and vegetables**; **take regular exercise and reduce weight**; **avoid alcohol and tobacco**; **attend the clinic regularly and take prescribed medicines** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: The advice must be practical and related to her condition.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) **A disease in which body cells divide in an uncontrolled way to form a growth that may spread** (1 mark).
- (ii) Any ONE of **lung, breast, cervical, prostate, liver or skin cancer** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The idea of uncontrolled growth of cells is essential in (i).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **a lump or swelling**; **a sore that does not heal**; **unusual bleeding or discharge**; **a change in a mole or wart**; **a lasting cough or hoarseness**; **difficulty in swallowing**; **a change in bowel or bladder habit**; **unexplained loss of weight** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Three distinct signs are required.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) Tobacco smoke contains **chemicals that damage the cells of the lungs and air passages**, which then grow uncontrollably (1 mark).
- (ii) **Ultraviolet rays damage the skin cells**, which may grow out of control as skin cancer (1 mark).
- (iii) Mouldy grain carries **poisons (aflatoxins) from fungi that damage the liver** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The idea of damage to cells must appear in (i) and (ii).*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- **At an early stage the growth is small and has not spread to other parts of the body** (1 mark).
- **It can then be removed or treated successfully, while a cancer that has spread is much harder to treat** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The idea of spreading must appear.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Ringworm** (accept tinea or athlete's foot for the toes) (1 mark).
- (ii) **Fungi** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Candidiasis (thrush)**, **nail infection** or **fungal eye infection** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Do not accept 'worm' or 'germ' for the group of organisms.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- W - **a shared comb carries infected hairs and skin scales from one scalp to another** (1 mark).
- X - **a shared towel rubs the fungus and skin scales on to another pupil's damp skin** (1 mark).
- Y - **a shared cap passes the fungus from head to head and keeps the scalp warm and sweaty** (1 mark).
- Z - **skin scales with the fungus are left on the wet floor and picked up by bare feet** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Each mark needs the idea of transfer of the fungus from one person to another.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **no sharing of combs, towels, caps, clothing or footwear**; **early treatment of infected pupils at the clinic**; **daily cleaning of bathrooms and wearing slippers in them**; **washing, sun-drying and ironing of clothing, towels and bedding**; **keeping the body clean and dry, especially between the toes**; **avoiding overcrowding and keeping the dormitory airy** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Three distinct measures; repeated ideas score once.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Personal cleanliness, no sharing of personal articles and early reporting for treatment** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Keeping the surroundings and public bathhouses clean, supporting education and encouraging treatment** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Providing clinics, medicines, trained workers, school screening and public health rules** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The role must match the level named.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **a short bold heading naming the disease**; **a clear drawing of the signs**; **short simple points on how it spreads**; **the steps to prevent it**; **where to go for treatment**; **large letters and few words, in a language the people read** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Three distinct features of a good poster.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Danger: **the real cause is not treated, so the disease spreads, and sand and hot leaves wound the skin and may cause further infection or scarring** (1 mark).
- Advice: **ringworm is caused by a fungus spread by contact and shared articles, and it is cured with antifungal medicine from the clinic** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The answer must name the fungus as the cause to earn the second mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 5: Humans and the Environment | **Sub-strand:** 2: Human Health | **Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)

**Content Standard:** **B9/JHS3.5.2.1** - Demonstrate knowledge of common non-communicable diseases of humans, their causes, symptoms, effects and prevention. **B9/JHS3.5.2.2** - Demonstrate understanding of the relationship of health and disease, the concept of common diseases in the environment and how to control them. **B9/JHS3.5.2.2** - Demonstrate knowledge of selected fungal diseases of humans, their causes, symptoms, effects and prevention.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 5: Humans and the Environment, Sub-Strand 2: Human Health, Basic 9, pages 115 to 117. Content standard B9/JHS3.5.2.1 carries indicator B9/JHS3.5.2.1.1, explain the symptoms, effects and prevention of some non-communicable diseases and analyse the risk factors associated with them, with the exemplars: describe what non-communicable diseases are and determine their common causes; identify symptoms, effects and prevention of non-communicable diseases associated with malnutrition, poor working environment and exposure to drugs; explain the causes, symptoms, effects and prevention of cancer; and identify common cancers that affect humans and link them to lifestyle. Content standard B9/JHS3.5.2.2 carries indicator B9/JHS3.5.2.2.1, explain the concepts of health and disease and show their relationship, with the exemplar: define health as stipulated by the World Health Organisation (WHO) and show the relationship between health and disease; and indicator B9/JHS3.5.2.2.2, explain the concept of common diseases in an environment, with the exemplars: conduct a survey about common diseases and analyse the findings to show what constitutes a common disease in a community; and identify causes, symptoms and prevention of common diseases. The curriculum then states a further content standard, printed with the same code B9/JHS3.5.2.2, demonstrate knowledge of selected fungal diseases of humans, their causes, symptoms, effects and prevention, with indicator B9/JHS3.5.2.2.1 on the nature of fungal diseases, with the exemplars: discuss the nature of fungal diseases; search for information and make presentations on ringworm, candidiasis and fungal eye infection and their mode of transmission from person to person, community to community and country to country; describe the symptoms, effects and prevention of these diseases; describe the role of individuals, community members and government in managing them; and design and produce a poster to educate community members on their incidence and control.

> Note: I1 (B9/JHS3.5.2.1.1) carries topics 17.2 and 17.3 and Questions 3 and 4; I2 (B9/JHS3.5.2.2.1) carries topic 17.1 and Question 1; I3 (B9/JHS3.5.2.2.2) carries topic 17.4 and Question 2; I4 carries topics 17.5 and 17.6 and Questions 5 and 6. In the published curriculum the code B9/JHS3.5.2.2 is printed twice, once for the content standard on health, disease and common diseases (pages 116) and again for the content standard on fungal diseases (page 117), and the indicator code B9/JHS3.5.2.2.1 likewise appears under both. The codes are reproduced here exactly as published and are distinguished in this paper as I2 and I4; no new code has been invented. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find these standards written as B9.5.2.1 and B9.5.2.2.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- The published curriculum prints the code B9/JHS3.5.2.2 twice on consecutive pages, once for the content standard on health, disease and common diseases and again for the content standard on fungal diseases, and the indicator code B9/JHS3.5.2.2.1 likewise appears under both. The codes have been reproduced exactly as published and are distinguished in the blueprint as I2 and I4. Teachers should expect to meet the same code twice in the official document.
- The WHO definition must be learnt word for word. Candidates who write only 'absence of disease' lose both marks, because the definition says expressly that health is more than that.
- The commonest error in this sub-strand is to confuse a cause, a symptom and a risk factor. Teach the three words together: a cause produces the disease, a symptom is what the patient feels or shows, and a risk factor is a habit or condition that makes the disease more likely.
- In Question 2(b)(ii) candidates must first decide which of the five diseases on the chart are non-communicable. High blood pressure and diabetes are the two; ringworm, although it is not spread by an insect, is communicable, and this is worth discussing in class.
- Question 5(b) is the heart of the fungal-disease indicator. Every mark turns on the transfer of the fungus from one person to another, so answers such as 'the comb is dirty' earn nothing.
- Question 6(c) touches a real belief in many communities. Candidates should be encouraged to answer with respect but with science: the fungus is the cause, the clinic has the cure, and cleanliness prevents it.
- Follow-up work: let the class carry out its own survey of the diseases reported at the nearest clinic for one month, draw the bar chart, calculate the percentages and classify each disease as communicable or non-communicable. Then let groups design and display posters on ringworm, candidiasis and nail infection, which is exactly the activity the curriculum asks for.

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) Accept the local name of a product or an industry (for example alata samina for local black soap) provided the meaning is clear. (3) Where a scientific process is asked for, the named process must be a process - evaporation, fermentation, saponification, filtration - and not simply 'heating things'. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **A group of firms producing the same kind of goods or services** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Primary (extractive), secondary (manufacturing) and tertiary (service) industries** (2 marks for all three; 1 mark for any two).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'extractive, manufacturing and service' in (ii).*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **Cocoa buying shed / cocoa growing** (accept the sawmill's timber felling) (1 mark).
- (ii) Any TWO of **bakery**, **palm oil mill**, **kente weaving**, **blacksmith's shop**, **sawmill** (1 mark each).
- (iii) **The taxi station** (transport) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A firm may be placed only once; mark each part on its own.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- Order: **harvesting the fruits → boiling and pounding → separating (skimming) the oil from the water and fibre → packaging and marketing** (2 marks for the full correct order; 1 mark if one pair is out of place).
- Scientific separation: **at the skimming stage, because oil is less dense than water and floats on it** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'pressing' for pounding and 'selling' for marketing.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) Raw material: **cassava roots** (1 mark); product: **gari** (1 mark).
- (ii) **B** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Only the letter is needed in (ii).*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **The pressing squeezes out the liquid** (1 mark); **the three days allow fermentation, which sours the mash and helps to remove the harmful (cyanide-producing) substance** (1 mark).
- (ii) **The heat drives off the remaining water as steam and cooks the starch** (1 mark); **the dry product does not support micro-organisms, so it keeps long** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'poisonous substance' for the cyanide-producing compound.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **Fermentation** (1 mark).
- (ii) Any TWO of: **a sour smell or taste develops**; **bubbles of gas escape**; **liquid drips from the bags**; **the mash becomes warm**; **the colour changes** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: The observation must be something that can be seen, smelt, tasted or felt.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO improvements each with a reason: **a motorised grater** - faster and gives an even mash (1 mark); **a screw or hydraulic press** - the same pressing force on every bag (1 mark); **a mechanical roaster or a fixed roasting time** - every batch roasted alike (1 mark); **better hygiene in the shed** - a safer product of steady quality (1 mark). Maximum 2 marks.
  - *Marking note: No mark for an improvement without a reason.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- P - **the channel (and gate) that lets sea water into the site** (1 mark).
- Q - **the reservoir pan holding the sea water** (1 mark).
- R - **the shallow crystallising pan in which the salt forms** (1 mark).
- S - **the heap of harvested salt** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'storage pan' for Q and 'salt pan' for R.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **Evaporation** (1 mark) and **crystallisation** (1 mark).
- (ii) **A wide, shallow pan gives a large surface area for evaporation** (1 mark); **the sun supplies heat and the wind carries away the vapour, so evaporation is faster** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'Boiling' is wrong; no boiling takes place in the pans.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **Dissolve the dirty salt in water and filter to remove the sand and rubbish** (1 mark).
- **Evaporate the filtrate to obtain clean salt crystals** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Both steps are needed; one step alone earns one mark.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) **An industry that uses local materials, simple tools and skills handed down in the community** (1 mark).
- (ii) Any ONE of **kente weaving, pottery, blacksmithing, basketry, shea butter extraction, gari processing, salt winning, fish smoking, adinkra printing** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Do not accept a modern factory in (ii).*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **To dissolve the alkali (potash) out of the ash** (1 mark); **the insoluble matter is left behind and strained off** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Saponification** (1 mark); **soap (and glycerol) is formed** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'lye' for the alkaline solution.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Test: **dip red litmus paper (or add a local plant indicator) into the solution** (1 mark).
- Result: **the red litmus turns blue** (accept the colour change of the local indicator) (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A test without the expected result earns one mark only.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO precautions each with a reason: **wear gloves and avoid splashes** - the alkali burns the skin (1 mark); **use a long ladle and keep the face away** - the hot mixture spits (1 mark); **work in the open air** - the smoke and fumes irritate the chest and eyes (1 mark); **keep children away from the fire** - to prevent burns (1 mark). Maximum 2 marks.
  - *Marking note: No mark for a precaution without its reason.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) **Removes suspended solid particles (mud, grit)** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Absorbs substances that give taste, smell and colour** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Kills bacteria and other germs** (1 mark).
- (iv) **Keeps out dust, germs and insects (and shows the bottle has not been opened)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Do not accept 'to make the water pure' alone in (i) or (ii).*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- (i) **Fermentation** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Carbon dioxide** (1 mark); **it forms bubbles that make the dough rise and give the bread a light, spongy texture** (1 mark).
- (iii) **The yeast is most active in warmth; in the cold it works too slowly** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'the yeast respires' for the process in (i) only if fermentation is named.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **the yeast was dead, too old or forgotten**; **the water was too hot and killed the yeast**; **the place was too cold**; **no sugar was added, so the yeast had no food**; **too much salt was added**; **the dough was not left long enough** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct reasons are required.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- Tools - weaver: **a simple wooden loom worked by hand and foot** (1 mark); factory: **power-driven machines** (1 mark).
- Quantity - weaver: **small output, a few cloths at a time** (1 mark); factory: **large output, many rolls a day** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The table must be copied; four correct entries earn the marks.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **little money or power needed to start and run**; **uses local materials and keeps local skills and culture alive**; **provides work in the village and trains apprentices**; **each cloth is unique and made to order**; **little waste and no industrial pollution** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Two distinct advantages are required.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **an improved or partly mechanised loom to weave faster while keeping his own designs**; **factory-spun, fast-dyed yarn of even quality**; **simple testing of colour fastness and strength**; **a mobile phone and the internet for orders and sales**; **electric lighting in the shed** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: The suggestion must keep the weaving itself in the hands of the weaver; 'buy power looms and close the shed' earns no mark.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 5: Humans and the Environment | **Sub-strand:** 3: Science and Industry | **Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)

**Content Standard:** **B9/JHS3.5.3.1** - Analyse the scientific concepts, principles and processes applied in industries in and outside their community. **B9/JHS3.5.3.2** - Demonstrate an understanding of the concept of industry, the science underpinning the processes of production in industries, and the technologies in indigenous industries and western industries.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 5: Humans and the Environment, Sub-Strand 3: Science and Industry, Basic 9, pages 118 and 119. Content standard B9/JHS3.5.3.1 carries indicator B9/JHS3.5.3.1.1, investigate the scientific concepts, principles and processes involved in industries in their environment, with the exemplars: identify products of industries within and outside their community and describe the process of production; and investigate and outline scientific concepts, principles and processes underlying the production of common everyday industrial products. Content standard B9/JHS3.5.3.2 carries indicator B9/JHS3.5.3.2.1, explain the concept of industry and distinguish between modern and indigenous industries, with the exemplars: identify an industry as individual firms producing the same commodity and give examples of industries in their community; and describe how technology affects industry and compare the technologies in indigenous and modern industries. The same content standard carries indicator B9/JHS3.5.3.2.2, examine indigenous industries in their communities and show the scientific processes in the stages of production, with the exemplars: discuss indigenous industries in their communities and identify the scientific processes, concepts and principles underlying the stages of production in the industries; and identify indigenous practices at home, school and the community and the science involved in the practices.

> Note: I1 (B9/JHS3.5.3.1.1) carries topics 18.2 and 18.3 and Questions 2 and 5; I2 (B9/JHS3.5.3.2.1) carries topics 18.1 and 18.6 and Questions 1 and 6; I3 (B9/JHS3.5.3.2.2) carries topics 18.4 and 18.5 and Questions 3 and 4. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find these standards written as B9.5.3.1 and B9.5.3.2.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- The curriculum defines an industry as individual firms producing the same commodity. Candidates who write that an industry is 'a factory' lose the mark in Question 1(a), and this definition should be learnt in the curriculum's own words.
- Question 2 is the backbone of the paper. The three days of pressing are not merely a local habit: they both remove liquid and allow fermentation, which is what makes the gari safe and sour. Classes that have watched the process answer this well.
- In Question 3(b) the answer is evaporation followed by crystallisation. Every year candidates write 'boiling'; there is no boiling in a salt pan, and the mark is lost.
- Saponification is the one technical term the soap-making question requires. Candidates should also know that the ash supplies the alkali; answers that say the ash is used 'for colour' earn nothing.
- Question 5 shows that the same scientific ideas - filtration, absorption, disinfection and fermentation - run through modern factories and village workshops alike. This is the main message of the sub-strand.
- Question 6(c) must be marked with care. A suggestion that replaces the weaver with machines answers a different question; the mark is for technology that helps the craftsman while the craft remains his.
- Follow-up work: let groups visit or describe one industry in their own town, draw a flow chart of its stages in the style of Fig. 1, and write beside each stage the scientific process at work. Displaying the charts side by side shows the class how much science their community already uses.

### Section B - Theory (summary answers; full detail in the Marking Scheme)

| Question | Expected Answer | Curriculum Area | Cognitive Level |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 (a) | (i) Climate is the average weather condition of a place taken over a long period, usually thirty years or more. (ii) Weather is the condition of the atmosphere of a place at a particular time and changes from day to day, while climate is the average of those conditions over many years. (iii) Climate change is a lasting change in the average weather pattern of a place or of the whole earth. | Climate, Climate Change and the Greenhouse Effect | Remember |
| 1 (b) | Longer and more severe dry spells and droughts; heavier rain falling in a short time and causing floods; rivers, streams and wells drying up earlier in the year; the disappearance of certain plants, birds, insects or fish from the area; crops failing or maturing at unusual times; stronger winds and more storms; and hotter nights as well as hotter days. | Climate, Climate Change and the Greenhouse Effect | Understand |
| 1 (c) | (i) Volcanic eruptions; changes in the energy given out by the sun; changes in ocean currents; changes in the earth's orbit and tilt; methane released from natural wetlands; and wildfires started by lightning. (ii) For example, a great volcanic eruption throws ash and gases high into the atmosphere, where they spread round the earth and block part of the sunlight, so that less heat reaches the surface and the earth is cooler for a year or more. | Natural Factors that Influence Climate Change | Analyse |
| 2 (a) | (i) P is the radiation (heat and light) coming from the sun to the earth's surface. (ii) Q is heat radiated from the warmed surface that passes through the layer and escapes into space. (iii) R is heat radiated from the surface that is absorbed by the layer and sent back to the earth's surface. (iv) S is the layer of greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour, in the atmosphere. | Climate, Climate Change and the Greenhouse Effect | Understand |
| 2 (b) | Carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour and nitrous oxide are the chief greenhouse gases. | Climate, Climate Change and the Greenhouse Effect | Remember |
| 2 (c) | (i) Without the layer, nearly all the heat radiated by the warmed surface would pass straight out into space, and none would be sent back; the surface would then lose heat rapidly, especially at night, and the average temperature of the earth would be far below freezing. (ii) The temperature rises, because more of the heat leaving the surface is trapped and returned. | Climate, Climate Change and the Greenhouse Effect | Understand |
| 2 (d) | Burning petrol and diesel in vehicles and generators, and burning coal or firewood, adds carbon dioxide. Cutting down and burning forest for timber, farming or charcoal adds carbon dioxide and removes the trees that would have absorbed it. Bush burning before planting adds carbon dioxide. Rearing large herds of cattle adds methane, and waste rotting in dumps and the flooding of rice fields also release methane. | Human Factors that Influence Climate Change | Analyse |
| 3 (a) | (i) 1985: 26.0 °C; 2025: 28.0 °C. (ii) Rise = 28.0 - 26.0 = 2.0 °C. (iii) 2.0 ÷ 4 = 0.5 °C per ten years. | Climate, Climate Change and the Greenhouse Effect | Apply |
| 3 (b) | The mean annual temperature has risen steadily throughout the forty years, with no fall at any point. This suggests that the district is becoming steadily warmer, that is, that its climate is changing and not merely that one year happened to be hot. | Climate, Climate Change and the Greenhouse Effect | Analyse |
| 3 (c) | Plant and protect trees and stop the felling of forest. Stop bush burning and clear farms by hoeing or composting instead. Use improved cook stoves, gas or solar energy instead of large quantities of firewood and charcoal. Share transport, walk, cycle or use buses instead of many private cars and motorcycles. Switch off lights and appliances not in use and change to LED lamps. Compost food waste or feed it to a biogas digester instead of burning or dumping it. | Minimising Human Activities that Cause Climate Change | Understand |
| 4 (a) | (i) A green economy is one that improves the well-being of people and provides them with a living while reducing the damage done to the environment and the waste of natural resources. (ii) Installing and maintaining solar panels; raising and planting tree seedlings; collecting and recycling plastics; building and servicing biogas digesters; organic farming; and ecotourism guiding. | The Green Economy | Remember |
| 4 (b) | The solar panels give electricity from sunlight, so less electricity from fuel-burning plants and less diesel from generators is used, and less carbon dioxide is released. The biogas digester captures the methane from the kitchen waste and burns it as cooking fuel, so a strong greenhouse gas does not escape into the air and less firewood or charcoal is needed. The trees take in carbon dioxide as they grow and store the carbon in their wood, and they also shade and cool the grounds. Recycling the plastics saves the energy and oil that would be used to make new plastic and keeps the waste out of dumps where it would be burnt. | The Green Economy | Understand |
| 4 (c) | Percentage = (60 ÷ 200) × 100 = 30%. | The Green Economy | Apply |
| 4 (d) | The monthly electricity bill and the number of units bought from the grid before and after the panels were fitted. The quantity of firewood, charcoal or gas bought for the kitchen each month before and after the digester was built. The number of the planted trees still alive and growing after a year or two, and their height. The mass of plastic collected and sold each term, and the money earned. The quantity of waste still being burnt or dumped by the school. | Climate Change and Green Economy Initiatives in Ghana and Beyond | Evaluate |
| 5 (a) | (i) Country M, with 55% of its electricity from renewable sources. (ii) Country L, with 40 000 hectares lost. (iii) 40 000 ÷ 2 000 = 20 times. | Climate Change and Green Economy Initiatives in Ghana and Beyond | Understand |
| 5 (b) | Country M acts on both sides of the problem at once. Its solar and wind farms mean that more than half of its electricity is produced without burning fuel, so little carbon dioxide is released, while its law against felling forest has kept its forest loss down to 2 000 hectares, the smallest of the three, so its trees continue to absorb carbon dioxide. The other two countries act on one side only: L plants trees for one day a year while losing 40 000 hectares, and N gives out solar lamps while still losing 18 000 hectares. | Climate Change and Green Economy Initiatives in Ghana and Beyond | Analyse |
| 5 (c) | The country loses 40 000 hectares of forest in the same year, far more than one planting day can replace, so its forest cover is still falling. Only 15% of its electricity comes from renewable sources, so most of its power still releases greenhouse gases. A planting day also says nothing about how many of the seedlings survive; without care and a count after a year or two, the trees planted may mostly die. | Climate Change and Green Economy Initiatives in Ghana and Beyond | Evaluate |
| 5 (d) | The Green Ghana Day, on which millions of seedlings are planted every year, restores forest cover and absorbs carbon dioxide. The ban on, and policing of, illegal mining in forest reserves and rivers protects both the trees and the water. The replacement of street lamps with solar and LED lamps cuts the electricity used for lighting. The distribution of improved cook stoves and the spread of liquefied petroleum gas reduce the firewood and charcoal burnt. Solar plants, such as those in the northern parts of the country, add clean electricity to the national grid. | Climate Change and Green Economy Initiatives in Ghana and Beyond | Create |
| 6 (a) | Example: a natural factor is a volcanic eruption (or a change in the sun's energy, ocean currents or the earth's orbit); a human factor is the burning of fossil fuels (or deforestation, bush burning or cattle rearing). Control: natural factors cannot be controlled by people, and communities can only prepare for and adapt to them, while human factors can be reduced or stopped by the choices people make. | Human Factors that Influence Climate Change | Analyse |
| 6 (b) | Plant and protect trees along streets, on school grounds and in degraded areas, which absorbs carbon dioxide, gives shade and provides nursery work. Make and enforce a by-law against bush burning and illegal mining, which saves the forest, the farms and the rivers. Provide and maintain buses or safe cycle paths, which cuts the fuel burnt by many private cars. Put up solar street lights and solar panels on public buildings, which cuts the electricity bought and the fuel burnt. Set up a composting or biogas site for market waste, which cuts methane from dumps and creates jobs and manure for farmers. | Minimising Human Activities that Cause Climate Change | Create |
| 6 (c) | Many of the actions cost little or nothing: stopping bush burning, planting and caring for seedlings, composting market waste and sharing transport save money rather than spend it. The green actions themselves create work and income - nursery work, recycling, solar installation and biogas - so they help the poor instead of burdening them. Doing nothing is more expensive in the end, because floods, failed harvests, dried-up streams and disease cost the district far more than prevention would have cost. The district can also obtain support from national green programmes and from organisations that fund such work. | Climate Change and Green Economy Initiatives in Ghana and Beyond | Evaluate |

## MARKING SCHEME - SECTION B (60 marks)

*General rules: (1) Accept any other correct and relevant answer. (2) A factor must be clearly placed as natural or human where the question asks for one of them; a human activity given as a natural factor earns no mark. (3) In calculations, award the method mark for correct working even when the arithmetic that follows is wrong, and award the final mark only when the unit or the percentage sign is given. (4) Where a candidate gives more answers than are asked for, mark only the first ones up to the number required. (5) Do not deduct marks for spelling unless the meaning is changed.)*

### Question 1 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **The average weather condition of a place over a long period** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Weather changes from day to day; climate is the average over many years** (1 mark).
- (iii) **A lasting change in the average weather pattern of a place or of the earth** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (ii) both halves of the comparison are needed.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE of: **longer droughts or dry spells**; **heavy rain in a short time causing floods**; **rivers, streams and wells drying up**; **certain plants or animals disappearing from the area**; **crops failing or maturing at unusual times**; **stronger winds and more storms**; **hotter nights** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: The sign must be a lasting change, not a single day's weather.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- (i) Any TWO of: **volcanic eruptions**; **changes in the sun's energy**; **changes in ocean currents**; **changes in the earth's orbit or tilt**; **methane from natural wetlands**; **wildfires started by lightning** (1 mark each).
- (ii) A correct explanation, for example **volcanic ash blocks sunlight so less heat reaches the earth** (1 mark) **and the earth cools for a period** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: A human activity named in (i) earns no mark.*

### Question 2 (12 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) **Radiation (heat and light) from the sun reaching the earth** (1 mark).
- (ii) **Heat from the earth escaping through the layer into space** (1 mark).
- (iii) **Heat from the earth sent back to the surface by the layer** (1 mark).
- (iv) **The layer of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: In (iii) the idea of the heat returning to the earth is essential.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **carbon dioxide**, **methane**, **water vapour**, **nitrous oxide** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: Oxygen and nitrogen are not greenhouse gases and earn no mark.*

**(c)** [3 marks]

- (i) **All the heat radiated by the surface would escape into space** (1 mark); **none would be returned, so the earth would lose heat and be very much colder** (1 mark).
- (ii) **The temperature rises (the earth becomes warmer)** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept 'global warming' in (ii).*

**(d)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE activities each with the correct gas: **burning petrol or diesel - carbon dioxide** (1 mark); **deforestation, charcoal burning or bush burning - carbon dioxide** (1 mark); **cattle rearing, rotting waste in dumps or flooded rice fields - methane** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: No mark for an activity without the gas it adds.*

### Question 3 (10 marks)

**(a)** [4 marks]

- (i) **26.0 °C** (1 mark) and **28.0 °C** (1 mark).
- (ii) **28.0 - 26.0 = 2.0 °C** (1 mark).
- (iii) **2.0 ÷ 4 = 0.5 °C per ten years** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The unit °C is required for the final two marks.*

**(b)** [2 marks]

- Trend: **the mean temperature rises steadily from 1985 to 2025** (1 mark).
- Meaning: **the district is becoming warmer - its climate is changing** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: 'The line goes up' alone earns the first mark only.*

**(c)** [4 marks]

- Any FOUR of: **plant and protect trees**; **stop bush burning**; **use improved stoves, gas or solar energy instead of much firewood and charcoal**; **share transport, walk, cycle or use buses**; **switch off lights and use LED lamps**; **compost waste or use a biogas digester instead of burning it** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: The action must reduce greenhouse gases, not merely tidy the town.*

### Question 4 (10 marks)

**(a)** [2 marks]

- (i) **An economy that improves people's well-being while reducing harm to the environment** (1 mark).
- (ii) Any ONE of **solar panel installer**, **tree nursery worker**, **recycling collector**, **biogas technician**, **organic farmer**, **ecotourism guide** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Accept any job whose work protects the environment.*

**(b)** [4 marks]

- Solar panels: **clean electricity from sunlight, so less fuel is burnt and less carbon dioxide released** (1 mark).
- Biogas digester: **the methane from the waste is captured and burnt as fuel instead of escaping, and less firewood is needed** (1 mark).
- Trees: **they absorb carbon dioxide as they grow and store the carbon** (1 mark).
- Recycling plastics: **saves the energy and oil needed to make new plastic and keeps waste from being burnt** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Each mark needs the link to greenhouse gases or energy saved.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- **(60 ÷ 200) × 100** (1 mark) **= 30%** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The percentage sign is required for the second mark.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **units of electricity bought before and after**; **firewood, charcoal or gas used by the kitchen before and after**; **number and height of surviving trees after one or two years**; **mass of plastic collected and sold each term**; **quantity of waste still burnt or dumped** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: The evidence must be something that can be measured and compared.*

### Question 5 (10 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- (i) **M** (1 mark).
- (ii) **L** (1 mark).
- (iii) **40 000 ÷ 2 000 = 20 times** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: Only the letter of the country is needed in (i) and (ii).*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- **M produces more than half its electricity without burning fuel, so little carbon dioxide is released** (1 mark).
- **Its law against felling has kept forest loss lowest, so its trees go on absorbing carbon dioxide** (1 mark).
- **It acts on both the source of the gas and the removal of the gas, while L and N act on one side only** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The answer must use figures from the table.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **it still loses 40 000 hectares of forest a year, far more than one day's planting can replace**; **only 15% of its electricity is from renewable sources, so most of its power still releases greenhouse gases**; **no figures are given for how many seedlings survive, so the planting may achieve little** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A reason must be supported by the table or by sound reasoning.*

**(d)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO actions each with a benefit: **Green Ghana Day tree planting** - restores forest cover and absorbs carbon dioxide (1 mark); **action against illegal mining in forests and rivers** - protects trees and water (1 mark); **solar and LED street lighting** - less electricity used (1 mark); **improved cook stoves and gas for cooking** - less firewood and charcoal burnt (1 mark); **solar power plants feeding the grid** - clean electricity (1 mark). Maximum 2 marks.
  - *Marking note: No mark for an action without its benefit.*

### Question 6 (8 marks)

**(a)** [3 marks]

- Example - natural: **volcanic eruption** (accept changes in the sun, ocean currents, earth's orbit) (1 mark); human: **burning of fossil fuels** (accept deforestation, bush burning, cattle rearing) (1 mark).
- Control: **natural factors cannot be controlled by people, while human factors can be reduced or stopped** (1 mark).
  - *Marking note: The table must be copied; both columns of the second row are needed for the third mark.*

**(b)** [3 marks]

- Any THREE actions each with a benefit: **plant and protect trees** - absorbs carbon dioxide and gives shade and work (1 mark); **a by-law against bush burning and illegal mining** - saves forest, farms and rivers (1 mark); **buses or cycle paths** - less fuel burnt (1 mark); **solar street lights and panels on public buildings** - less electricity bought (1 mark); **a composting or biogas site for market waste** - less methane and new jobs (1 mark). Maximum 3 marks.
  - *Marking note: No mark for an action given without its benefit.*

**(c)** [2 marks]

- Any TWO of: **many actions cost little or nothing and even save money**; **green actions create jobs and income in the district**; **doing nothing costs more later through floods, failed harvests and disease**; **support is available from national programmes and funding organisations** (1 mark each).
  - *Marking note: A bare 'it is important' earns no mark; an argument is required.*

## CURRICULUM ASSESSMENT BLUEPRINT

**Strand:** 5: Humans and the Environment | **Sub-strand:** 4: Climate Change and Green Economy | **Class:** Basic 9 (JHS 3)

**Content Standard:** **B9/JHS3.5.4.1** - Demonstrate an understanding of the natural and human factors that influence climate change and a green economy. **B9/JHS3.5.4.2** - Evaluate the effectiveness of initiatives that address the issue of climate change and green economy in Ghana and the world at large.

> Source: NaCCA Science Common Core Programme Curriculum (B7/JHS1-B9/JHS3), 2021 edition, Strand 5: Humans and the Environment, Sub-Strand 4: Climate Change and Green Economy, Basic 9, page 120. Content standard B9/JHS3.5.4.1 carries indicator B9/JHS3.5.4.1.1, examine various natural and human factors that influence climate change and green economy in their localities, with the exemplars: identify the natural factors that influence climate change; describe ways of minimising human activities that influence climate change; and compare natural and human factors that influence climate change and green economy. Content standard B9/JHS3.5.4.2 carries indicator B9/JHS3.5.4.2.1, assess data on climate change and green economy actions and activities globally including Ghana and other countries, with the exemplars: research into climate change and green economy actions in Ghana; access climate change and green economy actions in other countries; compare and contrast climate change and green economy actions in Ghana and other countries; and identify and write the effective initiatives that address climate change and green economy issues in Ghana and other countries.

> Note: I1 (B9/JHS3.5.4.1.1) carries topics 19.1 to 19.4 and Questions 1, 2 and 3; I2 (B9/JHS3.5.4.2.1) carries topics 19.5 and 19.6 and Questions 4, 5 and 6. The figures and the data table allow candidates to assess data, as the second indicator requires, without access to the internet in the examination room. Schools that use the shorter coded form will find these standards written as B9.5.4.1 and B9.5.4.2.

### EXAMINER NOTES

- The sub-strand joins two ideas that candidates often separate: the science of climate change and the economics of a green economy. Every green action in this paper is tied back to a greenhouse gas, and answers that stop at 'it is good for the environment' do not earn the mark.
- Natural and human factors must be kept apart. Volcanic eruptions, changes in the sun's energy, ocean currents and the earth's orbit are natural; everything that people burn, fell or rear is human. Question 1(c) and Question 6(a) both test the distinction, and a human activity written as a natural factor earns nothing.
- In Question 2 the three arrows must be distinguished carefully: P comes in from the sun, Q escapes to space, and R is returned to the earth by the layer. The greenhouse effect itself is natural and necessary; it is the increase in the gases that is the problem, and this point is worth stressing in class.
- Graph reading in Question 3 is straightforward, but the unit is part of the answer. A rise written as '2' without °C loses the mark.
- Question 5 is the data-assessment question the second indicator calls for. Candidates must quote figures from the table; an answer about country M that mentions no number cannot earn full marks.
- Question 5(c) and Question 6(c) ask for judgement. Candidates should learn that a launch ceremony is not a result: the test of an initiative is what can be measured a year or two later - trees alive, units of electricity saved, hectares of forest still standing.
- Follow-up work: let the class keep a record of the electricity units, firewood and water used in the school for one term, then introduce two simple changes and measure again. Let them also plant a small woodlot and count the survivors after the dry season. These two records turn the whole sub-strand into evidence the pupils have gathered themselves.
